## The Conservation of Mass-Energy Derivation of General Relativity
This section turns the conservation laws of Section 2 and the premises of Section 3 into general relativity: the clock, the rulers and the mass of every frame of reference around a body, and the clock around any arrangement of bodies, at rest or in motion. It is done for mass only. Charge and the other kinds of potential energy enter through their mass equivalent. Section 5 gives Einstein's derivation, and Section 6 sets the two side by side.

The whole derivation is one idea: the curvature between two points is the integral of f dot dr. The method has three steps:

- Figure out the integral of f dot dr.
- Figure out how much energy is gained. Get the mass equivalent and divide it by the mass.
- The curvature between the two points will be the same as the ratio in (2) above.

Here f is the force of gravity on the falling body; everywhere else in this paper \(f\) is the clock rate. The steps are done with an integral, so the calculation is continuous: at every small step the pull acts on the body's mass as it is at that moment, including the mass of the energy it has already gained.

1. The f dot dr idea gives the clock.

A body of rest mass \(m_0\) falls freely past frames held at rest. A frame held at rest reads its energy as \(mc^2=\gamma m_0c^2\) (premise 2). Over a step \(d\boldsymbol\ell\) on that frame's ruler the pull \(\mathbf g\) does work on the body's mass as it is at that moment. These are steps 1 and 2:

\[
\frac{dm}{m}=\frac{\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{c^2},\qquad
\ln\frac{m_B}{m_A}=\int_A^B\frac{\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{c^2}.
\]

The count does not change (premise 1), so the gain is canceled where it occurs (premise 3). The clock rate of the held frame falls by the same ratio. This is step 3:

\[
\frac{f_A}{f_B}=\frac{m_B}{m_A}=\exp\!\left(\int_A^B\frac{\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{c^2}\right),\qquad \gamma f=e\ \ \text{constant}.
\]

An energy that the held frame reads as \(E\) counts as \(fE\) in A's units. So the held frame's unit of energy is \(f\) times A's, its clock runs at \(f\) of A's, and light that climbs from it to A is redshifted by

\[
1+z=\frac1f .
\]

Nothing in the three steps asks what makes the pull. They hold between any two points, for any pull.

2. A frame held at rest reads the body that makes the pull at \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/f\).

The held frame's unit of energy is \(f\) times A's. So the count that A reads as \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\) reads, in the held frame's unit,

\[
\mathcal M_{\mathrm{held}}=\frac{\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}}{f}.
\]

The held frame gets the same number when it weighs the body with its own instruments: its own pull, times the square of the radius of its own circle around the body, over \(G\).

3. A frame that needs no force keeps the clock, the rulers and the mass of the frame it left.

No force acts on a body that falls freely: an accelerometer that falls with it reads zero. So in its own frame no work is done on it (premise 4). The frames held at rest that it passes read its energy growing (statement 1), and the clock rate where it is cancels that gain, so in A's units it keeps its count:

\[
e=\gamma f=f(r_1)\ \ \text{for a release from rest at } r_1,\qquad e=1\ \ \text{for a release from rest far away, with A}.
\]

For a release far away its energy in A's units stays \(m_0c^2\), the same number that it reads for itself at rest. It keeps the same mass and the same unit.

4. From stationary observers to free fall: the f dot dr in the field equals the f dot dr needed to generate the motion in the frame of reference.

Treat bodies in motion with each other as bodies at rest in frames of motion that require the same net force as it would be to create the motion. A body that moves is at rest in its own frame. If a force makes it move, then in that frame it sits at rest with that same force on it. If no force is needed, it is a frame that needs no force. What tells the two kinds of frame apart is what an accelerometer at rest in the frame reads.

Take a frame held at rest and a frame that falls past it from rest far away. In the field, the three steps give the falling body's mass ratio from the integral of f dot dr along its fall:

\[
\ln\gamma=\int_\infty^{r}\frac{\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{c^2}=\ln\frac1f .
\]

In a frame of reference with no pull, a force that sets a body in motion does the same kind of work on the body's mass as it is at that moment, and special relativity gives the same ratio for the same integral:

\[
\frac{dm}{m}=\frac{\mathbf F\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{mc^2},\qquad \ln\gamma=\int\frac{\mathbf F\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{mc^2}.
\]

Equate the two. The frame that falls past the held frame is in exactly the motion that the same f dot dr would generate there:

\[
\gamma=\frac1f,\qquad v=c\,\sqrt{1-f^2}.
\]

The falling frame needs no force, so it keeps A's clock, rulers and mass (premise 4). The two frames are in motion with each other, and special relativity between them, at the place, changes the clock and the ruler along the motion. It leaves the sideways rulers alone. So the held frame has

\[
\text{its clock at } f \text{ of A's},\qquad \text{its ruler along the force at } f \text{ of A's},\qquad \text{its sideways rulers the same as A's}.
\]

A step \(dr\) along the force on A's ruler therefore reads, on the held frame's own ruler,

\[
d\ell=\frac{dr}{f}.
\]

The same holds the other way round. A frame in motion at \(\gamma\) relative to a frame that needs no force has the clock and the rulers of a frame held at rest where the clock rate is \(f=1/\gamma\).

5. Anything can be represented by a point mass. So can the mass equivalent of potential energy.

Draw a closed surface around anything: a star, a swarm of bodies in motion, a spring, a pair of charges. The complete count inside, every kind of energy once (Section 2), has a mass equivalent, and it sets the pull through every surface outside (premise 1):

\[
\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}=\frac{E_{\mathrm{enc}}}{c^2},\qquad \Phi_g=4\pi G\,\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}} .
\]

That is the pull of a point mass \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\). Whatever happens inside the surface, the point mass does not change, because the count does not change.

Potential energy \(U\) has the mass equivalent \(U/c^2\), and it is represented by a point mass in the same way. Two bodies with the counts \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) and the potential energy \(U_{12}\) between them are, from outside, the point mass

\[
\mathcal M=\frac{E_1+E_2+U_{12}}{c^2}.
\]

A shell of rest mass \(m_0\) held at the radius \(R\) is the point mass \(\mathcal M=m_0-Gm_0^2/(2c^2R)\): its rest mass, and the mass equivalent of its own binding (derived in the physicist's box). An event horizon at the shell needs twice the rest mass that one would count without the binding, \(m_0=c^2R/G\).

For a round arrangement the point mass gives the pull exactly at every place outside. Any other arrangement is divided into pieces, each inside its own closed surface, each a point mass. For the surfaces far away a coarse division is enough. For the pieces close by a finer one is needed.

6. One point mass: \(f^2=1-L/r\).

The count sets the pull through every sphere around the point mass (premise 1). The pull is counted in A's units, \(f\,g_{\mathrm{hold}}\), where \(g_{\mathrm{hold}}\) is the acceleration that holds a frame at rest:

\[
4\pi r^2\,f\,g_{\mathrm{hold}}=4\pi G\,\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}},\qquad f\,g_{\mathrm{hold}}=\frac{G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}}{r^2}.
\]

In the frame of the calculation the counted pull is Newton's law, exactly, at every strength. With \(g_{\mathrm{hold}}=c^2\,d\ln f/d\ell\) (premise 3) and the ruler of statement 4, \(d\ell=dr/f\), the integral of f dot dr is

\[
f\,g_{\mathrm{hold}}=\frac{c^2}{2}\,\frac{dF}{dr},\qquad F=f^2=1-\frac Lr,\qquad L=\frac{2G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}}{c^2}.
\]

The clock rate is set to 1 far away, where clocks agree with A's. Between any two places the square of the clock rate changes by twice the integral of the counted force over the path, per unit of the probe's rest energy \(\mu c^2\):

\[
F(r_2)-F(r_1)=\frac{2}{\mu c^2}\int_{r_1}^{r_2}\frac{G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\,\mu}{r^2}\,dr .
\]

The falling frame passes the held one at \(v=c\sqrt{1-f^2}=\sqrt{2G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/r}\), Newton's speed of fall, and on its own clock the falling body obeys Newton's law exactly:

\[
\frac{d^2r}{d\tau^2}=-\frac{G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}}{r^2}.
\]

In the held frames' terms and in the falling frames' terms the same clocks and rulers read

\[
ds^2=-F\,c^2dt^2+\frac{dr^2}{F}+r^2d\Omega^2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
ds^2=-c^2dT^2+(dr+v\,dT)^2+r^2d\Omega^2,\qquad dT=dt+\frac{v}{c^2F}\,dr .
\]

The first is what the frames held at rest read, and it is general relativity's solution outside a round body (Section 7). The second is what the frames that need no force read, by premise 4: they have flat space and A's time \(T\), and the frames held at rest move through them at the speed \(v\) (the physicist's box, "A frame that needs no force"). Outside \(L\) the two say the same thing. What holds at \(L\) and beyond it comes from premises 7 and 8, and not from carrying either formula there (Section 2).

A worked example: the fall. \(L=1000\). A body is released at rest at \(r=2000\) and falls. Energies are per \(m_0c^2\), in A's units. The mass ratio is \(\gamma=m/m_0\).

\(r\) | Clock rate \(f\) | Mass ratio \(\gamma\) | Energy gained \((\gamma-1)f\) | Drop in \(f\) | \(\gamma f\) | 

2000 | 0.70711 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0.70711 | 

1500 | 0.57735 | 1.22474 | 0.12976 | 0.12976 | 0.70711 | 

1100 | 0.30151 | 2.34521 | 0.40560 | 0.40560 | 0.70711 | 

1010 | 0.09950 | 7.10634 | 0.60760 | 0.60760 | 0.70711 | 

At every step the energy gained equals the drop in the clock rate: the curvature cancels the gain exactly. From 2000 to 1100 the integral in step 1, divided by \(c^2\), is 0.852374, and \(e^{0.852374}=2.34521\), the mass ratio and the clock ratio both. Holding the mass fixed instead would give \(1+0.852374=1.852374\), and the count would not close.

The reading and the count: a rocket. Consider a rocket burning fuel to leave Earth orbit on a deep-space mission where 99% of its starting weight is fuel. Forgetting to check remaining propellant as the craft exits Earth orbit—and assuming the rocket's mass stays the same—barely disturbs a tiny burn, but wrecks the fuel budget on a long mission where most of the starting weight is consumed. In the exact same way, a calculation that takes the energy a frame reads for a falling body, \(\gamma m_0c^2\), as the body's mass-energy has frozen one entry of the account: the clock rate \(f\) of the frame that made the reading. The account of Section 2 counts the body's entry as the reading times the clock rate, \(\gamma f\,m_0c^2\), and statements 1 and 3 show that this entry never changes along the fall: the potential energy released is the kinetic energy gained, and the curvature at the body nullifies the increase. Far from the black hole \(f\) is close to 1 and the reading and the count agree: the small burn. At the event horizon \(f\) is zero: the reading grows without bound while the count stays fixed, and the frozen reading does there what a frozen formula does outside its range: it blows up. The divergence of an energy at \(r=L\) is the reading mistaken for the count; the body's entry in the account does not diverge, and the account's total does not change. What does go to zero there is the far observer's clock factor \(f\), in the Schwarzschild solution and here alike.

For a mission the same mistake costs the factor \(1/f\). The energy that braking the body yields where the clock rate is \(f\), and that lifting it back then costs, is \((e-f)\,m_0c^2\) in A's units, finite everywhere. A plan that takes the local stopping energy \((\gamma-1)\,m_0c^2\) for it is wrong by the factor \(1/f\): 31.6 at \(r=1001\) for a body released from rest at 1100, and without bound at \(L\) (the teacher's box).

7. The general case: any arrangement of point masses. The squared-clock deficits add exactly.

Take point masses \(\mathcal M_a\) at the places \(\mathbf x_a\), at rest in the frame of the calculation. Each \(\mathcal M_a\) is the count that the pull through a closed surface around that piece alone shows, in that frame's units. The counts of the pieces add up to the complete count of the whole, with the potential energy of every pair counted once. The count sets the pull through every closed surface (premise 1). The calculation is done in one frame, with that frame's ruler, scale and clock. At every place the frame held at rest has its ruler along the force at \(f\) (premise 5), and the pull is counted through the areas across the force as that one frame's grid measures them. For one point mass statement 4 derives that those areas are unchanged; for several point masses this is carried over, and the premise table names it. The factor of the ruler along the force and the factor of the counted pull cancel, and what is left is Newton's law for every point mass, with the pulls adding:

\[
f\,\mathbf g_{\mathrm{hold}}=\frac{c^2}{2}\,\nabla F=\sum_a\frac{G\mathcal M_a\,(\mathbf x-\mathbf x_a)}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf x_a|^3}.
\]

The integral of f dot dr then gives the clock at every place:

\[
F(\mathbf x)=f^2=1-\sum_a\frac{L_a}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf x_a|},\qquad L_a=\frac{2G\mathcal M_a}{c^2}.
\]

This is superposition. The deficit \(1-f^2\) of each point mass adds to the deficits of the others, exactly, with the ruler, the scale and the clock of the frame in which the calculation is done.

A worked example: two point masses. \(L_1=1000\) at 0 and \(L_2=500\) at 10,000, on one line.

Place on the line | \(L_1/r_1\) | \(L_2/r_2\) | \(F=1-\) their sum | Clock rate \(f\) | 

4000 | 0.250000 | 0.083333 | 0.666667 | 0.816497 | 

5857.9 | 0.170711 | 0.120711 | 0.708579 | 0.841771 | 

8000 | 0.125000 | 0.250000 | 0.625000 | 0.790569 | 

At 5857.9 the two pulls cancel. A frame there needs no holding force, and its clock still runs at 0.841771 of A's.

The count of a pair. Two bodies of rest masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), each the count of its body when it is alone, are held at rest at the separation \(d\). From outside they are one point mass. A small body held near a large one enters the count at the large one's clock rate, \(f\,dm\); the count is the same when the two bodies are exchanged; and it is taken to be a power series in the two masses. These three give the count through the second order (the physicist's box):

\[
\mathcal M=m_1+m_2-\frac{Gm_1m_2}{c^2d}-\frac{G^2m_1m_2\,(m_1+m_2)}{2c^4d^2}-\dots
\]

The potential energy of the pair is in it once. The sum of the two rest masses, each at the clock rate that the other makes, would hold it twice.

8. The motion: bodies in motion with each other.

A body in motion is at rest in its own frame (statement 4). In the frame of the calculation its count holds the energy of its motion: the frame it passes reads \(\gamma m_0c^2\), and in A's units that is \(e\,m_0c^2\) with \(e=\gamma f\). So a body that moves through the pull of bodies at rest in the frame of the calculation is the point mass

\[
\mathcal M_a=e_a\,m_a .
\]

While it falls freely it keeps \(e_a\) (premise 3). The gain of its motion is canceled by the clock rate where it is, so its point mass does not change while it falls.

When two bodies move freely in each other's pull, both move, and the clock rate where each one is changes also because the other has moved. Then each \(e_a\) changes, and each \(m_ae_a\) holds the potential energy of the pair. What stays constant is the complete count of the pair, with that energy counted once. This holds for any free motion of the two, a fall toward each other and an orbit alike. To the first order in the two small numbers below, where it is Newton's conservation of energy read as a count of mass, in the frame where the centre of the pair is at rest (what is left out is of the second order in the two small numbers of the problem, the potential over the speed of light squared and the speeds squared over the speed of light squared):

\[
m_1e_1+m_2e_2+\frac{Gm_1m_2}{c^2d}=\text{constant}.
\]

The rulers are updated instantaneously (premise 6). At every moment \(T\), the time that the frames with no force share, the pull through every closed surface is set by the count inside it at that moment, and the pull on each body points to where the other bodies are at that moment:

\[
\Phi_g(T)=4\pi G\,\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}(T),\qquad \frac{d\mathbf P}{dT}=\sum_i\mathbf F_i(T)=0 .
\]

The pulls on two bodies are then equal and opposite at every moment, so the total momentum never changes. And the general case holds at every moment, with each body's place and count at that moment and the ruler along the force of that moment (premise 5):

\[
F(\mathbf x,T)=1-\sum_a\frac{L_a(T)}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf x_a(T)|} .
\]

With nothing crossing a closed surface around all the bodies, the count inside is constant. Through every surface outside, the pull of the whole is that of one point mass at every moment, whatever the bodies inside do.

9. The result obeys the conservation laws.

Conservation test | Result | 

A free body's count along its fall through the pull of bodies at rest | constant, exactly | 

The pull through closed surfaces, counted in A's units | the same through every surface that holds the same count, and zero through the surface of an empty volume, exactly | 

The count of a closed system when a shell is built up piece by piece | closes exactly | 

The mass a held frame reads, by count and by weighing | the same, \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/f\) | 

The total momentum of bodies in motion, with the pulls on two bodies equal and opposite at every moment (premise 6) | constant, exactly | 

The complete count of two bodies in free motion in each other's pull, a fall or an orbit | constant, to the first order (Newton's conservation of energy, read as a count of mass) | 

10. Where this derivation and Einstein's part.

For one point mass at rest, outside its event horizon, the clocks and the rulers above are the ones Einstein's derivation gives. What Einstein assumes there and this section derives is listed line by line in Section 6. The two part in three places.

For several point masses at different places the squared-clock deficits add exactly here, in the grid of the frame of the calculation (statement 7 and the premise table). In Einstein's equations they do not: for bodies at rest on one line and held apart his clock rates multiply (Weyl's solutions, with each body's rate taken in his coordinates). For the same two deficits the two give the same clocks to first order, and they part at the second, by the product of the two deficits. A measurement of clock rates between two bodies can tell them apart, once the place between them is named by measurements (Section 10, Part 16; Section 17).

When the count moves, premise 6 holds: the rulers are updated instantaneously, and the sum of statement 8 holds at every moment. In Einstein's derivation a change moves at the speed of light.

At \(L\) and beyond it, premises 7 and 8 hold: what two frames read is real for each from its own frame of reference, an inferred measurement across \(L\) has two solutions, and objects move beyond their event horizon. General relativity's step there is to take one metric for all observers and to continue the same solution, with the same mass, across \(L\) (Section 9). Nothing outside \(L\) requires that step. It is the error that this paper names (Section 18), and it is not used.

## For a child
A ball falls toward a heavy body and speeds up. Its extra energy has mass, so the ball gets a little heavier. But the box around everything is sealed, so the total inside can't change, and neither can the pull of the box. Something has to make up for the ball's extra mass, exactly. It is the clock where the ball is: it runs slower, by exactly the share the ball got heavier. Do that one small step at a time, all the way down, and you get how fast every clock runs at every place around the body.

Now picture two people at the same place near the body. One is held there, standing on a platform. The other is falling past. Nobody holds the one who falls, so that one keeps the clock and the ruler they started with. How fast is the faller going? Exactly as fast as if someone had pushed them, in empty space, with the same push over the same distance that the pull gave them on the way down. So the two are simply moving past each other, and for two people who move past each other we already know the rule: the clock changes, and the ruler along the motion changes, and the rulers across it stay the same. That gives the held person's clock and rulers.

Last, picture a bag with anything in it: stones, springs wound up tight, things flying around. From outside the bag you cannot tell what is in it. You can only tell the total, and the total pulls on you like one small heavy point. Wound-up springs count too: their stored energy is part of the total. Many bags are many points, and their effects on your clock simply add. If the bags move, you use where each one is right now.

Imagine a rocket where 99 out of 100 pounds at launch is fuel, and someone forgets to check how much fuel is left after leaving Earth orbit because they pretend the rocket's weight never changes. On a tiny trip, pretending the weight stays the same barely shows up, but on a long trip where almost all the weight is fuel, that guess gets the fuel needed completely wrong. Reading the stone's speed-energy as if nothing else had changed is the same mistake in the black hole calculation. Far away it barely shows up. Near the edge, the speed-reading blows up, but the clock there has slowed by exactly as much, and when you write both down, as the jar rule of Section 2 says to, the total never changes. The blow-up is in the reading, not in what is there. Count everything, and the rocket comes out right, and so does the black hole.

## For a high school physics teacher
The three steps, for a body moving a small step \(d\boldsymbol\ell\) along the pull:

- Step 1, the work. The pull does work \(dW=\mathbf F\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=m\,\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell\) on the body, where \(m\) is its mass at that moment.
- Step 2, the mass of the energy gained, over the mass. The work becomes the body's energy, so its mass grows by \(dm=dW/c^2\). Dividing by the mass, \(dm/m=\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/c^2\). Adding up the small steps, \(\ln(m_B/m_A)=\int_A^B\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/c^2\).
- Step 3, the curvature. The clock rate of a frame held at rest falls by the same ratio: \(f_A/f_B=m_B/m_A\). So \(mf\), the body's energy as A counts it, never changes.

Far from the mass, \(\mathbf g\) is Newton's pull, and the clock rate is \(f\approx1-G\mathcal M/(c^2r)\): the familiar gravitational redshift.

From stationary observers to free fall. The same work, done by a force on a body in empty space, gives the same mass ratio: \(\ln\gamma=\int\mathbf F\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/(mc^2)\) is the work-energy theorem of special relativity. So the frame that falls from rest far away passes the held frame at \(\gamma=1/f\). The falling frame needs no force and keeps A's clock and rulers. Special relativity then gives the held frame's: its clock at \(1/\gamma=f\) of A's, its ruler along the force at \(f\) of A's, and its sideways rulers unchanged.

Anything is a point mass. Gauss's law for the pull: outside a closed surface only the total inside counts, \(\mathcal M=E/c^2\), with every kind of energy in \(E\). Potential energy counts with its mass equivalent \(U/c^2\), which is negative for a bound pair.

One point mass. In A's units the counted pull is Newton's, \(G\mathcal M/r^2\), and with the ruler \(d\ell=dr/f\) the three steps give \(f^2=1-2G\mathcal M/(c^2r)\). A held frame reads the body at \(\mathcal M/f\), heavier than A does: at twice \(L\) it reads 1.414 times A's value.

The reading, the count, and a rocket. A mission calculation that takes one frame's reading for the count, as the rocket's frozen-mass formula takes the starting mass \(M_0\) for the mass along the flight, breaks down whenever what it ignores changes substantially. A rocket of starting mass \(M_0\) and exhaust speed \(v_e\): the frozen-mass formula keeps the mass at \(M_0\) throughout, so the speed gained is \(\Delta v=v_e\,\Delta M/M_0\). The account counts the exhaust as it leaves: conservation of momentum on the closed system, rocket plus exhaust, gives \(M\,dv=-v_e\,dM\), which integrates to the rocket equation \(\Delta v=v_e\ln(M_0/M_f)\):

Fuel burned, fraction of \(M_0\) | Frozen mass: \(\Delta v/v_e=\Delta M/M_0\) | Mass free to change: \(\Delta v/v_e=\ln(M_0/M_f)\) | Frozen formula's error | 

1% | 0.0100 | 0.0101 | 0.5% low | 

10% | 0.1000 | 0.1054 | 5.1% low | 

50% | 0.5000 | 0.6931 | 27.9% low | 

99% | 0.9900 | 4.6052 | a factor 4.65 low | 

The frozen formula is right to half a percent on the small burn and wrong by a factor of 4.65 on the 99% mission. Its error is set by one thing: how much of the baseline changes.

The same mistake at the black hole, and the account that fixes it: the frozen calculation reads \(\gamma=1+(\text{kinetic energy})/m_0c^2\) and takes \(\gamma m_0c^2\) for the body's mass-energy. The account multiplies the reading by the clock rate of the frame that made it: the body's entry in the count is \(\gamma f\,m_0c^2\), and it never changes (statements 1 and 3). For a body released from rest at \(r=1{,}100\), with \(L=1{,}000\):

Place \(r\) | Clock rate \(f\) | Frozen reading \(\gamma\) | The body's entry \(\gamma f\) (\(\times m_0c^2\)) | Schwarzschild \(e\) | Reading's growth \(\gamma-1\) | Braking yield = lift cost, far units, \(e-f\) | Frozen plan's factor \(1/f\) | 

1,100 | 0.3015 | 1.000 | 0.3015 | 0.3015 | 0.00 | 0.0000 | 3.3 | 

1,050 | 0.2182 | 1.382 | 0.3015 | 0.3015 | 0.38 | 0.0833 | 4.6 | 

1,020 | 0.1400 | 2.153 | 0.3015 | 0.3015 | 1.15 | 0.1615 | 7.1 | 

1,005 | 0.0705 | 4.275 | 0.3015 | 0.3015 | 3.27 | 0.2310 | 14.2 | 

1,001 | 0.0316 | 9.539 | 0.3015 | 0.3015 | 8.54 | 0.2699 | 31.6 | 

\(\to L\) | \(\to0\) | \(\to\infty\) | 0.3015 | 0.3015 | \(\to\infty\) | 0.3015 | \(\to\infty\) | 

Far away, for a release from rest at 100,000, the reading has grown by 2% at \(r=20{,}000\) while the entry has not moved, the small burn:

Place \(r\) (released from rest at 100,000) | Clock rate \(f\) | Frozen reading \(\gamma\) | The body's entry \(\gamma f\) | Reading's growth \(\gamma-1\) | 

100,000 | 0.99499 | 1.00000 | 0.99499 | 0.00000 | 

50,000 | 0.98995 | 1.00509 | 0.99499 | 0.00509 | 

20,000 | 0.97468 | 1.02084 | 0.99499 | 0.02084 | 

At \(r=1{,}001\) the reading has grown by a factor 9.5 while the entry has not moved; at \(r=L\) the reading is unbounded and the count is still \(0.3015\,m_0c^2\). Every number in the entry column is Schwarzschild's \(e\): the account and the Schwarzschild calculation agree outside the horizon, to every figure.

Mission consequence: the energy, in far units, that braking the body at \(r\) yields, and that lifting it back to 1,100 then costs, is \((e-f(r))\,m_0c^2\), finite everywhere and \(0.270\,m_0c^2\) at \(r=1{,}001\); a plan that takes the local reading \((\gamma-1)\,m_0c^2\) for that energy is wrong by the factor \(1/f(r)\), 31.6 at 1,001 and unbounded at the horizon. For a spacecraft mission such as a NASA flight plan, assuming a frozen mass baseline miscalculates impulse, energy, and propellant margin rather than tracking real mass change.

Many point masses. The counted pulls add as in Newton's theory, so \(f^2=1-\sum_a2G\mathcal M_a/(c^2r_a)\). Where two pulls cancel, the clock still runs slow by both deficits.

Bodies in motion. A moving body's count includes its energy of motion. At every moment the same sum holds with the bodies' places at that moment, and the pull on each points to where the others are then, which is what keeps the total momentum constant.

## For a theoretical physicist

### What this derivation uses
# | What is used | Where | 

1 | The conservation of mass-energy and of momentum (Section 2) | The count; the three steps; the motion; the tests | 

2 | Premise 1: the pull through a closed surface is set by the complete count inside, at every strength of the pull. The pull is counted in A's units, \(f\,g_{\mathrm{hold}}\): the work of holding a probe, per unit of its rest mass and per unit of the held frame's length, converted to A's units | The point mass; one point mass; the general case | 

3 | Premise 2, with special relativity at one place: a frame reads a moving body's energy as \(\gamma m_0c^2\); the work of a force on a moving body; between two frames in motion the clock and the ruler along the motion change; light moves at \(c\) on each frame's own clock and ruler | Steps 1 and 2; statement 4 | 

4 | Premise 3: the gain is canceled at the body, \(\gamma f=e\); \(d\ln f=g\,d\ell/c^2\) | The clock; bodies in motion | 

5 | Premise 4: a frame that needs no force keeps the same clocks, rulers and mass | The frames that fall; statement 4 | 

6 | Premise 5: where a force is required, clocks, rulers and mass follow from the work of the force; the ruler along the force is at \(f\) | The clock; the unit of energy; the mass a held frame reads; the general case | 

7 | Premise 6: the rulers are updated instantaneously | The motion | 

8 | Planck's relation with one constant in every frame | The clock from the unit of energy | 

9 | Newton's law far from the mass | \(G\); the far normalization | 

Nothing else is used. In particular: no equation of Einstein's, no one geometry shared by all observers, no general covariance, no condition that the equations be of second order, and no assumption that the arrangement is the same at every time.

### Steps 1 and 2: the work, and the mass of the energy gained
A body of rest mass \(m_0\) passes a frame held at rest, which reads its energy as \(E=\gamma m_0c^2=mc^2\). Over a step \(d\boldsymbol\ell\) on that frame's ruler the pull does work \(dW=m\,\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell\). The pull acts on the current mass, gained energy included. With \(dm=dW/c^2\),

\[
\frac{dm}{m}=\frac{\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{c^2},\qquad
\ln\frac{m_B}{m_A}=\int_A^B\frac{\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{c^2}.
\]

Done in 10 steps from 2000 to 1100 (with \(L=1000\)), the pull taken at the middle of each step, the mass ratio is 2.187647; in 1,000 steps 2.343624; in 100,000 steps 2.345192. The continuous calculation is the limit, 2.34521.

### Step 3: the curvature between two points
By the curvature between two points this paper means the ratio of the clock rates at the two points: the ratio of a falling body's masses there, which the integral of f dot dr between them fixes. The curvature at one point is the second derivative of the clock rate along the local ruler (Section 12), and integrating it twice from one point to the other gives the same ratio (Section 12, statement 3).

The pull of the closed system does not change, so the body's gain is canceled where it occurs. The clock rate of the held frame falls by the same ratio:

\[
\frac{f_A}{f_B}=\frac{m_B}{m_A},\qquad d\ln f=\frac{\mathbf g_{\mathrm{hold}}\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{c^2},\qquad \gamma f=e\ \text{constant}.
\]

Here \(\mathbf g_{\mathrm{hold}}=-\mathbf g\) is the acceleration that holds a frame at rest. Released potential energy and gained energy cancel exactly. Counted in A's units, the body's energy \(e\,m_0c^2\) never changes.

### The unit of energy, the clock and the redshift
The unit of energy. An energy that the held frame reads as \(E\) counts as \(fE\) in A's units. So the held frame's unit of energy is \(f\) times A's.

The clock. A clock counts the ticks of a transition, and the energy of the transition's light is Planck's constant times its frequency. Take the same transition in the held frame and with A. The held frame reads for its own transition the same energy that A reads for A's. Converted to A's units it is \(f\) times that. With the same Planck's constant its frequency in A's terms is \(f\) times A's. So the held frame's clock runs at \(f\) of A's.

The light that climbs. In an arrangement at rest every crest takes the same time to climb from the held frame to A. So A receives the crests at the rate at which they were sent, counted in A's time: \(1+z=1/f\).

### The mass a held frame reads
The count converted to the held frame's unit is \(\mathcal M/f\). The direct weighing, with the same value of \(G\) as A and the rulers of statement 4, gives the same:

Held at | Clock rate \(f\) | Weighed on its own instruments | The count in its own unit, \(\mathcal M/f\) | 

1.5 L | 0.577350 | 1.732051 ℳ | 1.732051 ℳ | 

2 L | 0.707107 | 1.414214 ℳ | 1.414214 ℳ | 

5 L | 0.894427 | 1.118034 ℳ | 1.118034 ℳ | 

50 L | 0.989949 | 1.010153 ℳ | 1.010153 ℳ | 

The weighing is the count rule read the other way: the one power of \(f\) in the pull that A counts, \(f\,g_{\mathrm{hold}}\), and the one power of \(f\) in the unit of energy are the same choice.

What follows for stars. The redshift of light leaving a star is \(1/f-1\) at its surface, with the far mass and the star's radius. The far mass goes into the formula; putting the held frame's heavier reading into it would count the conversion twice.

Star | Surface clock rate | Redshift | 

1.4 suns, radius 12 km | 0.809601 | 23.5% | 

2.08 suns, radius 12.4 km | 0.710363 | 40.8% | 

The figures use the measured product \(GM_\odot=1.32712440\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}\).

### From stationary observers to free fall, step by step

- In the field. A body falls from rest far away to the held frame at \(r\). The three steps give \(\ln(m/m_0)=\int\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/c^2=\ln(1/f)\).
- In a frame of reference with no pull. A force \(\mathbf F\) sets a body in motion. Its work goes into the body's energy, \(d(mc^2)=\mathbf F\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell\), so \(dm/m=\mathbf F\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/(mc^2)\) and \(m/m_0=\gamma\).
- Equate the two integrals. The falling frame passes the held frame with \(\gamma=1/f\). It is the motion that the same net force would create there.
- The falling frame needs no force and keeps A's clock, rulers and mass (premise 4).
- Special relativity between the two, at the place, changes the clock, and the ruler along the motion. It leaves the sideways rulers alone.
- So the held frame has its clock at \(1/\gamma=f\) of A's, its ruler along the force at \(f\) of A's, and its sideways rulers the same as A's.

The held clock, as the falling frame reads it with its own rule for "at the same time", runs at \(1/\gamma=f\): the same number as the three steps give, reached by another route.

### A frame that needs no force
Its mass and its unit of energy. A body that falls freely keeps \(\gamma f=e\). For a body that started at rest far away, with A, \(e=1\): its energy in A's units stays \(m_0c^2\), the same number it reads for itself at rest. A body released from rest at a held frame at \(r_1\) has \(e=f(r_1)\): it keeps that frame's unit.

Its clock. The frames that fall from rest far away share a time \(T\), which is A's time carried inward, \(dT=dt+v\,dr/(c^2F)\) with \(v=c\sqrt{L/r}\). Each of their clocks reads \(T\) exactly, \(d\tau=dT\). For a fall from 50 L to 1.5 L: \(\tfrac23\,(50^{3/2}-1.5^{3/2})=234.477515524\) L/c on its own clock and in the shared time.

Its rulers. With the held rulers of statement 4, the frames that fall freely from rest far away have rulers that are exactly A's, in every direction, and their space is flat everywhere outside:

Place | Falling frame's step along the fall, per unit of A's | Its sideways ruler, per unit of A's | Curvature of its space | 

1.5 L | 1.000000 | 1.000000 | 0 | 

2 L | 1.000000 | 1.000000 | 0 | 

5 L | 1.000000 | 1.000000 | 0 | 

50 L | 1.000000 | 1.000000 | 0 | 

A frame released from rest at any held frame. Let a family of frames fall from rest at \(r_1\), with \(e=f(r_1)\) and \(q=\sqrt{e^2-F}\). In that family's own terms the same clocks and rulers read

\[
ds^2=-c^2dT_e^2+\frac{(dr+c\,q\,dT_e)^2}{e^2}+r^2d\Omega^2,\qquad dT_e=e\,dt+\frac{q}{cF}\,dr .
\]

Each member's clock reads \(T_e\), which at a fixed place runs at \(e\) of A's far time. Its ruler along the fall is \(e\) of A's, and its sideways rulers are A's. The count of its rest energy stays \(e\,m_0c^2\). These are the clock rate, the ruler along the force, the sideways rulers and the unit of the held frame it left: 0.707107 all the way down for a release at 2 L, 0.894427 for a release at 5 L, 1 for a release far away. So premise 4 holds for every place of release.

No redshift inside one small falling laboratory. Between two clocks at rest in a small laboratory that falls freely, a distance \(d\) apart, the shift of the first order in \(d\) is zero. What is left is the tide, of the order \(L\,d^2/r^3\).

### Anything as a point mass
The pull through a closed surface is the same for every content with the same count (premise 1). For a round content it is the same at every place of every sphere around it, so the point mass is exact there. For a content that is not round, the pull at a given place is that of its pieces added (statement 7), not that of one point mass: two equal point masses \(\mathcal M\) at \(x=\pm a\) pull, at \(x=2a\) on their line, \(20/9\) as strongly as one point mass \(2\mathcal M\) at the centre, while the pull through every closed surface around both is the same. For bodies about one centre the counts add: \(L=\sum_jL_j\) outside all of them, with every interaction, motion and support entry counted once.

Potential energy. A probe of rest mass \(\mu\) held where the clock rate is \(f\) enters A's count at \(\mu f\): its gravitational potential energy is already in the count, as the clock rate. For any other kind of potential energy between two bodies, the pair's length is \(L=2G(E_1+E_2+U_{12})/c^4\), with the three entries counted apart. For a spinning body the count takes the mass equivalent of all the potential energy that could be converted into kinetic energy.

A shell built up piece by piece. Build a shell at the radius \(R\) piece by piece. When its count is \(\mathcal M'\), a further piece of rest mass \(dm\) held at rest at \(R\) enters A's count at \(f\,dm\), with \(f=\sqrt{1-2G\mathcal M'/c^2R}\) the clock rate there due to the matter already present. The count grows by exactly what is brought in (premise 1), \(d\mathcal M'=\sqrt{1-2G\mathcal M'/c^2R}\;dm\). Integrated from nothing to the rest mass \(m_0\), for \(m_0\) up to \(c^2R/G\), with \(L=2G\mathcal M/c^2\):

\[
\sqrt{1-\frac LR}=1-\frac{Gm_0}{c^2R},\qquad \mathcal M=m_0-\frac{Gm_0^2}{2c^2R}.
\]

The second term is Newton's energy of a shell in its own pull, \(-Gm_0^2/2R\). The work taken out while the pieces are lowered is an entry of the account of whatever received it (Section 2). With \(y=2Gm_0/c^2R\): \(L/R=1-(1-y/2)^2\) and \(\mathcal M/m_0=1-y/4\).

\(y=2Gm_0/c^2R\) | Clock rate at the shell, \(1-y/2\) | \(L/R\) | Count \(\mathcal M/m_0\) | 

0.5 | 0.7500 | 0.4375 | 0.8750 | 

1 | 0.5000 | 0.7500 | 0.7500 | 

1.5 | 0.2500 | 0.9375 | 0.6250 | 

2 | 0.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.5000 | 

The event horizon reaches the matter, \(L=R\), when \(y=2\), that is \(m_0=c^2R/G\): twice the \(c^2R/2G\) that the count needs, because at that point half the rest mass is canceled by its own binding. Pieces in motion at \(R\) enter at \(\gamma f\,dm\), and for a common \(\gamma\) the same integration gives \(\sqrt{1-L/R}=1-\gamma Gm_0/c^2R\). The place of the event horizon depends on the energy of what is inside, light included: energy \(E\), in A's units, that is sent in from outside adds \(2GE/c^4\) to \(L\).

The count of a pair. Two bodies of rest masses \(m_1\), \(m_2\) are held at rest at the separation \(d\). Rest mass means here the count of each body when it is alone, \(B(m,0)=m\). Write \(a=G/(c^2d)\) and \(s(m)=\sqrt{1-2am}\). Three things fix the count \(B(m_1,m_2)\) of the pair: it is the same when the two bodies are exchanged; a small body brought to a large one enters at the large one's clock rate, \(B(m,dm)=m+s(m)\,dm\) up to terms in \(dm^2\); and \(B\) is a power series in the two masses, with no other mass in it. Every term of the first degree in one of the masses is then fixed, and a free term has to be of the second degree in each. The first such term is of the order \(a^3\), with a number \(\lambda\) that the premises leave free:

\[
B=m_1+m_2-a\,m_1m_2-\tfrac12a^2m_1m_2(m_1+m_2)-\tfrac12a^3m_1m_2(m_1^2+m_2^2)+\lambda\,a^3m_1^2m_2^2+\dots
\]

The force between the two, in A's units, is the change of the count with the separation: \(c^2\,dB/dd=(c^2/d)\,[\,a\,m_1m_2+a^2m_1m_2(m_1+m_2)+\dots]\), Newton's force first. For \(m_1=500\), \(m_2=250\), \(d=10{,}000\) (with \(G=c=1\); each body alone has the length \(2m\), 1000 and 500): \(B=737.5\) to first order and \(737.03125\) to second. The lengths \(L_a\) of statement 7 are the counts in the arrangement, so for this pair they add up to \(2B=1474.06\), and not to 1500. The sum of the two rest masses, each at the clock rate that the other makes, is \(m_1s(m_2)+m_2s(m_1)=724.51\): to the leading order it holds the potential energy of the pair twice. Building the pair in order, the second body entering at the clock rate of the first, gives 737.17 or 737.34, according to which body is brought in: right to first order, and not the same in the two orders at the second.

The division into pieces. A division is a choice of closed surfaces. The count inside each is its point mass, and the counts of all pieces add up to the count of the whole. The count of the whole is what the pull through a closed surface around all of it shows (premise 1). Written in the rest masses of two bodies, the three things above give it through the second order, and the term \(-\tfrac12a^3m_1m_2(m_1^2+m_2^2)\) of the third. They do not fix how the potential energy of a pair is divided between its two bodies, nor the number \(\lambda\) and what follows it in the pair's count: that takes a law for the work of bringing two bodies of any size together, and a rule for where the potential energy is counted. Both have to be stated with the division.

### One point mass
With the pull counted in A's units and the rulers of statement 4,

\[
4\pi r^2\cdot\frac{c^2}{2}\,\frac{dF}{dr}=4\pi G\mathcal M
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r^2F'=L,\qquad F=1-\frac Lr .
\]

Integrating the flux law and the clock step inward from far away, with no formula for \(f\) assumed, reproduces \(\sqrt{1-L/r}\) to six figures at 2000, 1500, 1100 and 1010. The second line element of statement 6 follows from the first by putting \(dt=dT-v\,dr/(c^2F)\).

On the body's own clock, with \(e=\gamma f\) and \(d\ell=dr/f\), \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-F)=c^2(e^2-1)+2G\mathcal M/r\). Differentiating, \(d^2r/d\tau^2=-G\mathcal M/r^2\): Newton's law, exactly, with \(r\) the circumference of the circle over \(2\pi\).

### The reading, the count, and a rocket
The rocket from the account. Closed system: rocket plus exhaust, in the nonrelativistic rocket calculation. Conservation of momentum, with the exhaust counted as it leaves at the speed \(v_e\) relative to the rocket: \((M+dM)(v+dv)+(-dM)(v-v_e)=Mv\), so \(M\,dv=-v_e\,dM\) and \(v=v_e\ln(M_0/M)\). Conservation of energy: the chemical bond energy released is the kinetic energy of the rocket and of the exhaust plus heat, every entry on the list of Section 2; the account closes. The frozen formula uses \(M_0\) for \(M\) throughout, \(\Delta v=v_e\,\Delta M/M_0\). For \(\Delta M/M_0=0.01,0.10,0.50,0.99\) the frozen formula gives 0.0100, 0.100, 0.500, 0.990 and the account 0.0101, 0.105, 0.693, 4.605 (in units of \(v_e\)): accurate to 0.5% on the small burn, wrong by a factor 4.65 on the 99% mission. The error is set by the fraction of the baseline that changes. [DERIVED from conservation of momentum; OBSERVED on every launch]

The falling body from the account. The frame held at rest at \(r\) reads \(\gamma m_0c^2\); the count in the far observer's units is the reading times that frame's clock rate, \(\gamma f\,m_0c^2\), and \(d(\gamma f)=0\) along a free fall through the pull of a body at rest (statements 1 and 3). In Schwarzschild's form, with \(d\tau=f\,dt/\gamma\), \(e=(1-L/r)\,dt/d\tau=f^2\cdot\gamma/f=\gamma f\): the body's entry in the account is the conserved \(e\). The reading is \(\gamma=e/f\): it grows without bound as \(f\) goes to zero at \(r=L\), and only there; the body's entry does not. Mission numbers: the braking yield at \(r\), and the cost of the lift back to \(r_0\), is \((e-f(r))\,m_0c^2\) in far units, since the local stopping energy \((\gamma-1)m_0c^2\) is worth \(f\) times that to the far observer; a plan that uses \((\gamma-1)m_0c^2\) unconverted is off by the factor \(1/f\). [DERIVED]

### The general case: why the deficits add
Let \(\mathbf x\) be the flat grid of the frame of the calculation, and \(f(\mathbf x)\) the clock rate of the frame held at rest at \(\mathbf x\), as a share of that frame's clock. The held frame's ruler along the force is \(f\) of the calculation frame's (premise 5), and its rulers across the force are taken as unchanged: statement 4 derives that for one point mass, and for several it is carried over with the grid of the frame of the calculation (the premise table). Let \(n\) be the direction of the force. The holding acceleration is \(g_{\mathrm{hold}}=c^2\,\partial\ln f/\partial\ell\), and one unit of the held ruler along \(n\) is \(f\) units of the grid, so

\[
f\,g_{\mathrm{hold}}=c^2\,f\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}=\frac{c^2}{2}\,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_n},\qquad f\,\mathbf g_{\mathrm{hold}}=\frac{c^2}{2}\,\nabla F .
\]

The factor \(1/f\) of the ruler along the force has canceled against the factor \(f\) of the counted pull. A surface element counts only its part across the force, and that part is measured with the unchanged rulers. So the pull counted through any closed surface is, in the flat grid,

\[
\oint f\,\mathbf g_{\mathrm{hold}}\cdot d\mathbf A_h=\frac{c^2}{2}\oint\nabla F\cdot d\mathbf A=4\pi G\,\mathcal M_{\mathrm{inside}}
\]

by premise 1. In empty space \(\nabla^2F=0\). For point masses, with \(F\to1\) far away,

\[
\boxed{F(\mathbf x)=1-\sum_a\frac{L_a}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf x_a|}}
\]

The equation is linear in the counts, so the deficits add exactly. Both checkers agreed this result on 24 November 2026: with the paper's ruler, scale and clock updated to the frame of the calculation, the squared-clock deficits add exactly in that frame's grid, for the complete counted energy assigned to its places.

Of the three ways to put two clock rates together that Section 10, Part 16, lists (the shifts add; the rates multiply; the deficits \(1-f^2\) add), this is the third. For bodies about one centre only deficit addition gives the exact exterior of the whole.

### The motion
A body in motion as a point mass. The frame that a body passes reads its energy as \(\gamma m_0c^2\), and that frame's unit is \(f\) of A's. So in A's units the body counts as \(e\,m_0c^2\) with \(e=\gamma f\), the energy of its motion included. Along a free fall through the pull of bodies at rest in the frame of the calculation \(e\) is constant (premise 3): the point mass of that freely falling body does not change. A body set in motion by a force gains the work of that force, and the count of whatever supplied the work falls by the same amount (Section 2).

Two bodies that fall toward each other. Now the clock rate where each body is changes also because the other body moves: the same work step gives \(d\ln(\gamma f)/dT=\partial_T\ln f\), which is not zero. Release two bodies from rest at the separation \(d_0\), in the frame where their centre is at rest, and write \(S=m_1+m_2\), \(D=1/d-1/d_0\). To the first order, where the balance is Newton's conservation of energy read as a count of mass,

\[
v_{\mathrm{rel}}^2=2GSD,\qquad v_a=\frac{m_b}{S}\,v_{\mathrm{rel}},\qquad e_a=1+\frac{v_a^2}{2c^2}-\frac{Gm_b}{c^2d},\qquad \Delta e_1=\Delta e_2=-\frac{Gm_1m_2D}{Sc^2},
\]

and the complete count of the pair is

\[
m_1e_1+m_2e_2+\frac{Gm_1m_2}{c^2d}=\text{constant}.
\]

Each \(m_ae_a\) holds the potential energy of the pair, through the clock rate, so the sum holds it twice, and the last term puts one of the two back. For \(m_1=500\), \(m_2=250\) (with \(G=c=1\)), released far apart and now at \(d=10{,}000\): \(v_1^2=1/60\), \(v_2^2=1/15\), \(e_1=e_2=59/60\), and the count is \(737.5+12.5=750\), the sum of the two rest masses, as it was at the start.

The same holds for any free motion of the two, an orbit included. Whatever the two velocities are, the work step gives to this order

\[
\sum_am_a\,\frac{de_a}{dT}=\sum_am_a\,\partial_T\ln f_a=-\frac{Gm_1m_2}{c^2}\,\frac{d}{dT}\Big(\frac1d\Big).
\]

For the same two bodies on Newton's orbit between the separations 324,503 and 1,000,000, \(m_1e_1+m_2e_2\) changes by 0.2607 along the orbit and the complete count by 0.0005. On an orbit ten times as wide the first is ten times smaller and the second a hundred times: what is left out is of the second order.

At every moment. By premise 6 the pull on a body at the moment \(T\) is the pull toward where the other bodies are at that moment, with their counts of that moment. For two bodies the pulls are equal and opposite, \(\dot{\mathbf p}_1=-Q\,\mathbf n=-\dot{\mathbf p}_2\) with \(\mathbf n\) along the line that joins them, so the total momentum is constant, exactly, and so is the angular momentum of the pair about any point when each momentum is along its body's velocity: \(d\mathbf P/dT=\sum_i\mathbf F_i(T)=0\). Why the pull cannot point to where the other body was at an earlier time is the argument of premise 6 (Section 3). The time \(T\) is constructed above for the frames that fall toward one point mass. For two bodies that move it is not yet constructed in this section: two times of that kind differ across the separation \(d\) by about \(vd/c^2\), in which the other body moves by about \((v^2/c^2)\,d\). So the direction of the pull is carried here to the leading order, and the count to the first order does not depend on it. The size of the pull, \(Q\), is Newton's to the leading order. For two bodies at rest its next order follows from the count of the pair above. For bodies in motion its terms beyond Newton's, the relation between a body's momentum and its velocity in the frame of the calculation, and the energy of the pair there wait for the same two laws as the division into pieces. The clock at every place follows from the same integral of f dot dr, taken through the arrangement of that moment, with the ruler along the force of that moment (premise 5):

\[
F(\mathbf x,T)=1-\sum_a\frac{L_a(T)}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf x_a(T)|},\qquad \sum_a\mathcal M_a(T)=\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\ \ \text{constant}.
\]

The counts of the pieces, with the binding between them counted once, add up to the count of the whole, and that does not change.

A frame in motion. A frame that moves at \(\gamma\) past a frame that needs no force is a frame at rest that required the work of statement 4 to create its motion. Its clock is at \(1/\gamma\) of that frame's, its ruler along the motion at \(1/\gamma\), and its sideways rulers are the same.

### In Einstein's terms
For one point mass the clocks and rulers of statement 6 satisfy Einstein's equations in empty space, \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\) (Section 5, equations (29), (35) and (36)). In the terms of Section 5, part 11: a small cloud of free particles in empty space, with no motion between its particles at release, keeps its volume at first, at rest and in any motion. This was checked by brute force, with no formula for curvature in the check: seven free particles integrated along the straightest paths of these clocks and rulers (Einstein's assumption A6, on the comparison side; for motion across the pull this paper has not yet derived the paths, Section 6), the volume measured at equal times on their own clocks, for clouds at rest and clouds moving along and across the pull at \(0.3c\) and \(0.6c\). Every one keeps its volume at first, to \(3\times10^{-7}\) in units of \(c^2/L^2\).

For several point masses premise 1, written at a point in the grid of the frame of the calculation, is \(\nabla^2F=0\) in empty space. In Einstein's equations, for bodies at rest on one line and held apart, the logarithms of the clock rates add in Weyl's coordinates, so his clock rates multiply. Here the deficits add. The two give the same clocks to first order and part at the second, by the product of the two deficits.

The rulers between two bodies, and why the frame of the calculation has to be updated. The sum of statement 7 is worked out in one frame, the far observer's, and it gives the clock at every place. It does not by itself give the lengths, the areas and the light paths near a body that sits in the pull of others. Suppose the far observer's grid were kept for those too, at every place, with the ruler along the force shortened by the clock rate that all the bodies together make there. With those rulers the clock equation (35) of Section 5 would hold exactly, as \(\Delta_hf=0\), and equation (36) would not. On the line between two point masses the surface of equal clock rate has, in the flat grid, the two curvatures \(C/|B|\), with \(B=dF/dx\) and \(C=\sum_aL_a/r_a^3\); the sideways rulers are unchanged, so its own geometry is unchanged; and the ruler along the force at \(f\) multiplies its bending by \(f\). Gauss's relation between the two then gives, with \(A=\sum_aL_a/r_a=1-F\), the curvature of space in the plane across the line:

\[
K=(1-f^2)\Big(\frac CB\Big)^2=A\Big(\frac CB\Big)^2\qquad(B\ne0) .
\]

Einstein's equations (35) and (36) would require \(K=-f_{;nn}/f=C\) of the same clocks and rulers. Around one point mass both are \(L/r^3\). For the two point masses of statement 7:

Place on the line | \(K\) with one far grid, \(A(C/B)^2\) | What Einstein's equations would require of the same clocks and rulers, \(C\) | 

2000 | \(1.52\times10^{-7}\) | \(1.26\times10^{-7}\) | 

4000 | \(4.54\times10^{-8}\) | \(1.79\times10^{-8}\) | 

8000 | \(1.30\times10^{-7}\) | \(6.45\times10^{-8}\) | 

Where the two pulls cancel, at 5857.9, \(B=0\): the force has no direction there, premise 5 names no ruler to shorten, and \(K\) as written grows as \(A/4(x-x_*)^2\) on the way to that place \(x_*\), while the clock rate stays finite.

Read in that way, for lengths, areas and light paths, the one far grid is not this paper's rule. It keeps one frame's ruler, scale and clock for every place, which is the mistake of the static mass in another form. Near a body that sits in the pull of others, the ruler, the scale and the clock have to be updated to the frame in which the calculation is done. For the Sun in the Galaxy the difference is measured: with the far ruler of the Galaxy kept, light that grazes the Sun would bend by \(2.775''\), and with the units updated to the Sun's own surroundings it bends by \(1.7512''\), the observed value, whatever the Galaxy's deficit (both checkers agreed this on 24 November, with a rule for converting units that this paper has still to derive from its own premises). The table shows how large the same mistake would be between two bodies of comparable pull. Outside one point mass the ruler along the force and the ruler along the motion of the frames that fall from far away (statement 4) are one and the same; around two bodies, off the line that joins them, they can be two different directions. The rule for the rulers between two such bodies is the first item of "Not yet in this section". It bears on the sum of statement 7 as well: the sum counts the pull through areas across the force as the far grid measures them, and a rule that changed those areas between two bodies could change the sum with them; a rule that changes the rulers and keeps the sum is given there. For the Sun in the Galaxy, where the Galaxy's deficit is the same all around the Sun, the update leaves the clocks of the sum as they are.

With \(C_n=(1/f)\,\partial^2f/\partial\ell_n^2\) for the curvature of the clock rate along a direction and \(K_{ab}\) for the curvature of space in a plane, the curvatures around one point mass are, with a prime for the change per unit of distance on the local ruler, so that \(r'=f\):

\[
C_r=\frac{f''}{f}=-\frac{L}{r^3},\qquad C_\theta=C_\varphi=\frac{f'r'}{fr}=+\frac{L}{2r^3},
\qquad
K_{r\theta}=K_{r\varphi}=-\frac{r''}{r}=-\frac{L}{2r^3},\qquad K_{\theta\varphi}=\frac{1-r'^2}{r^2}=+\frac{L}{r^3}.
\]

Each is one or two derivatives of the clock rate. With \(L=1000\), at \(r=2000\), in units of 1 over length squared:

Curvature | Value | Formula | 

Clock rate, along the pull | \(-1.25\times10^{-7}\) | \(-L/r^3\) | 

Clock rate, across the pull (two directions) | \(+6.25\times10^{-8}\) each | \(+L/2r^3\) | 

Space, the two planes that hold the radius | \(-6.25\times10^{-8}\) each | \(-L/2r^3\) | 

Space, the plane of the sphere | \(+1.25\times10^{-7}\) | \(+L/r^3\) | 

The three curvatures of the clock rate add up to zero, and so do the three curvatures of space. The curvature of space is the curvature, from place to place, of the wave function's rate of oscillation (Section 10).

### Steps add, and frames chain
Frames chain. For three frames held at rest, \(f_{AC}=f_{AB}\,f_{BC}\), and the ratio between two frames does not depend on the path between them. If two paths gave different ratios, a mass lowered along one and raised along the other would come back with energy left over, while everything else is as it was. That is energy from nothing.

Steps add. Each small step \(d\boldsymbol\ell\) changes \(\ln f\) by \(-\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/c^2\): the clock rate falls along the pull.

### Does the result obey the conservation laws?
Conservation test | Result | Scope | 

A free body's count along its fall through the pull of bodies at rest | constant, exactly | premise 3, carried out | 

The pull through closed surfaces, counted in A's units | the same through every surface that holds the same count, and zero through the surface of an empty volume, exactly | the pull counted with the clock rate, \(f\,g_{\mathrm{hold}}\) | 

The count of a closed system when a shell is built up | closes exactly | the shell, above; the work taken out is an entry of the account of whatever received it | 

The mass a held frame reads, by count and by weighing | the same, \(\mathcal M/f\) | with the same \(G\); the one power of \(f\) in the counted pull and the one power of \(f\) in the unit of energy are one step, so this row shows that the step is carried through, not a separate test | 

The total momentum of bodies in motion | constant, exactly | the pulls on two bodies equal and opposite at every moment (premise 6) | 

The complete count of two bodies in free motion in each other's pull, a fall or an orbit | constant, to the first order (Newton's conservation of energy, read as a count of mass) | 737.5 + 12.5 = 750 in the worked case of "The motion"; on the orbit there, a change of 0.0005 against 0.2607 | 

### What is shown and what is not yet in this section
Shown, from what the first table lists:

- The three steps, done continuously, are the clock step: the curvature between two points equals the ratio of the falling body's masses.
- A frame that needs a force: clock \(f\), unit of energy \(f\), mass read \(\mathcal M/f\), ruler along the force \(f\), and near one point mass the sideways rulers unchanged.
- From stationary observers to free fall: the frame that falls is in the motion that the same f dot dr would generate, \(\gamma=1/f\), and it keeps the clock, the rulers and the mass of the frame it left.
- Anything inside a closed surface sets the pull through every closed surface around it as one point mass would, with the mass equivalent of its complete count, potential energy included. Outside a round content it is one point mass at every place; otherwise each of its pieces is one, and their pulls add (statement 7).
- The reading and the count: the energy that a frame held at rest reads for a falling body, \(\gamma m_0c^2\), grows without bound at \(L\), and the body's entry in the count, \(\gamma f\,m_0c^2\), does not change; a calculation that takes the reading for the count is wrong by the factor \(1/f\), as a rocket calculation that freezes the rocket's mass is wrong by the share of the mass that it burns.
- One point mass: \(F=1-L/r\); the counted pull is Newton's, exactly; the fall obeys Newton's law exactly on the body's own clock.
- Any arrangement of point masses: the squared-clock deficits add exactly in the frame of the calculation, for the counts of the pieces, with the pull counted through the areas of that frame's grid (derived for one point mass and for every round arrangement, carried over for other arrangements: the premise table).
- A shell built up piece by piece: \(\mathcal M=m_0-Gm_0^2/(2c^2R)\), exactly; an event horizon at the shell needs the rest mass \(c^2R/G\).
- The count of a pair of bodies at rest, to the second order and with one of the two terms of the third, with its potential energy counted once.
- Bodies in motion: the same sum at every moment, with the count of each body including the energy of its motion; the total momentum constant, exactly; the complete count of two bodies in free motion in each other's pull, a fall or an orbit, constant, to the first order, where it is Newton's conservation of energy read as a count of mass.
- The result passes the conservation tests of the table above.

Not yet in this section:

- The rule for the rulers between bodies: which frame of the calculation applies there. It sets the lengths across the pull, the areas and the light paths there. The sum of statement 7 counts the pull through areas across the force as the grid of the frame of the calculation measures them. Statement 4 derives that for one point mass, Section 17 for every round arrangement, and for other arrangements it is carried over, so a rule that changed those areas between two bodies could change the sum with them. Premise 5 shortens the ruler along the force, and where the pulls of two bodies cancel the force has no direction. A rule that changes the rulers and keeps the sum exists. The second reviewer built one on 26 November 2026: with \(b_i=\partial_iF\), \(S=\sum_aL_a/r_a^2\), \(w=|b|^2/S^2\) and \(A=F+(1-F)\,w\), the rulers \(h_{ij}=A\,\delta_{ij}+A(1-F)\,b_ib_j/(F\,S^2)\) are those of statement 6 for one point mass, are regular where the pulls cancel (there \(h_{ij}=F\,\delta_{ij}\)), and satisfy \(\sqrt{\det h}\,h^{ij}\partial_jf=\tfrac12\partial_iF\), so the pull counted through their own areas is the sum's. It is a candidate, not derived from the premises, and not the only such rule. It keeps the flux identity. In the far grid its length along the force is \(A\,|dx|/f\), and premise 5 gives \(|dx|/f\): for one point mass \(A=1\) and the two are the same; between bodies, identifying them needs a conversion of frames. The frame near a body that sits in the pull of others, such as the Sun in the Galaxy, was agreed on 24 November with a rule for converting units that this paper has still to derive from its own premises; there the update leaves the clocks of the sum as they are.
- How the potential energy of a pair is divided between its two bodies, and the number \(\lambda\) in the third order of a pair's count, with what follows it. Both take a law for the work of bringing two bodies of any size together.
- For bodies in motion: the construction of the time \(T\) for two bodies that move (above it is constructed for the frames that fall toward one point mass), the size of the pull beyond Newton's, and the relation between a body's momentum and its velocity in the frame of the calculation.
- The paths of light and of planets in these clocks and rulers, with the figures for the Sun.

What holds at \(L\) and beyond it is not a gap of this section. It is derived in Section 3, under premises 7 and 8, and Section 9 sets it against general relativity's step there.

### The premises of general relativity this touches
General relativity reaches the same clocks and rulers for one body at rest from one geometry shared by all observers, the equivalence principle, general covariance and the requirement that the equations be of second order (Section 5, part 1). Here they follow from the conservation laws and the premises of Section 3. Three of its premises are not used and are contradicted by what this section derives. The first is the class of equations that Einstein chose (A9 of Section 5): they are not linear, and for bodies at rest on one line and held apart they make the clock rates multiply where the deficits add here, in the grid of the frame of the calculation (against statement 7, with the premise table). The second is that his equations go on holding while the arrangement changes (A4, A9 and A10 of Section 5); from that, changes of clocks and rulers obey a wave equation and move at the speed of light (Section 5, part 13; against statement 8). The third is the step taken when his solution for one body is continued across \(L\): one metric for all observers, the same solution and the same mass on both sides. It is the step that merges the frames' different values into one event horizon, and it is the error that this paper names (against premises 7 and 8; Section 18). Section 6 sets the two derivations side by side, line by line.
