## Why the Contradiction Is Hard to Spot
The contradiction is easy to miss because outside the horizon the two agree exactly, standard textbook notation makes the reading of one frame look like the count, and no direct observation ever probes the inside of a horizon, where the mismatch turns into a sharp breakdown. When every familiar check passes far from the source, the step that carries the static form inside the horizon looks like routine algebra rather than a premise. The same three things hide the contradiction of Section 1: a count that nobody inside is left to keep.

### Context and Core Idea
A contradiction built into a formula rarely announces itself where the formula already works. Outside the horizon the Schwarzschild solution is exactly what conservation gives (Section 4), and normalizing by mc^2 looks like standard dimensionless unit scaling. Because the breakdown appears only inside an unvisited horizon, reached by a change of coordinates fourteen parts into the derivation (Section 7, parts 15 to 17)—and because textbook language treats e and γ as familiar labels—the underlying clash between a count and a quantity nobody reads stays out of sight.

## For a child
When a magic trick works every single time in the backyard, nobody thinks to check what happens inside a locked box nobody has opened. Out where gravity is gentle, the numbers line up with normal adding and subtracting, and writing things in neat shorthand makes the hidden rule easy to skip right over.

## For a high school physics teacher
The contradiction is easy to overlook for three practical reasons:

Agreement outside masks the premise: Outside the horizon the Schwarzschild solution and conservation give the same numbers to every figure (Section 4), and far from the mass, expanding mc^2e = mc^2(1 − L/r) dt/dτ to first order gives mc^2 + ½mv^2 − Gℳm/r, matching everyday energy conservation and tests like Pound–Rebka or GPS clocks.

Dimensionless units look like routine arithmetic: Dividing by mc^2 and treating e as a per-mass constant looks like routine unit normalization rather than taking one frame's reading for the count (Section 4).

No direct check inside: Inside the event horizon—where 1 − L/r flips sign—there are no direct measurements to force a second look at the step that carries the static form across (Section 7, parts 15 to 17).

## For a theoretical physicist
The clash between the Schwarzschild continuation inside the horizon and conservation of mass-energy remains obscured by how standard derivations are structured and checked:

Exterior fidelity: Outside the horizon the conservation derivation (Section 4) reproduces the Schwarzschild exterior exactly, and in the regime L/r ≪ 1, v/c ≪ 1 the first-order expansion of (1 − L/r) dt/dτ reproduces Newtonian energy conservation and passes every test, giving no reason to question the continuation inside.

Notation and specific-quantity conventions: Writing geodesic conservation in specific form (e = −p_t/m in geometric units) and normalizing local quantities by mc^2 embeds the reading of one frame inside standard algebraic conventions where it reads as the count.

Lack of empirical constraint inside: The sign inversion of g_(tt) and g_(rr) for r < L, the absence of any frame at rest there, and a conserved e that is a momentum, which no observer at rest exists to read as an energy (Section 9, statement 3), occur in a region where no direct measurement has yet been made, allowing the extrapolation of the static form across the horizon to go unchallenged in standard treatments.

14 / RESEARCH NOTES

## Can Objects Escape the Event Horizon with the Updated Schwarzschild/Conservation of Mass-Energy Solution?
Can anything get out past the event horizon? Yes. Objects can (and do) move beyond their event horizon (premise 8, Section 3). A body in free motion keeps its count \(e=\gamma f\) and has, on its own clock, the speed \(c\,e\) at \(L\), which is not zero; it gets there in a finite time of its own, by the same law in both directions. A body let go at rest inside \(L\) comes out through \(L\), and from \(L/2\) or deeper it goes away for good (Part 6). A body that falls in from outside turns back inside \(L\) and comes out again (Part 7). Light sent outward at \(L\) by a source on its way out reaches an observer far away with the count \(2eE\). What that observer cannot do is observe the passage: on its clock the passage has no finite time. And what one frame of reference works out about an event beyond its causal boundary, through intermediate frames of reference, has two solutions, and they are complex (premise 7). This section works these out on one thought experiment.

### Context and Core Idea
The updated solution says it in the count: the event horizon at a radius \(R\) is where the entries inside, each a reading times a clock rate, add up to \(c^4R/2G\) (Section 4, the physicist's box). Nothing that moves toward the edge loses its entry; what grows without bound at the edge is each frame's reading of it. Nothing in the account stops anything at the edge.

The thought experiment. Take \(L=1{,}000\), held fixed: while a photon of far-counted energy \(E\) is inside, \(L\) is larger by \(2GE/c^4\) (Part 1), which the factors below leave out. Here A is a frame held at rest inside \(L\), not the far observer that Section 3 calls A; every clock rate \(f\) below is a share of the far observer's clock. A at 200 and B at 900 are frames held at rest inside \(L\). C at 1,000 is the event horizon of every frame held at rest, A's included: there a frame at rest would need the speed of light to escape (premise 8). No frame is held at rest at C itself: a frame held at rest feels the pull \(G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/(r^2f)\) (Section 9, statement 2), which has no bound where \(f=0\). D at 1,100 is held at rest outside. Each frame reads with its own clock, ruler and scale, and its readings are real. A emits photon 1 with the energy \(E_0\) on its own scale. B reads it and emits photon 2, with the energy it read, toward C. A frame at \(C-\delta\), on B's side, reads photon 2; a frame at \(C+\delta\), on the other side of C, reads it too and emits photon 3, with the energy it read, to D. One rule converts every reading: premise 7's factor, the ratio of the two frames' clock rates, with the clock rate \(f^2=1-L/r\) that the conservation laws give (Section 4, statement 6). A reading \(E_Q\) made by a frame Q is, in the frame P,

\[
E_P=\frac{f_Q}{f_P}\,E_Q,\qquad \frac{f_Q^{\,2}}{f_P^{\,2}}=\frac{1-L/r_Q}{1-L/r_P}.
\]

On one side of C the ratio of the squares is positive and the factor is real. Across C it is negative, and the factor is \(\pm i\) times a real number.

### The Proof
Part 1. The horizon as a condition on the count. For the far observer the horizon is at \(L=2G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/c^2\), and \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}c^2\) is the sum of the entries inside. The horizon reaches a radius \(R\) when

\[
\sum\text{entries inside }R\ \ge\ \frac{c^4R}{2G}.
\]

For matter held at rest, in a shell built up at fixed \(R\), that takes the rest mass \(c^2R/G\), twice \(c^2R/2G\), half of it being cancelled by its own binding; motion lowers the rest mass needed, and a shell that falls with its count fixed reaches \(R=L\) (Section 4, the physicist's box). Light counts too: a photon sent in from outside with far-counted energy \(E\) adds \(2GE/c^4\) to \(L\). The place of the horizon depends on the energy of what is inside, the photon's included. [DERIVED from H1 to H3]

Part 2. Photon 1, A to B, on one side of C. For A at 200 and B at 900, \(f_A^{\,2}=1-1{,}000/200=-4\) and \(f_B^{\,2}=-1/9\): both are negative, and their ratio is positive. B's reading of photon 1 is

\[
E_B=\frac{f_A}{f_B}\,E_0=\sqrt{\frac{-4}{-1/9}}\;E_0=6\,E_0,
\]

a real number: A and B are on the same side of C, and neither is beyond the other's causal boundary. [DERIVED: premise 7's factor]

Part 3. Photons 2 and 3, across C through intermediate frames. B emits photon 2 with \(6E_0\). The frame at \(C-\delta\) is on B's side and reads it at

\[
E_{C^-}=\frac{f_B}{f_{C-\delta}}\,6E_0=2E_0\sqrt{\frac{L-\delta}{\delta}},
\]

a real number, \(19.900\,E_0\) at \(\delta=10\). The frame at \(C+\delta\) is on the other side of C. What A works out for its reading is

\[
E_{C^+}=\frac{f_{C-\delta}}{f_{C+\delta}}\,E_{C^-}=\pm\,2i\,E_0\sqrt{\frac{L+\delta}{\delta}}:
\]

two solutions, and they are complex (premise 7). The frame at \(C+\delta\) emits photon 3 with the energy it read, and what A works out for D's reading is

\[
E_D=\frac{f_{C+\delta}}{f_D}\,E_{C^+}=\pm\,2\sqrt{11}\,i\,E_0=\pm\,6.633\,i\,E_0,
\]

the same for every \(\delta\). The intermediate frames drop out. Each one's clock rate enters once above the line and once below it, so what A works out for D's reading is \(E_0f_A/f_D\) whatever the intermediate frames are and wherever they stand: neither the place of the boundary zone nor its width enters. The one factor that is complex is the one across C. D's own reading, made with D's own clock, ruler and scale, is real (premise 7). [DERIVED: premise 7's factor, leg by leg]

The twist: one photon. Carry the same photon through the three legs instead, given energy at each step: at each step it carries on the energy that the frame there reads, and no energy is added from outside. Each frame reads it with the same factor as in the relay, the ratio of the clock rates of the frame it comes from and of the frame that reads it, so every reading is the same: \(6E_0\) at B, \(2E_0\sqrt{(L-\delta)/\delta}\) at \(C-\delta\), and, worked out by A, \(\pm6.633\,i\,E_0\) at D. Three photons keep each step plain; one photon gives the same numbers. [DERIVED: premise 7's factor]

Part 4. Does the edge depend on the photon's energy? Through the factors, no. Every reading is \(E_0\) times a ratio of clock rates, and \(E_0\) does not enter the ratio: double \(E_0\) and every reading on every leg doubles, D's included, while the place where the factors vanish or grow without bound, C, stays where it is. Through the count, yes, and only there: while the photon is inside the surface its far-counted energy \(E\) is an entry, \(L\) is larger by \(2GE/c^4\), and when it has left, the entry leaves with it (Part 1). [DERIVED: premise 7's factor and H1]

Part 5. Matter, outward. A body in free motion keeps its count \(e=\gamma f\) (premise 3) and, on its own clock, obeys the law of premise 8, one law on both sides of \(L\) (Part 7):

\[
\Big(\frac{dr}{d\tau}\Big)^2=c^2\Big(e^2-\Big|1-\frac Lr\Big|\Big),\qquad\text{outside } L:\ \ c^2\Big(e^2-1+\frac Lr\Big).
\]

Its numbers below are on its own clock and in the radius of the circles, with \(e\) in the far observer's units. Moving outward at \(L\), it has the speed \(c\,e\) there, which is not zero. It got there in a finite time of its own (\(c\,\Delta\tau=744.3\) for \(e=0.5\) from its inner turn at 800, \(L/(1+e^2)\), deeper than which a body with this count never is), and it moves beyond \(L\). Outside, it climbs while \(e^2-1+L/r\gt0\): to \(r=L/(1-e^2)\) and back if \(e\lt1\), and away for good if \(e\ge1\). The speed it still needs at \(L\) to escape is \(c\,(1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\) for \(e\le1\), and none for \(e\gt1\): less than the \(c\) that a frame at rest there needs, so the causal boundary depends on the frame of reference. On the clock of an observer at rest far away the passage has no finite time:

\[
\Delta t=\int\frac{e\,dr}{c\,(1-L/r)\sqrt{e^2-|1-L/r|}}\ \longrightarrow\ \infty\quad\text{at }L .
\]

For \(e=0.5\), \(c\,\Delta t\) from \(L(1+\epsilon)\) to 1,100 is 2,608 for \(\epsilon=10^{-2}\), 7,243 for \(10^{-4}\) and 11,849 for \(10^{-6}\). Inside \(L\), what the far observer works out for the reading of a frame held at rest there is \(\gamma=e/f=\mp ie/\sqrt{L/r-1}\), two complex solutions, while that frame's own reading is real, \(e/\sqrt{L/r-1}\) (premises 3 and 7; Part 6). The same law holds in both directions (premise 8). [DERIVED in Section 3, premise 8; inside \(L\), from the reading of the frames held at rest with the ruler rule (Part 7)]

Part 6. Bodies inside, as the frames held at rest there read them. Each frame held at rest inside \(L\) reads a passing body with its own clock, ruler and scale, and its reading is real (premise 7). Between two such frames premise 7's factor is real, the factor of Part 2. A free body keeps \(\gamma f\) (premise 3, which holds between any two points, for any pull: Section 4, statement 1), so the readings of two such frames stand in the inverse ratio of their clock rates:

\[
\gamma(r)=\gamma_0\sqrt{\frac{L/r_0-1}{L/r-1}}\qquad(0\lt r,\ r_0\lt L).
\]

Released at rest at \(r_0\) (\(\gamma_0=1\)), the body would be read below its rest energy one step further in, which no speed allows (H2, \(\gamma\ge1\)). So a free body at rest inside \(L\) cannot fall inward: it can only move outward. Released at rest at 990, the frames it passes read it at 1.42 at 995, 3.18 at 999 and 10.05 at 999.9; at 985 it would be read at 0.81, which no speed allows. Thrown inward at \(\gamma_0\), it is read slower as it goes in and turns back where the reading is its rest energy, at \(L/r-1=\gamma_0^2(L/r_0-1)\): thrown inward at \(\gamma=2\) from 990, it turns at 961.2. The same factor reads light: photon 1 of Part 2 is read at B at six times A's energy, so a photon sent inward from B is read at A at \(1/6\) of B's: light going inward inside \(L\) is read redder, while outside a body falling inward is read bluer. The sign of the energy change in free fall flips at \(L\). [DERIVED: premises 3 and 7 and H2; no ruler is used]

What the far observer works out for such a body is complex. Its count converted with the clock rate that the far observer works out, \(\gamma f=\pm i\,\gamma\sqrt{L/r-1}\), is \(\pm i\) times a real number, the same at every place (premise 7), and so is its step along the radius as the far observer works it out from their rulers, \(f\,d\ell=\pm i\,dr\): \((f\,d\ell/d\tau)^2=c^2f^2(\gamma^2-1)=-(dr/d\tau)^2\) is below zero wherever the frames held at rest read \(\gamma\gt1\). The outward motion that they read, real on their own clocks and rulers, is in the far observer's working-out a motion in the complex dimension. [DERIVED: premises 3, 5 and 7, with the ruler rule]

Let go at rest inside \(L\), the body comes out: the pull there points outward (Part 10). Its motion on its own clock follows from what the frames held at rest read: with the reading above, \(\gamma=k_0/k\), where \(k=\sqrt{L/r-1}\) and \(k_0=k(r_0)\), special relativity at one place, \(\gamma^2=1+(d\ell/c\,d\tau)^2\), and the ruler rule \(d\ell=dr/k\) (Part 10),

\[
\Big(\frac{dr}{d\tau}\Big)^2=c^2\big(k_0^2-k^2\big)=c^2L\,\frac{r-r_0}{r\,r_0}.
\]

It reaches \(L\) in a finite time of its own, \(c\,\Delta\tau=529.1\) from A (200), 579.6 from B (900) and 198.3 from 990, at the speed \(c\,k_0\) on its own clock. There premise 8's law takes over: at \(L\) a body's speed on its own clock is \(c\,e\), so it leaves \(L\) with the count \(e=k_0=\sqrt{L/r_0-1}\), the real size of the clock rate where it was let go, the same real size that the ruler rule gives the ruler. From \(L/2\) or deeper, \(e\ge1\) and it goes away for good: let go at A, \(e=2\), and it arrives far away at \(0.866\,c\). Let go between \(L/2\) and \(L\), it climbs to \(L/(1-e^2)\) and falls back: from B, \(e=1/3\), to 1,125. An observer far away never observes the passage (premise 8): on its clock the body on its way out has been just outside \(L\) since the earliest times. [DERIVED: the reading of the frames held at rest (premises 3 and 7, H2), special relativity at one place, the ruler rule, and premise 8 at \(L\)]

Part 7. Matter, inward: it turns back and comes out, the turn as the far observer sees it, and why there are two solutions. A body falling in from outside keeps its count \(e=\gamma f\) outside \(L\). Inside, the frames held at rest read it with their own clocks and rulers at the real \(\gamma=e/\sqrt{L/r-1}\) (Part 6, with premise 8's one speed \(c\,e\) at \(L\)), and with the ruler rule and special relativity at one place its motion on its own clock is one law on both sides of \(L\):

\[
\Big(\frac{dr}{d\tau}\Big)^2=c^2\Big(e^2-\Big|1-\frac Lr\Big|\Big),\qquad \frac{dt}{d\tau}=\frac eF,\qquad F=1-\frac Lr .
\]

On its own clock it passes \(L\) at the speed \(c\,e\) and moves on inward, slowing, for inside \(L\) the pull points outward (Part 10). It comes to rest where \(|F|=e^2\), at \(L/(1+e^2)\), and goes back out: it passes \(L\) outward with the same count \(e\) and goes away for good if \(e\ge1\); if \(e\lt1\) it climbs to \(L/(1-e^2)\) and falls back, so on its own clock it goes on between \(L/(1+e^2)\) and \(L/(1-e^2)\), through \(L\) both ways. Nothing with \(e\gt0\) reaches the centre. That it cannot go deeper rests on no ruler: the frames held at rest read it at \(\gamma=q/\sqrt{L/r-1}\), with \(q\) its real count inside, and \(\gamma\ge1\) bars it from where \(\sqrt{L/r-1}\gt q\) (Part 6); the law above and the outward pull (Part 10) bring it there in a finite time of its own and turn it back. Its count inside is its count outside, \(q=e\), by premise 3 at the real size of the clock rate. A ruler sets only how fast it moves: with a real ruler \(d\ell=\lambda\,dr/\sqrt{L/r-1}\), \(\lambda\gt0\), the same speed \(c\,e\) on both sides of \(L\) would give \(q=\lambda e\) and the turn at \(L/(1+\lambda^2e^2)\); the ruler rule, \(\lambda=1\), agrees with premise 3, and the turn is at \(L/(1+e^2)\). For \(e=0.5\): \(c\,\Delta\tau=223.3\) from D to C, \(744.3\) from C to the turn at 800, and \(744.3\) back to C; it never reaches A. It is back at D after \(c\,\tau=1{,}935.3\) of its own time, and it goes from its inner turn to its outer turn at 1,333.3 and back in \(c\,\tau=4{,}434.3\). The law that would carry it on inward, premise 8's law outside carried inside \(L\) with a real \(e\), \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-1+L/r)\), is not what the frames held at rest read: with it they would read its count \(\gamma\sqrt{L/r-1}\) as \(\sqrt{e^2+2(L/r-1)}\), changing along the path, against premise 3. It is general relativity's law for the inside of its continued solution, which at the turn still has the body moving inward, with \((dr/d\tau)^2=2c^2e^2\). On the far observer's clock, time flips at the causal boundary: \(dt/d\tau\) is positive outside \(L\), has a pole at \(L\) and is negative inside. So on the way in the far observer's \(dr/dt\) is negative outside and positive inside: as the far observer's time runs on, the part of the path inside \(L\) runs back toward \(L\). That is the turn as the far observer sees it; on the way out the signs are the other way round. Each passage reaches \(L\) only as the far observer's time runs without bound, to \(+\infty\) on the way in and \(-\infty\) on the way out: the far observer cannot and does not observe either passage (premise 8). [DERIVED: the reading of the frames held at rest (premises 3 and 7, H2), special relativity at one place, the ruler rule, and premise 8 at \(L\), with premise 3 at the real size of the clock rate for its count across \(L\); the far clock as the far observer works it out, \(f\,dt=(e/f)\,d\tau\); general relativity's law on the comparison side]

The body also moves in the complex dimension. Inside \(L\) the clock rate of a frame held at rest, as the far observer works it out across its causal boundary, is \(f=\pm i\sqrt{L/r-1}\) (premise 7). So the body's steps, as the far observer works them out, are complex: its reading \(e/f\), its step on the clocks of the frames held at rest, \((e/f)\,d\tau\), and its step on their rulers, \(dr/f\), each \(\mp i\) times what those frames read with their own clocks and rulers. At B, on the way in for \(e=0.5\), where the frames held at rest read \(\gamma=3/2\), they are \(\mp3i/2\), \(\mp3i\,d\tau/2\) and \(\pm i\sqrt5\,c\,d\tau/2\). This is why an event past the causal boundary has two solutions: there the clock rate is the square root of a negative number, \(F\lt0\), which has two roots, \(+i\) and \(-i\) times a real number, and every quantity worked out through it comes in the same two forms. The two are complex conjugates. What depends only on \(F\), such as the speed \(dr/dt\), or on neither root, such as the ratio of the two steps (\(-\sqrt5\,c/3\) at B), is real and the same for both. [DERIVED: premises 3, 7 and 8; Section 4, statements 4 and 6]

The far observer's time itself moves into the complex dimension. Premise 8's integral for the far time of the passage has a pole at \(L\); continued around it by the rule of Part 10, with its logarithm on the half-turn and its finite parts matched at equal distances from \(L\) on the two sides, as for light, it gains \(\mp i\pi L/c\) inside \(L\), with the sign that goes with the root of the clock rate. With \(t=0\) at D and \(e=0.5\), on the way in: \(c\,t=2{,}608.1\) at 1,010; at 990, \(c\,t=2{,}628.1\mp3{,}141.6\,i\); at B, \(192.5\mp3{,}141.6\,i\), where \(f_B=\pm i/3\); at the turn, \(-1{,}164.2\mp3{,}141.6\,i\). On the way in the real part grows without bound toward \(L\) from both sides and runs backward inside: the turn as the far observer sees it. On the way out it runs on to \(-2{,}520.9\) at B and \(-4{,}956.5\) at 990, and falls without bound toward \(L\) from both sides. Carried on through the outward crossing, the far time gains the offset once more, \(\mp2\pi iL/c\) in all outside on the way back, unless the outward leg is given its own origin of real far time; either way neither passage has a finite far time. The match of the finite parts fixes only the far time's constant inside \(L\): no reading, rate or turn depends on it, and the far time between two points on one side comes out the same by direct integration (\(-2{,}435.6\) from 990 to B). [DERIVED: premise 8 and the joining rule of Part 10, with the finite parts matched at equal distances from \(L\)]

Part 8. Light, outward. Light sent outward at \(r\), read as \(E\) by its source, reaches an observer far away with the count (Section 3)

\[
f\,E\ \ \text{(source at rest)},\qquad \big(e-\sqrt{e^2-F}\,\big)E\ \ \text{(falling in)},\qquad \big(e+\sqrt{e^2-F}\,\big)E\ \ \text{(on its way out)},\qquad F=1-\frac Lr .
\]

At \(L\) the first two are zero and the third is \(2e\,E\): light sent at the event horizon by a source on its way out arrives far away with a real, finite count, \(E\) itself for \(e=0.5\). It also arrives at a finite time on the far observer's clock, while the passage of its source has none: light sent outward at \(L(1+\epsilon)\) by a source on its way out with \(e=0.5\) reaches 1,100 ahead of the source by 215.5, 235.6 and 235.8 (\(c\,\Delta t\)) for \(\epsilon=10^{-2}\), \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-6}\): the two far times that grow without bound cancel. [DERIVED in Section 3, premise 8, with the far times of Part 5 and Part 10]

Part 9. At the edge itself. No frame is held at rest at C (the thought experiment, above), and a factor to a frame there would be zero or without bound. As Section 1 puts it: "Rather than evaluating events at a causal boundary where no rest frame is held, physics beyond a frame's causal boundary can be calculated indirectly by stepping through intermediate frames of reference." Here they stand one on each side of C (Part 3), and the passage itself is calculated on the clock of what passes (Parts 5 and 7). [DERIVED: no frame is held at C, from \(f=0\) there; the method as Section 1 states it]

Part 10. Where the light turns. The light turns around at the event horizon. Previously, the light ended because we reached a singularity. After the singularity, the light returned. In numbers, on the ruler and clock of an observer at rest far away: a frame at rest at \(r\) has the clock rate \(f\) and, along the radius, the ruler \(d\ell=dr/f\) (Section 4, statements 4 and 6), and light moves at \(c\) on each frame's own clock and ruler (premise 2). So on the far observer's ruler and clock, light along the radius moves at

\[
\frac{dr}{dt}=\pm\,c\,f^2=\pm\,c\Big(1-\frac Lr\Big).
\]

Its speed falls to zero at \(L\), from both sides, and on that observer's clock the passage has no finite time (premise 8). Inside \(L\) the clock rate of a frame held at rest, as the far observer works it out across its causal boundary, has two solutions, \(f=\pm i\sqrt{L/r-1}\) (premise 7); the speed \(c\,f^2\) is real and the same for both, and its sign is the opposite of its sign outside. The light's speed on that ruler and clock changes sign at \(L\) and nowhere else. In units of \(c\), with the sign it has for light that moves outward outside \(L\): \(0.0909\) at 1,100, \(0.0099\) at 1,010, \(0.0010\) at 1,001, zero as the limit at 1,000, \(-0.0010\) at 999, \(-0.0101\) at 990 and \(-0.111\) at 900. Nothing ends at \(L\): a body that reaches it has the speed \(c\,e\) on its own clock, which is not zero, and gets there in a finite time of its own (Parts 5 and 7). We no longer have the singularity. [DERIVED: outside \(L\), from Section 4, statements 4 and 6, and premise 2 (special relativity at one place, an import named in Section 4), for light along the radius; inside \(L\), with premise 5's ruler and premise 7]

How the two sides join. On each side of \(L\) the time equation of the light leaves its own constant, and the pole at \(L\) does not fix them. This paper adopts one rule that joins the two sides (26 November 2026): the far observer's time and the clock rate are continued past \(L\) along the same half-turn about \(L\), above or below, with no further winding. The far time then gains exactly \(\pm i\pi L/c\) across \(L\), for light and for matter, and the two half-turns are premise 7's two roots: one gives \(f=+i\sqrt{L/r-1}\) inside, the other \(f=-i\sqrt{L/r-1}\). For light moving outward, with \(t=0\) at D and \(H(r)=r+L\ln|r/L-1|\):

\[
c\,t=H(r)-H(D)\quad(r\gt L),\qquad c\,t=H(r)-H(D)\pm i\pi L\quad(r\lt L).
\]

From A to D the far time is \(c\,\Delta t=900-1000\ln8\mp i\,1000\pi=-1{,}179.4\mp3{,}141.6\,i\). Scaled by A's clock rate, \(f_A=\pm2i\), it is \(6{,}283.2\mp2{,}358.9\,i\): two solutions, complex, with the same real part, \(2000\pi\), on both. [PREMISE: the joining rule, adopted on 26 November 2026; the rest DERIVED from it with premise 7 and Section 4, statement 6]

Why there are two solutions once the light reaches the causal boundary. Three steps, each in the mathematics above. First, the clock rate. The conservation laws fix its square, \(f^2=F=1-L/r\) (Section 4, statement 6). Outside \(L\) the square is positive and the clock rate is its positive root; at \(L\) it is zero; past \(L\) it is negative, so the clock rate that a frame works out across its causal boundary has two roots, \(+i\sqrt{L/r-1}\) and \(-i\sqrt{L/r-1}\), and the premises prefer neither (premise 7). Second, time flips. \(F\) changes sign at \(L\), so on the far observer's ruler and clock the light's speed \(c\,f^2\) changes sign there, and inside \(L\) the far time runs the other way along the light's path (the speeds above). Third, the complex dimension. The far time of the light, \(c\,dt=dr/F\), grows without bound toward \(L\) from both sides, and the pole there does not say how the two sides join: every way around it adds an odd multiple of \(i\pi L/c\) to the far time, never a real amount. The rule that joins them carries the far time and the clock rate past \(L\) together, along one half-turn about \(L\), above or below: the far time gains \(+i\pi L/c\) or \(-i\pi L/c\), and the clock rate takes the root that goes with that half-turn. So once the light has passed the causal boundary, every value worked out for it across the boundary, through the clock rate or the far time, comes in two forms, complex conjugates of each other, one for each half-turn: what A works out for D's reading of its photon, \(\pm6.633\,i\,E_0\) (Part 3); the photon's far time from A to D, \(-1{,}179.4\mp3{,}141.6\,i\); and that time scaled by A's clock rate, \(6{,}283.2\mp2{,}358.9\,i\). Where a value depends only on \(F\), such as the light's speed, or on the ratio of two clock rates on one side of \(L\), the two forms are one. The two solutions belong to what a frame works out across its causal boundary; each frame's own readings are real and single (premise 7), as A's own clock shows next. [DERIVED: the two roots from premise 7 and Section 4, statement 6; the sign change from Section 4, statements 4 and 6, and premise 2; the two half-turns and their pairing with the roots from the joining rule]

What is shown. The horizon is a condition on the count, and its place depends on the energy inside, light included (Part 1). Readings between frames on one side of C are real; what A works out for D's reading, beyond A's causal boundary and through intermediate frames, is \(\pm6.633\,i\,E_0\): two solutions, complex, whatever the intermediate frames (Parts 2 and 3). The edge does not depend on the photon's energy through the factors, only through the count (Part 4). Objects move beyond their event horizon: a body moving outward passes \(L\) at the speed \(c\,e\) on its own clock and climbs to \(L/(1-e^2)\), or goes away for good if \(e\ge1\), and light sent at \(L\) by a source on its way out reaches an observer far away with \(2eE\), at a finite time on that observer's clock (Parts 5 and 8). Read by the frames held at rest inside \(L\), a free body at rest there cannot fall inward, a body thrown inward turns back, and the energy change in free fall flips sign at \(L\); the outward motion they read is, in the far observer's working-out, a motion in the complex dimension, its step along the radius \(f\,d\ell=\pm i\,dr\) (Part 6). A body let go at rest inside \(L\) comes out: it reaches \(L\) in a finite time of its own and leaves with the count \(e=\sqrt{L/r_0-1}\), for good if it was let go at \(L/2\) or deeper (Part 6). A body falling in from outside passes \(L\) on its own clock, turns back at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and comes out again with its count \(e\): nothing with \(e\gt0\) reaches the centre; on the far observer's clock time flips at \(L\) and the inside part of its path runs back toward \(L\), and its values inside come in two complex conjugate forms, the two roots of the clock rate (Part 7). No frame is held at the edge, and an observer far away never observes the passage (Parts 5, 7 and 9). On the far observer's ruler and clock the light's speed changes sign at \(L\) and nowhere else, and nothing ends at \(L\); with the rule that joins the two sides, the far time gains \(\pm i\pi L/c\) across \(L\), one sign for each root of the clock rate (Parts 7 and 10). That is why there are two solutions once the light has passed the causal boundary: the clock rate's square is negative past \(L\), so it has two roots, and the far time is carried past \(L\) on one of two half-turns, each with its root (Part 10). On A's own clock the light sent outward from A never reaches C, A's causal boundary; on A's side A's clock runs opposite to the far time, and what the far observer works out for it is \(\mp i\) times A's own reading (Part 10). Frames held at rest inside \(L\) read the pull pointing outward (Parts 6 and 10). What this rests on: H1 to H3, premises 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 and 8, Section 4, the rule that joins the two sides of \(L\), and the rule for the scale of the ruler of a frame held at rest inside \(L\) (Part 10). The premises of general relativity this touches are the one-way surface shared by every frame and the fall of everything inside to the centre, which follow from the static form carried inside, with the direction of time that the continuation chooses there (Section 9, statement 3; Section 18). The two part at a calculated event: where the body here comes to rest, at \(L/(1+e^2)\), the continued solution has it still moving inward, with \((dr/d\tau)^2=2c^2e^2\) (Part 7). Nothing has tested them; the observation that decides is anything, light or matter, arriving outside from inside an event horizon.

## For a child
Can things get out? Yes. Things can move beyond the edge, and they do. A stone moving outward reaches the edge still moving, after a short time on its own watch, and keeps going; a slow one comes back down, a fast one never does. A flash sent outward right at the edge by something on its way out reaches people far away. Inside the edge, people standing still see a stone that starts at rest move only outward; thrown inward, it slows, stops and comes back. Let go deep enough inside, a stone goes out through the edge and never comes back. A stone falling in from outside goes through the edge with speed to spare, slows down inside, stops and comes back out through the edge. Someone far away, working out its path with their own clock, finds the clock running backwards past the edge, so the stone's path inside seems to come back toward the edge: that is the turn they see. Past the edge their numbers come in two forms, because they come from the square root of a negative number. There is a second reason: the far clock's time cannot go straight through the edge, so it has to go around it, one way or the other, and each way gives one of the two forms. People standing still inside the edge each have one real watch reading of their own. To them the pull points outward, and a flash they send outward never reaches the edge on their watches. Nobody far away ever sees the crossing itself, and nobody can stand still exactly on the edge.

## For a high school physics teacher
One rule converts every reading: a frame P reads what a frame Q read times \(f_Q/f_P\), with \(f^2=1-L/r\) (premise 7). With \(L=1{,}000\), A at 200 and B at 900 inside: \(f_A^2/f_B^2=(-4)/(-1/9)=36\), so B reads A's photon at \(6E_0\). For D at 1,100 outside, \(f_A^2/f_D^2=(-4)/(1/11)=-44\): what A works out for D's reading is \(\pm\sqrt{44}\,i\,E_0=\pm6.633\,i\,E_0\), two solutions. Passing the photon through frames on the two sides of the edge gives the same, because each frame's clock rate cancels.

A free body obeys \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-|1-L/r|)\) on both sides of \(L\): at \(L\) its speed on its own clock is \(ce\), it gets there in a finite time of its own, outside it climbs to \(L/(1-e^2)\), and inside, where the pull points outward, it turns at \(L/(1+e^2)\). Light sent outward at \(L\) by a source on its way out arrives far away with \(2eE\). Inside \(L\), frames held at rest read a free body at \(\gamma\propto1/\sqrt{L/r-1}\), so a body at rest there can only move outward and a body thrown inward turns back. With the ruler rule, \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(k_0^2-k^2)\), \(k^2=L/r-1\): let go at rest at \(r_0\), it reaches \(L\) at the speed \(c\,k_0\) on its own clock and leaves with \(e=k_0=\sqrt{L/r_0-1}\), for good if \(r_0\le L/2\). A body falling in from outside slows inside \(L\), turns at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and comes back out; nothing with \(e\gt0\) reaches the centre. On the far clock \(dt/d\tau=e/F\) changes sign at \(L\): the inside part of its path runs back toward \(L\); inside, \(f=\pm i\sqrt{L/r-1}\), and every value worked out through \(f\) comes in two conjugate forms. The far time of light, \(c\,dt=dr/F\), has a pole at \(L\); it is carried past it on one of two half-turns, adding \(\pm i\pi L/c\), each with its root of \(f\): that is why there are two solutions. A frame held at rest inside reads its own real ruler, \(d\ell=dr/\sqrt{L/r-1}\); on the clock of A at 200 its photon is at B at \(c\,T=2{,}758.9\) and never reaches C; and the frames held at rest inside read the pull pointing outward. On the far observer's clock nothing is seen to cross, and the light's speed on that observer's ruler and clock, \(c(1-L/r)\), is zero at \(L\) and changes sign across it.

## For a theoretical physicist
Frames: \(f^2=1-L/r\) (Section 4, statement 6). A reading converts as \(E_P=(f_Q/f_P)E_Q\) (premise 7): real on one side of \(L\); across \(L\), \(f_Q/f_P=\pm i\sqrt{(L/r_Q-1)/(1-L/r_P)}\) for \(r_Q\lt L\lt r_P\). Chains telescope, \(E_{P_n}=E_{P_0}\prod_k f_{P_k}/f_{P_{k+1}}=E_{P_0}f_{P_0}/f_{P_n}\), so the intermediate frames drop out: for \(R_A=200\), \(R_B=900\), \(R_D=1{,}100\) and \(L=1{,}000\), \(E_B=6E_0\) and \(E_D=\pm2\sqrt{11}\,iE_0\), for every boundary zone \(C\mp\delta\). No frame is held at \(L\): the holding pull \(G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/(r^2f)\) has no bound as \(f\to0\).

Motion: outside, \(e=\gamma f\) and \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-1+L/r)=c^2f^2(\gamma^2-1)\); inside, the held frames read \(\gamma=e/k\), \(k^2=L/r-1\), and with the ruler rule \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-k^2)\): one law, \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-|F|)\), with turns at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and, for \(e\lt1\), at \(L/(1-e^2)\) (with a ruler \(d\ell=\lambda\,dr/k\), \(\lambda\gt0\), the inner turn is at \(L/(1+\lambda^2e^2)\)); \(|dr/d\tau|_L=ce\); \(\Delta\tau\) to \(L\) finite; \(dt/d\tau=e/F\), so \(\Delta t=\int e\,dr/(c(1-L/r)\sqrt{e^2-|F|})\to\infty\) at \(L\), and \(dt/d\tau\lt0\) inside; the speed still needed at \(L\): \(c\) at rest; for a free frame with \(e\le1\), \(c(1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\) along its motion, falling in or on the way out, and none for \(e\ge1\) (to turn a frame falling in back at \(L\) itself would take \(c\)). Inside \(L\), read by frames held at rest (premises 3 and 7, H2): \(\gamma(r)=\gamma_0\sqrt{(L/r_0-1)/(L/r-1)}\), so no inward motion from rest and a turn at \(L/r-1=\gamma_0^2(L/r_0-1)\); for such a body the converted count \(\gamma f\) is imaginary and \((f\,d\ell/d\tau)^2=c^2f^2(\gamma^2-1)=-(dr/d\tau)^2\lt0\) where \(\gamma\gt1\). In the held frames' own account, with the ruler rule, \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(k_0^2-k^2)\): a finite own time to \(L\) and the speed \(ck_0\) there, so premise 8 outside gives \(e=k_0\), and escape for \(r_0\le L/2\). For a body from outside, the far-inferred \(\gamma=e/f=\mp ie/\sqrt{L/r-1}\), clock step \((e/f)\,d\tau\) and ruler step \(dr/f\) are imaginary and conjugate on the two roots; \(dr/(e\,d\tau)\) is real. Light from outside \(L\): the far counts \(fE\), \((e-\sqrt{e^2-F})E\) falling in and \((e+\sqrt{e^2-F})E\) on the way out, the last \(2eE\) at \(L\); from inside, \(fE\) and \(\pm i\) times the other two with \(|F|\) for \(F\). Light along the radius on the far observer's ruler and clock: \(dr/dt=\pm cf^2=\pm c(1-L/r)\), real on both sides for both of premise 7's solutions, with one change of sign, at \(L\). The joining rule (adopted): the far time and \(f\) are continued past \(L\) on the same half-turn, so \(c\,t_{\rm in}-c\,t_{\rm out}=\pm i\pi R\) with the residue \(R=\sigma L\) for light and \(R=-L\) for a body falling in, the finite parts of the two sides matched at equal \(|r-L|\) (for a body the regular parts of \(c\,dt/dr\) on the two sides of \(L\) differ, \(1\pm1/2e^2\), so the whole outside differential is not continued: that would give back general relativity's law inside), and \(f=\pm i\sqrt{|F|}\) on the same half-turn. Two solutions: \(s_{PQ}^2\lt0\) across \(L\) gives the two roots; the far time's logarithmic divergence at \(L\) leaves the constants of the two sides free; the joining rule (one half-turn, no further winding) selects the two offsets \(\pm i\pi L/c\) and pairs each with a root. A held frame's own radial ruler inside \(L\): with \(h=f/f_A\) and \(d\ell=\kappa\,dr/h\), premises 1, 3 and 5 give \(r^2h\,g_{\rm hold}=G\mathcal M/(F_A\kappa)\), so \(\kappa\) is constant; the rule \(d\ell=dr/|f|\) gives \(\kappa=1/|f_A|\). Then \(c\,T_A=|f_A|[H(R_A)-H(r)]\), \(dT_A/dt=-|f_A|\) along the outgoing ray, \(f_A\,dt=\mp i\,dT_A\), \(g_{\rm hold}=-G\mathcal M/(r^2|f|)\), and the counted flux is \(-4\pi G\mathcal M/|f_A|\) in A's units.

## Part II, Testing the Solution: NASA's NICER Data, and How We Test with It
The figures are from the project's records of 22 to 24 November 2026, measured on one laptop.

Part I is a great deal of mathematics. Part II tests it. This section describes the first test: a real calculation that NASA's NICER mission needs, with known answers, done with the clocks and rulers of this paper. The test has two aims, in the author's words:

- "(a) check the math with a complex, real world challenge with know answers to see if the physics is correct"
- "(b) Check to see if it's useful. Can we use the math to speed up the calculation."

1. The problem.

NICER is NASA's X-ray telescope on the International Space Station. It records the X-ray light of hot spots on spinning neutron stars. The star turns, the spots come into view and go out of view, and the light pulses. On its way out the light passes clocks and rulers that the star has changed, so the shape of the pulse depends on the star's mass and radius. To read the mass and the radius from NICER's counts, the expected pulse has to be calculated for millions of trial stars. One such calculation is called a pulse profile. It is a pure calculation of clocks, rulers and light paths, and each one is costly.

2. What is calculated, and from what.

For a star with the count \(\mathcal M\) and the radius \(R\), with \(L=2G\mathcal M/c^2\), the program calculates, from Section 4:

\[
f=\sqrt{1-\frac Lr},\qquad d\ell=\frac{dr}{f},\qquad 1+z=\frac1f,
\]

then the path of each ray of light in these clocks and rulers, the time each ray takes, the motion of the star's surface, the number of photons expected in each of NICER's bins of phase and energy, and the likelihood of NICER's counts. The path of light uses one law more, the angular momentum law for light, which the author accepted as a premise on 23 November 2026 and which this paper has still to derive from its own premises.

3. The control.

The control is X-PSI, the public program that the NICER collaboration's work uses for pulse profiles (github.com/xpsi-group/xpsi; version 3.5.0b1 was run). Both programs get the same stars and the same instrument. The test stars have known answers. The comparison is made bin by bin and in the likelihood.

4. What this test can show, and what it cannot.

It tests the solution outside a star, at redshifts of 20 to 40 percent, in every detail of light's path. Outside one round body the conservation derivation and the Schwarzschild derivation give the same clocks and rulers (Section 9), so this test cannot tell the two apart. What it can show is that the mathematics of Part I, rebuilt from the conservation laws, gives the known answers in a hard, real calculation, and that it is useful: the same answers, faster.

5. The ways the mathematics is used to save time.

- Using the mathematics as it is: the clock, the ruler and light's path in closed form, counted at the place where the light leaves.
- The curvature integrated directly: the clock rate, the ruler and light's two path integrals from one integration of the curvature from far away inward (Section 10, Part 9; Section 12).
- Superposition: what does not change between two trial stars is calculated once (Section 4, statement 7, for several bodies).
- The heatmap: more calculation where the approach has more error, and less where it has little.
- The approximation built with the search: point masses, fine near and coarse far (Section 4, statement 5).

6. Where the work is.

The programs, the checks and the measured figures are public: github.com/ChrisBergstromBeamish/fast-nicer-pulse-profile-modeling. Section 16 gives the results.

## For a child
A neutron star is a star squeezed down to the size of a city. Some of them spin many times a second, with hot patches that glow. A telescope on the Space Station counts the light from those patches. Because the star is so heavy, clocks near it run slow and light bends on its way out, so the glow rises and falls in a special pattern. To learn how big and how heavy the star is, a computer has to work out that pattern again and again, millions of times. We gave that job to the rules of this paper. First we check that they get the answers that are already known. Then we see whether they get them faster.

## For a high school physics teacher
The data. NICER counts X-ray photons from the hot spots of millisecond pulsars, sorted by the phase of the star's turn and by energy.

The calculation. Light from a spot leaves a surface where the clock rate is \(f=\sqrt{1-L/R}\), about 0.8 for a typical neutron star, so it arrives redshifted by 20 to 40 percent. Its path bends, so more than half of the star's surface is seen at any moment. The surface moves at a good fraction of the speed of light, so the spot is brighter when it comes toward us. A pulse profile adds all of this up for every piece of the spot, every phase and every energy.

The control. The same calculation is done by X-PSI, the public program of the field, on the same stars. The two results are compared bin by bin.

What it shows. Outside a star the conservation derivation gives the same clocks and rulers as the Schwarzschild solution, so this is a test of the mathematics and of its usefulness. It is not a test that could tell the two derivations apart.

## For a theoretical physicist
Inputs taken as given. The test problems' inputs are taken as the control has them: the star's mass and equatorial radius, its spin, the place, size and temperature of the spots, the atmosphere table, the instrument's response, and the flattened shape of a spinning star, whose formula was made to match general relativity's star models. The round star is tested first.

Premises. Section 4, statements 1, 4 and 6, for the clock and the ruler; light at \(c\) on each frame's own clock and ruler; the angular momentum law for light, \(b=r\sin\alpha/f\), an IMPORT accepted as a premise by the author on 23 November 2026; special relativity at one place for the moving surface (an IMPORT on the review list).

The gates fixed before the runs. Agreement with the test stars to 0.1 percent; the likelihood within 0.1 on the example counts; a speed ratio above 1 with an interval that excludes 1; each way of saving time reported alone.

What general relativity this touches. None of its premises is tested here: outside one round body both derivations give the same numbers. The premise touched is a practical one, that these calculations need the field equations and their solutions as data. The program takes neither.

Still to be written here: the derivation page of the public repository brought into the paper's terms; the list of the test stars; the exact statement of each way of saving time with its measured share; the plan for the runs on NICER's public counts.

Ours, compiled | 0.423 ms | 116 to 131 times | 

The gate of Section 15 asked for a speed ratio above 1 with an interval that excludes 1. The twelve stars give 116 to 131 times; the interval itself is still to be reported. On all the cores of the same laptop the compiled program does 2,096 stars a second, against 406 on one core (24 November 2026). The fastest public program is not the control. It is a program for a graphics card, which its authors report at 1.8 to 5.3 ms for a profile on one RTX 4080.

3. What the results show, and what they do not.

They show that the clocks and the rulers of Part I, calculated from the conservation laws with no field equation and no solution taken as data, together with two inputs that are not yet derived here (the angular momentum law for light, and for a spinning star the flattened shape, which is made to match general relativity's star models; Section 15), give the known answers of a hard, real calculation to the control's own tolerances, and give them about a hundred times faster on the same core. This paper's own stricter gate on the likelihood, 0.1, is met in the first check and not in the second. They do not tell the conservation derivation from the Schwarzschild derivation: outside one round body the two give the same numbers (Section 9).

## For a child
We gave our rules the same homework that NASA's helpers give their own program: work out how a spinning star's glow should look. Our rules got the answers the helpers already knew were right. And they finished about a hundred times sooner on the same computer.

## For a high school physics teacher
Right answers. The expected counts agree with the control's, and where the two differ a little, the control's numbers move toward ours when it is asked to work more finely. The likelihood, which is what a search for the star's mass and radius uses, agrees within the control's own tolerance.

Faster. One evaluation takes the control about 50 thousandths of a second and our compiled program 0.4 thousandths, on one core of the same laptop.

The limit of the test. These stars redshift light by 20 to 40 percent, which is a great deal, and the conservation derivation and the Schwarzschild solution still give the same numbers there, because the light leaves from outside one round body.

## Part II, Testing the Solution: High-Redshift Observations
The observations are listed in the Appendix (Section 19); not every one has yet been checked at its source.

For Chris, before this stub is filled. Your sentence: "Ours predict higher redshifts." What the mathematics of Section 4 gives is this. First, a higher redshift than a calculation with the mass held static, everywhere. Second, a higher redshift than Einstein's equations in the two cases with more than one count that are worked out here: for the same two deficits of two bodies at rest on one line, and, wherever both clock rates are real, at every place inside an evenly spread body. Third, for the light that leaves the surface of one round body at rest, calculated from its far mass and its radius, the same redshift as Schwarzschild's formula as the textbooks and the published analyses use it. Your columns 4 and 5 are in the table of statement 2 as the calculation with the mass held static and the conservation-based formulas, after your words of 24 November: "Schwarzchild held the mass as static." and "We're comparing it to the uncorrected schwarzschild equations which diverge." A last column shows Schwarzschild's formula as published. It gives the figures of column 5. Which of the two the paper calls general relativity without corrections is yours to say. The physicist's box shows what the choice hangs on: the power of the clock rate in the counted pull.

The heavier and smaller a body is, the more the light that leaves it is redshifted. Far from the mass every way of calculating gives the same redshift. At high redshift the ways come apart. This section says how, lists the observations with the highest redshifts, and sets the calculations beside them.

1. Three calculations of the redshift of light that leaves a body.

Take one round body at rest, with the count \(\mathcal M\) as read far away and the radius \(R\), and write \(x=2G\mathcal M/(Rc^2)=L/R\).

The mass held static. Every frame held at rest puts the same mass, the far one, into its own law of the pull. With the clock step and the held frame's ruler of Section 4, or with nothing updated at all, that gives

\[
1+z=\frac{1}{1-x/2}\qquad\text{or}\qquad 1+z=e^{x/2}.
\]

The conservation derivation. A frame held at rest reads the body at \(\mathcal M/f\), heavier than the frame far away does (Section 4, statement 2). With that reading in its law of the pull, the integral of f dot dr gives \(f^2=1-x\) (statement 6):

\[
1+z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x}} .
\]

Schwarzschild's formula. The Schwarzschild solution gives the same expression as the conservation derivation, \(1+z=(1-x)^{-1/2}\). The correction is already inside it (Section 9, statement 2).

So for the light that leaves one round body at rest, the conservation derivation predicts a higher redshift than a calculation that holds the mass static, and the same redshift as Schwarzschild's formula from the same far mass and radius:

Conservation derivation, and Schwarzschild's formula | Mass held static, the ruler updated | Mass held static, nothing updated | 

0.0269% (Sirius B) | 0.0269% | 0.0269% | 

1.0% | 1.00% | 0.99% | 

10.0% | 9.50% | 9.07% | 

20.0% | 18.03% | 16.51% | 

23.5% (1.4 suns, 12 km) | 20.81% | 18.80% | 

40.8% (2.08 suns, 12.4 km) | 32.92% | 28.11% | 

80.0% | 52.83% | 41.29% | 

100.0% | 60.00% | 45.50% | 

Below 1 percent the three differ by less than a hundredth part of the redshift itself. At 20 percent the static calculations fall short by a tenth and a sixth of the redshift, and at 80 percent by a third and a half. Where more than one count pulls, the conservation derivation and Einstein's equations part as well (statement 3).

2. The observations.

The table holds the observations with a redshift above 20 percent for which a mass and a radius have been published, with the best-measured white dwarf for comparison. In three of the four the mass and the radius do not come from the redshifted line itself. The redshift in the last three columns is calculated from that mass and radius. The fourth column holds the mass static: every frame puts the far mass into its own law of the pull. The fifth is the conservation derivation, with the mass that each frame reads. The sixth is Schwarzschild's formula as the published analyses use it, and it gives the figures of the fifth.

4U 1820−30, NICER, 23 August 2021 | 1.58 suns (9.11 km) | 72% ± 5% | 34.4% | 43.2% | 43.2% |

In every row above 20 percent the observed redshift is higher than every calculation. (For X 1636−536 the published mass and radius had the line itself among their inputs, with an assumed motion of the gas, so that row is not independent of the line.) The conservation-based figure is closer to it than the static one. Three cautions go with the rows above 20 percent, and the Appendix gives them row by row: in each the line's identification is disputed or was not reproduced; the mass and the radius come from the analysis of X-ray bursts, which rests on a model of the star's atmosphere and on general relativity's relations at the surface; and the stars spin, which no calculation here has in it yet. For Sirius B, where none of the three applies, the observed redshift and the calculations agree within the one percent of the measurement.

3. Where the conservation derivation and general relativity part at high redshift.

In two places, and in both the conservation derivation gives the higher redshift.

Where more than one count pulls. The squared-clock deficits add exactly in the grid of the frame of the calculation (Section 4, statement 7). That the pull between two bodies is counted through that grid's areas is carried over from one point mass (Section 4, the premise table). In Einstein's equations, for bodies at rest on one line and held apart, the clock rates multiply (Weyl's solutions, with each body's rate taken in his coordinates). So for light that leaves a place where two counts pull, with the same two deficits,

\[
1+z=\Big(1-\frac{L_1}{r_1}-\frac{L_2}{r_2}\Big)^{-1/2}\ \text{here},\qquad 1+z=\Big[\Big(1-\frac{L_1}{r_1}\Big)\Big(1-\frac{L_2}{r_2}\Big)\Big]^{-1/2}\ \text{there}.
\]

The first is the higher, always. With the deficits 0.25 and 0.0833 it is 22.5 percent against 20.6. With 0.3 and 0.3 it is 58.1 percent against 42.9. The squares of the two clock rates differ by the product of the two deficits, so the difference shows only where both are large. To compare the two at one and the same place, named by measurements, takes the rulers between two bodies, which are not yet stated (Section 4).

Inside a body. A body is an arrangement of many counts. For a round body the sum needs only the spheres around the centre: the pull through each is set by the count inside it (premise 1), and the ruler is along the pull (premise 5). Inside a round body at rest whose count is spread evenly, at the distance \(s\) from the centre, the exact sum gives

\[
F(s)=1-\frac{L}{2R}\Big(3-\frac{s^2}{R^2}\Big),\qquad F(0)=1-\frac{3L}{2R}.
\]

General relativity's solution for its own evenly spread body has a faster clock at the centre, wherever both clock rates are real:

Body | Redshift of the light from the surface, in both | Redshift of a clock at the centre, the exact sum | The same, general relativity's solution | 

1.4 suns, 12 km | 23.5% | 43.9% | 40.0% | 

2.08 suns, 12.4 km | 40.8% | 97.3% | 76.8% | 

\(R=\tfrac53L\) | 58.1% | 216% | 123% | 

\(R=1.5\,L\) | 73.2% | no finite value | 173% | 

\(R=1.125\,L\) | 200% | | no finite value | 

With the exact sum the clock rate at the centre, as the observer far away reads it, reaches zero when \(R=\tfrac32L\). The light from the surface is then redshifted by

\[
z_{\mathrm{surface}}=\sqrt3-1=73.2\% .
\]

That is where the causal boundary of the observer far away, which is also the event horizon, first appears: at the centre of the body, while the surface is still well outside \(L\). In a smaller body it is a sphere inside the body, of the radius \(R\sqrt{3-2R/L}\), and it reaches the surface when \(R=L\). In general relativity's solution the clock rate at the centre reaches zero at \(R=\tfrac98L\), at a surface redshift of 200 percent.

A body whose count is denser toward its centre gets there at a larger radius. So for every round body at rest whose count is nowhere denser farther out than farther in: at a surface redshift of 73.2 percent or more, the causal boundary of the observer far away lies inside the body.

Is 73.2 percent a limit? For the light that the far observer reads from the surface of a body at rest of this kind, yes. A frame cannot be held at rest where its clock rate, as read far away, is zero while the pull is not: the force that would hold it has no finite value on its own scale (the physicist's box). This result takes that as its premise. A body at rest is filled with pieces held at rest, so for \(L\le R\lt\tfrac32L\) one of them would sit on that sphere. So a round body at rest whose count is nowhere denser farther out, and whose surface lies outside \(L\), has \(R\ge\tfrac32L\) and a surface redshift of at most 73.2 percent. General relativity allows up to 200 percent (Buchdahl's limit, for a fluid with the same pressure in every direction, a finite pressure at the centre and none at the surface).

A body that lies wholly inside \(L\) has no such sphere in it, and the premise says nothing about it. Its surface is beyond the far observer's causal boundary, and the redshift that this observer would infer for its light has two solutions, both complex (premise 7). To exclude such bodies would take a further premise, and none of the eight of Section 3 gives one. General relativity's premise that no frame is at rest inside \(L\) would do it, and this paper denies that premise (Section 3). So the result is: every surface line that the far observer reads with a real redshift, from a round body at rest whose count is nowhere denser farther out, is redshifted by at most 73.2 percent.

An observation can decide: one confirmed line from the surface of a body at rest of this kind, with a redshift between 73.2 and 200 percent, would refute the exact sum inside a body together with this premise, and general relativity's equations would still stand. Two things bound the statement. The premise is not among the eight of Section 3; without it, the sum says where the causal boundary is, and no more. The limit does not hold for a body whose count is denser farther out: inside a shell (Section 4) the clock rate is the same everywhere, and the redshift of its surface has no limit before \(R=L\). The sum inside the body uses premise 5 inside matter, which the derivation of Section 4, statement 4, gives there as outside; it makes the centre of the body a conical point (the physicist's box).

The highest surface redshifts that the search found are 72% ± 5%, 65% ± 3% and 64.2% ± 3.2% (the first three rows of the table). They need a radius of 1.51, 1.58 and 1.59 times \(L\), just outside one and a half. With the exact sum that leaves little room: the average of \(R/u\) over the star's count, which is 1.5 for an even spread, has to stay below 1.511 for the centre of a star with a line at 72 percent to be on our side of the causal boundary. So if one of these lines is confirmed as a surface line, the spread of the star's count, measured in some other way, says where the star's centre is.

## For a child
Light that climbs away from a very heavy star gets tired: it arrives redder than it left. The heavier and smaller the star, the redder. There are different ways to work out how much redder. One way forgets that things get heavier when you measure them close to the star. That way always comes out too low, and the heavier the star, the more it is off. Our way does not forget, and for the outside of one star it gives the same answer as the famous black-hole formula.

Then we looked at what telescopes have seen. For a few very heavy stars the light looks even redder than every calculation says. Nobody is sure yet that those telescopes read the light correctly.

Our rules say something new about the inside of a star. Squeeze a star smaller and smaller. There comes a point where, for someone far away, the very middle of the star sits on the edge of what they can ever see. With our rules that happens when the star's light is 73 parts in 100 redder. With the old rules it happens at 200. Holding a piece of the star still, right on that edge, would take a push with no end. If no piece can be held there, then a star that stands still, and that we can still see, cannot be squeezed past that point. The reddest light of this kind that we found a report of is 72.

## For a high school physics teacher
The formulas. With \(x=2G\mathcal M/(Rc^2)\): the conservation derivation and Schwarzschild's formula both give \(1+z=1/\sqrt{1-x}\). A calculation that keeps the mass the same for every frame gives \(1+z=1/(1-x/2)\). To first order in \(x\) all agree: \(z\approx G\mathcal M/(Rc^2)\), the formula used for white dwarfs.

Where the difference comes from. A frame held at rest near the body reads the body's mass as \(\mathcal M/f\), heavier than a far frame does, because its unit of energy is smaller. That heavier reading is what the pull at its place goes with. Leaving it out lowers the redshift: 20.8 percent in place of 23.5 percent for a neutron star of 1.4 suns and 12 km.

The observations. For the white dwarf Sirius B the measured redshift, 80.65 km/s as a speed, matches the calculation within the one percent of the measurement. For four neutron stars with claimed lines the measured redshift is above every calculation, and each of those lines is disputed.

Where this paper and general relativity part. For the light from the surface of one star the two give the same redshift. They part where more than one mass pulls, and the inside of a star is such a place. Here the deficits \(1-f^2\) of the pieces add, and that makes the clock at the centre slower than in general relativity's solution. With the deficits adding, the clock at the centre of an evenly filled star stops, as read from far away, when \(R=1.5\,L\): the surface light is then redshifted by 73.2 percent. In general relativity's solution for an evenly filled star that happens at \(R=1.125\,L\) and 200 percent. The force needed to hold a piece of the star at rest where the clock stops has no finite value there. With the premise that no piece is held there, a star at rest whose matter is nowhere denser farther out, and whose light the far observer reads with a real redshift, has a surface redshift of at most 73.2 percent.

## For a theoretical physicist

### The three calculations, and the power of the clock rate
All use the clock step \(d\ln f=g_{\mathrm{hold}}\,d\ell/c^2\) (premise 3) and the held frame's ruler \(d\ell=dr/f\). They differ in the mass that the held frame puts into its own law of the pull, \(\mathcal M/f^{\,n}\):

\(n\) | The held frame's law of the pull | Result | 1.4 suns, 12 km | 2.08 suns, 12.4 km | 

0: the mass held static | \(g_{\mathrm{hold}}=G\mathcal M/r^2\) | \(f=1-x/2\) | 20.8% | 32.9% | 

1: the conservation derivation (Section 4, statements 2, 4, 6) | \(g_{\mathrm{hold}}=G(\mathcal M/f)/r^2\) | \(f^2=1-x\) | 23.5% | 40.8% | 

2: the reading entered twice | \(g_{\mathrm{hold}}=G(\mathcal M/f^2)/r^2\) | \(f^3=1-3x/2\) | 27.4% | 57.3% | 

In general \(f^{\,n+1}=1-(n+1)\,x/2\) for \(n\ne-1\); at \(n=-1\) the same step gives \(f=e^{-x/2}\), which is also the result with the mass held static and the ruler not updated either, \(d\ell=dr\).

Section 4 derives the row \(n=1\): the held frame reads the body at \(\mathcal M/f\), by count and by weighing (statement 2). The Schwarzschild solution has the same pull on a frame held at rest, \(g_{\mathrm{hold}}=G\mathcal M/(r^2\sqrt{1-L/r})\). So its formula for the redshift is the row \(n=1\), although the solution has one constant \(M\) for every frame. The row \(n=2\) is derived nowhere in this paper. It is in the table because it is the only one of the three that gives a higher redshift than Schwarzschild's formula for the surface of one body. The second reviewer derived the rows \(n=0\) and \(n=1\) independently on 25 November 2026 and the figures agree.

Around one body at rest the emitter's motion multiplies \(1+z\) by \(D=\gamma(1-\beta\cos\theta)\), with \(\theta\) the angle between the light and the emitter's velocity in the frame held at rest (Section 4, statement 8).

### Inside a round body
Let \(\ell(u)\) be the count, as a length, inside the radius \(u\), with \(\ell(R)=L\), and let \(u\) be the radius of the circles around the centre. The pull through the sphere at \(s\) is set by the count inside it (premise 1), \(f\,g_{\mathrm{hold}}=G\mathcal M(s)/s^2\), and with the ruler along the pull, \(d\ell=ds/f\) (premise 5), the clock step gives

\[
\frac{dF}{ds}=\frac{\ell(s)}{s^2}\ge0,\qquad F(s)=1-\frac{\ell(s)}{s}-\int_s^R\frac{d\ell(u)}{u}.
\]

This is the exact sum of Section 4, statement 7, for a round arrangement, where the average of \(1/|\mathbf x-\mathbf x_a|\) over a sphere of radius \(u\) is \(1/\max(s,u)\). For a round body it needs only the spheres around the centre. \(F\) is lowest at the centre, for every spread of the count. If the count is nowhere denser farther out than farther in, then \(\ell(u)\ge L\,(u/R)^3\), and an integration by parts gives

\[
1-F(0)=\frac LR+\int_0^R\frac{\ell(u)}{u^2}\,du\ \ge\ \frac{3L}{2R},
\]

with equality for the even spread, where \(F(s)=1-(L/2R)(3-s^2/R^2)\). The second reviewer derived the same inequality, independently, on 25 November 2026.

So for \(L\lt R\lt\tfrac32L\) the sum gives \(F(0)\lt0\lt F(R)\). \(F\) then rises from below zero at the centre to \(1-L/R\) at the surface, and it is zero on a sphere inside the body: for the even spread at \(s_0=R\sqrt{3-2R/L}\), where \(dF/ds=Ls_0/R^3\gt0\). That sphere is the causal boundary of the observer far away, by the criterion of premise 8: a body at rest where the clock rate is \(f\) needs the speed \(c\sqrt{1-F}\) to escape (from \(e=\gamma f=1\), premise 3), and that is \(c\) where \(F=0\). Inside it the square of the clock rate that this observer infers is negative, and by premise 7 the inferred clock rate has two solutions, \(\pm\,i\sqrt{-F}\).

The force. On its own scale, the force per unit of mass that holds a piece at rest is

\[
g_{\mathrm{hold}}=c^2\,\frac{\partial\ln f}{\partial\ell}=\frac{c^2}{2f}\,\frac{dF}{ds}=\frac{c^2\,\ell(s)}{2f\,s^2}.
\]

On the sphere where \(f=0\) the pull is not zero, so this has no finite value: it grows without bound as the sphere is approached. At \(R=\tfrac32L\) exactly, for the even spread, the zero is at the centre, where the pull is zero as well. There the force tends to the finite value \(c^2\sqrt{L/2R^3}\) as the centre is approached, and the distance to the centre along the held rulers, \(\int ds/f\), has no finite value. The limit needs one premise: no piece of a body at rest is held where the far-read clock rate is zero and the pull is not. For a body whose count is nowhere denser farther out and whose surface lies outside \(L\), a radius below \(\tfrac32L\) gives \(F(0)\lt0\lt F(R)\), which puts such a piece inside the body, with \(\ell(s_0)\gt0\). So with that premise a body of this kind whose surface lies outside \(L\) has

\[
R\ge\frac32\,L,\qquad 1+z_{\mathrm{surface}}=\Big(1-\frac LR\Big)^{-1/2}\le\sqrt3 ,
\]

with equality only for the even spread. For \(R\lt L\), \(F\lt0\) everywhere in the body, the zero of \(F\) lies outside it at \(s=L\), and the premise says nothing. The far observer would infer for the light of such a surface \(1+z=1/f\) with \(f^2=1-L/R\lt0\): two solutions, both complex (premise 7). Excluding such bodies would take a further premise, and none of the eight of Section 3 gives one; general relativity's premise that no frame is at rest inside \(L\) would do it, and Section 3 denies that premise. So the result, with its one premise, is: every surface line that the far observer reads with a real redshift, from a round body at rest whose count is nowhere denser farther out, has \(z\le\sqrt3-1\).

For a spread that is not even the condition is sharper. With \(\langle R/u\rangle\) the average of \(R/u\) over the count,

\[
F(0)\gt0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Big\langle\frac Ru\Big\rangle\lt\frac RL .
\]

The even spread has \(\langle R/u\rangle=1.5\). A line at 0.72 has \(R/L=1.511\), so it allows \(\langle R/u\rangle\) only up to 1.511.

Body | Radius | Surface redshift | 

Count spread evenly: the far observer's causal boundary appears at the centre (the exact sum) | \(1.5\,L\) | 73.2% | 

Count spread evenly: the clock rate at the centre reaches zero in general relativity's solution (comparison) | \(1.125\,L\) | 200% | 

Needed by the line of 4U 1820−30 at 0.72, in both | \(1.511\,L\) | | 

Needed by the line of X 1608−52 at 0.65, in both | \(1.581\,L\) | | 

Needed by the line of X 1636−536 at 0.642, in both | \(1.590\,L\) | | 

What this uses: that the counts of the pieces are the only sources of the pull inside a body that is held up by its own pressure, each count positive and holding its share of the binding and of whatever holds the body up; that every piece is at rest; and that the count, per unit of volume of the grid, is nowhere denser farther out than farther in. With the held frame's unit of energy at \(f\) and its ruler along the pull at \(f\), the count per unit of grid volume is the density that the held frames read in their own units. So the last condition is of the same kind as the one in general relativity's limit on the comparison side, a density read by the held frames; what each of the two densities includes has still to be matched. How the potential energy is divided among the pieces (Section 4, "Not yet in this section") changes the spread of the count, not the result for a given spread. The spin of a real star is not in it.

The centre of the body. The clock step above uses premise 5 inside matter: the ruler along the pull at \(f\), the rulers across it unchanged, so \(ds/d\ell=f\) with \(s\) the radius of the circles. At the centre the pull goes to zero where the density there is bounded (the count inside \(s\), as a length, falls faster than \(s^2\)), while \(f(0)\) stays below 1. So near the centre a sphere at the distance \(d\) measured on the held rulers has the area \(4\pi f(0)^2d^2\), less than \(4\pi d^2\) by the share \(1-F(0)\) when \(0\lt F(0)\lt1\), and the curvature of space in the planes across the radius, \((1-F)/s^2\), grows without bound there: the centre is a conical point. For the even spread the share is \(3L/2R\): 45 percent for \(L/R=0.3\). At \(R=\tfrac32L\), where \(F(0)=0\), the clock rate near the centre is \(f=a\,s\) with \(a=\sqrt{L/2R^3}\), and the centre lies at an unbounded distance on the held rulers, \(d=a^{-1}\ln(s_*/s)\). Premise 5 holds inside matter by the derivation that gives it outside (Section 4, statement 4), on the same round grid: wherever a frame that falls from rest far away passes a piece held at rest, with a clock rate \(0\lt f\le1\), the piece's ruler along the pull is at \(f\) and its rulers across it are unchanged; nothing is added that the outside does not use. Section 10, Part 16, finds the same ruler inside a wave, with the same deficit at the centre, and the 73.2 percent limit rests on it. General relativity's interior ruler, \(ds/d\ell=\sqrt{1-\ell(s)/s}\) with \(\ell(s)\) the count inside \(s\) as a length, is regular at the centre; with it the clock inside becomes general relativity's interior solution and the limit becomes 200 percent. It is not a repair of this derivation but the premise under comparison.

The opposite case is the shell of Section 4: all the count at one radius. Inside it \(F\) is the same everywhere as at the shell, the far observer's causal boundary appears at the shell itself, at \(R=L\), and the redshift of its surface has no limit before that. So without the condition on the spread there is no figure of 73.2 percent.

General relativity, on the comparison side. Its solution for a body of the same density everywhere has the clock rate \(f(s)=\tfrac32\sqrt{1-L/R}-\tfrac12\sqrt{1-Ls^2/R^3}\), which is zero at the centre when \(R=\tfrac98L\). At the distance \(s\) from the centre the squares of the two clock rates differ by \(\tfrac34\big(\sqrt{1-Ls^2/R^3}-\sqrt{1-L/R}\big)^2\). So the square of the exact sum's clock rate is the lower at every place inside the body and at every size, and wherever both clock rates are real the exact sum's clock is the slower. (For \(R\lt\tfrac32L\) the exact sum's \(F\) is below zero at the centre while general relativity's clock rate there is still real: at \(R=\tfrac43L\), \(F(0)=-\tfrac18\) and \(f_{\mathrm{GR}}(0)=\tfrac14\).) At the centre the difference of the squares is \(\tfrac34\big(1-\sqrt{1-L/R}\big)^2\). Buchdahl's limit: for a round body at rest made of a fluid with the same pressure in every direction, whose energy density is nowhere greater farther out than farther in, with a finite pressure at the centre, joined to empty space at a surface where the pressure is zero, \(R\gt\tfrac98L\) and \(z_{\mathrm{surface}}\lt2\).

### What is shown, and the premises of general relativity this touches
Shown. For the light from the surface of one round body at rest: the conservation derivation gives a higher redshift than a calculation with the mass held static, by the figures of the first table, and the same redshift as Schwarzschild's formula from the same far mass and radius. In the two cases with more than one count that are worked out here, the exact sum gives a higher redshift than Einstein's equations, at the second order in the deficits: for the same two deficits of bodies at rest on one line, with the pull counted through the areas of the grid of the frame of the calculation (Section 4, the premise table), and, wherever both clock rates are real, at every place inside an evenly spread round body, where the sum needs only the spheres around the centre. In a round body at rest whose count is nowhere denser farther out than farther in, the far observer's causal boundary appears at the centre at a surface redshift of at most 73.2 percent; in general relativity's solution for an evenly spread body the clock rate at the centre reaches zero at 200 percent. With the premise that no piece is held where the far-read clock rate is zero and the pull is not, every surface line that the far observer reads with a real redshift from such a body is redshifted by at most 73.2 percent. In the four observations above 20 percent that have a published mass and radius, the observed redshift is above every calculation.

Not shown. The comparison between two bodies at one and the same place, named by measurements, and an ordering for every arrangement of several bodies. That any of the four lines is a line from the star's surface. What the conservation-based formulas give once the spin and the burst analyses are redone. Whether a body can be at rest with pieces beyond the far observer's causal boundary: wholly inside \(L\), where the premise says nothing, or across \(L\), when the premise is not taken. What holds a body up, and so which bodies exist. The same for a spinning body.

The premises of general relativity this touches. The first is its equations inside matter. They give the clock at the centre of a body, and for a fluid with the same pressure in every direction, whose energy density is nowhere greater farther out than farther in, with a finite pressure at the centre and none at the surface, they allow a body at rest up to a surface redshift of 200 percent (Buchdahl). The exact sum gives a slower clock at the centre wherever both clock rates are real, a lower square of the clock rate at every size, and it puts the far observer's causal boundary at the centre at 73.2 percent. The burden is on the premise that general relativity's equations hold inside matter at such redshifts, which no observation has tested: the highest surface redshift that the search found is 0.72 ± 0.05. The second is the class of equations that Einstein chose (A9 of Section 5), which makes the clock rates of bodies at rest on one line and held apart multiply, where the deficits add here in the grid of the frame of the calculation.
