## Conclusion
We found an error in the Schwarzschild solution, fixed it, and reconciled the solution with conservation of mass-energy. The error is one step. The Schwarzschild form is derived outside the event horizon; general relativity then carries it inside by a change of coordinates, and with that step gives every frame one mass \(\mathcal M\) and one event horizon, leaves no frame at rest inside, and, with the direction of time it chooses there, sends everything to the centre (Section 7, parts 15 to 17; Section 9, statement 3). The fix keeps the solution outside \(L\), because the count gives the same; makes its assumption that nothing changes with time a result, with no field equation; and puts premises 7 and 8 in the place of its continuation across \(L\), one account for every frame of reference (Section 9, statement 4).

With the error fixed, the Schwarzschild solution and conservation of mass-energy give identical results inside and outside the event horizon. Outside, around one body at rest, they give the same clocks, the same rulers and the same count of a free body, to every figure (Section 9, statement 1). At the event horizon and inside it, both take premises 7 and 8 in the place of the continuation: what each frame reads is real for it; a value worked out across \(L\) has two solutions, and they are complex; objects move beyond their event horizon, by the same law in both directions; an observer at rest far away cannot and does not observe the passage; and the causal boundary depends on the frame of reference (Sections 3, 9 and 14). In both, an event beyond a frame's causal boundary is calculated through an intermediate frame of reference, and an event at the causal boundary is not: no frame is held there (Section 14).

### What Is Shown

- Outside, the Schwarzschild solution is conservation of mass-energy. From H1 (the complete count inside a closed surface is constant), H2 (special relativity in the frame a body passes) and H3 (potential energy is the clock rate), with the ruler rule: \(f^2=1-L/r\), \(L=2G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}/c^2\), with \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\) constant because nothing crosses the surface, not because the field is assumed the same at every time; a free body keeps \(\gamma f\) constant, and that is Schwarzschild's \(e\). No field equation is used (Section 4, statements 1 to 6). [DERIVED]
- Across the causal boundary: premises 7 and 8. Between two frames at rest the factor is \(f_Q/f_P\), with \(f_Q^{\,2}/f_P^{\,2}=(1-L/r_Q)/(1-L/r_P)\) from the clock rate that conservation gives: positive on one side of \(L\), negative across it, so a reading worked out across \(L\) has two solutions, \(\pm i\) times a real number. A free body keeps its count \(e\) and obeys \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-|1-L/r|)\) on both sides of \(L\): at \(L\) its speed on its own clock is \(c\,e\), it gets there in a finite time of its own, and it moves beyond \(L\); on the clock of an observer at rest far away the passage has no finite time. The speed a frame still needs at \(L\) to escape is \(c\) at rest, and, for a frame in free motion with count \(e\le1\), \(c\,(1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\) along its motion, falling in or on its way out; with \(e\ge1\) it needs none (Section 3, premises 7 and 8; Section 9, statement 3). [DERIVED in Section 3 on premises 7 and 8; inside \(L\) with premise 3, H2 and the ruler rule]
- Bodies inside, as the frames held at rest there read them. Their readings are real, and between two of them premise 7's factor is real; with premise 3 a free body is read at \(\gamma(r)=\gamma_0\sqrt{(L/r_0-1)/(L/r-1)}\). With \(\gamma\ge1\), a free body at rest inside \(L\) cannot fall inward, and a body thrown inward turns back where the reading is its rest energy (961.2 for \(\gamma=2\) from 990, with \(L=1{,}000\)); light going inward inside \(L\) is read redder, so the energy change in free fall flips sign at \(L\). The outward motion these frames read is, in the far observer's radius, a motion in the complex dimension (Section 14, Part 6). [DERIVED on premises 3 and 7 and H2] The pull that these frames read points outward, for every real ruler they carry; on A's own clock the light that A sends outward never reaches C, A's causal boundary, and A's clock runs opposite to the far time; what the far observer works out for A's clock is \(\mp i\) times A's own reading (Section 14, Part 10). [DERIVED on premises 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7; the scale of the ruler on the ruler rule, adopted on 26 November 2026] A body let go at rest inside \(L\) comes out: it reaches \(L\) in a finite time of its own and leaves with the count \(e=\sqrt{L/r_0-1}\), for good if it was let go at \(L/2\) or deeper (Section 14, Part 6). [DERIVED on premises 3, 7 and 8, H2 and the ruler rule]
- A body falling in from outside. It passes \(L\) on its own clock at the speed \(c\,e\), slows inside \(L\), where the pull points outward, turns at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and comes back out with its count \(e\): nothing with \(e\gt0\) reaches the centre. Where it comes to rest the continued solution still has it moving inward, with \((dr/d\tau)^2=2c^2e^2\). On the far observer's clock time flips at \(L\) (\(dt/d\tau=e/F\) changes sign), so the inside part of its path runs back toward \(L\): the turn as the far observer sees it. Inside, the far observer's values for it, worked out through the clock rate \(f=\pm i\sqrt{L/r-1}\), come in two complex conjugate forms; that is why an event past the causal boundary has two solutions. With the rule that joins the two sides of \(L\), adopted on 26 November 2026, the far time itself gains \(\mp i\pi L/c\) inside, one sign for each root (Section 14, Parts 7 and 10). The light's values past \(L\) come in the same two forms, one for each half-turn of the far time with its root of the clock rate (Section 14, Part 10). [DERIVED on premises 3, 7 and 8, H2 and the ruler rule; the far time on the joining rule]
- Through intermediate frames. With \(L=1{,}000\), A at 200 and B at 900 inside and D at 1,100 outside, B reads A's photon at \(6E_0\), a real number, and what A works out for D's reading is \(\pm6.633\,i\,E_0\), two complex solutions, the same through any intermediate frames, because each one's clock rate cancels. A body moving outward at \(L\) climbs to \(L/(1-e^2)\), or goes away for good if \(e\ge1\); light sent at \(L\) by a source on its way out reaches an observer far away with the count \(2eE\). No frame is held at rest at the edge; events beyond it are calculated through intermediate frames (Section 14). [DERIVED on premises 7 and 8]
- What conservation adds: the mass an event horizon needs. The Schwarzschild solution leaves \(\mathcal M\) as a number to be measured. Conservation fixes it from the source: a shell of rest mass \(m_0\) held at \(R\) counts as \(\mathcal M=m_0-Gm_0^2/2c^2R\), so the horizon reaches the matter at \(m_0=c^2R/G\), twice \(c^2R/2G\), half of it cancelled by its own binding; light sent in adds \(2GE/c^4\) to \(L\) (Section 4, the physicist's box). [DERIVED]
- The frozen yardstick. The divergence at the horizon is one frame's reading, \(\gamma m_0c^2\), taken for the count; the body's entry in the count, \(\gamma f\,m_0c^2\), never changes (Section 4). [DERIVED]
- Why the error had to be fixed. With the static form carried inside, no frame at rest is left there, and the conserved \(e\) is a momentum along a spacelike direction, which no observer at rest exists to read; as this paper defines the account, a count kept by an observer (Section 2), the uncorrected inside keeps no count of mass-energy (Section 9). [DERIVED on the paper's definition of the account, a premise]

### The Error: the Premises of General Relativity the Fix Removes
(1) The static form carried inside the horizon. The form \(1-L/r\), derived outside, is continued to \(r\lt L\) by a change of coordinates (Section 7, parts 15 to 17), where the far observer's clock factor is imaginary and nothing has tested it. The inward fall of everything, the absence of a frame at rest and the one horizon for every frame follow from this one step and the extension's choice of the direction of time.

(2) No frame can be held at rest inside the event horizon. A consequence of (1): a frame at rest there would have a spacelike four-velocity. This paper keeps "rest frames with their local clock, ruler, and energy relations intact" (Section 1): what each reads is real for it, and between frames on the two sides of \(L\) the values worked out are premise 7's, with two complex solutions (Section 3; Section 14). Read by those frames, a free body at rest inside \(L\) cannot fall inward (Section 14, Part 6), and a body falling in from outside turns back at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and comes out, where the continued solution still has it moving inward (Section 14, Part 7), against general relativity's fall of everything inside to the centre.

(3) One event horizon for every frame, crossed one way only. One \(L=2G\mathcal M/c^2\), measured far away, is given to every frame, inside and out, and nothing crosses it outward. Here the causal boundary depends on the frame of reference: at \(L\) only a frame at rest needs the speed of light to escape; a frame in free motion with count \(e\le1\), falling in or on its way out, needs \(c\,(1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\) along its motion, and with \(e\ge1\) none; and objects move beyond their event horizon, by the same law in both directions (Section 3, premise 8; Section 14).

These three are the error, and the burden is on them. None of them is needed outside the horizon, where the solution was already right.

### Observations That Could Decide
Around one body at rest, outside the event horizon, the clocks and rulers of the fixed solution are those of the unfixed one to every figure (Section 9, statement 1), so the tests of the redshift made so far are passed by both; the orbits and the paths of light are not yet derived from Section 4. For several bodies, and when the count moves, the two part outside \(L\) as well (Section 6, statement 3). For one body at rest, what decides is the inside. Anything, light or matter, arriving outside from inside an event horizon: forbidden by premise (1), which makes the horizon one-way; in this paper objects can, and do, move beyond their event horizon, by the same law in both directions (premise 8; Section 14). A frame held at rest inside an event horizon, or any signal from one: forbidden by premise (2); this paper keeps such frames (premise 7). No observation has yet been made at or inside an event horizon; until one is, for one body at rest the two are separated only by the premise.

## For a child
We found a mistake in the black-hole formula and fixed it. The formula is right outside the black hole: it is the rule that the total in the jar never changes, with clocks that slow down deep in the pull. The mistake was pushing the formula across the edge in a way that makes everything fall to the middle, leaves nobody standing still inside, and gives everyone the same edge, which nothing can cross on the way out. Fixed, the formula says the same thing as the jar rule everywhere, outside and inside. What you measure with your own clock, ruler and scale is real. You cannot measure anything exactly on the edge, but you can work out what happens across it by passing the message through friends on each side, and then you always get two answers. Things can move beyond the edge, and they do, in both directions, and the edge depends on who is looking and how they move. Inside, people standing still see a stone at rest move only outward, and a stone that falls in slows down, stops and comes back out. Someone far away, following a stone that falls in, finds their clock running backwards past the edge. Nobody ever sees anything cross their own edge.

## For a high school physics teacher
Outside: \(f^2=1-L/r\) from conservation and the clock step, and \(\gamma f=e\) is the conserved count of a falling body. The error: carrying that form inside by a change of coordinates, which gives every frame one mass and one horizon and removes every frame at rest. The fix: keep the outside, and across \(L\) use premises 7 and 8; then the solution and conservation give identical results inside and outside. Between two frames at rest the factor is \(f_Q/f_P\), with \(f_Q^2/f_P^2=(1-L/r_Q)/(1-L/r_P)\): positive on one side of \(L\) and negative across it, so a reading converted across \(L\) has two solutions, \(\pm i\) times a real number. A free body obeys \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-|1-L/r|)\) on both sides of \(L\), in both directions: at \(L\) its speed on its own clock is \(ce\) and it gets there in a finite time of its own, while on the far observer's clock the passage has no finite time, and inside \(L\) that clock runs backward along the body's path (\(dt/d\tau=e/F\lt0\)). Frames held at rest inside read a free body at \(\gamma\propto1/\sqrt{L/r-1}\), so a body at rest there can only move outward, and a body falling in from outside turns at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and comes out. The test: anything arriving outside from inside an event horizon.

## For a theoretical physicist
Exterior: \(4\pi r^2fg=4\pi G\mathcal M_{\mathrm{enc}}\) (H1 for the force the far observer counts), \(g=c^2\,d\ln f/d\ell\) (H3), \(d\ell=dr/f\) (the ruler rule) give \(f^2=1-L/r\) with no field equation; \(\gamma f=e\). Source: \(d\mathcal M=f\,dm\) as the shell is built, \(\sqrt{1-L/R}=1-Gm_0/c^2R\), horizon at the matter for \(m_0=c^2R/G\). Across \(L\) (premises 7 and 8): \(E_P=(f_Q/f_P)E_Q\), with \(f_Q/f_P=\pm i\sqrt{(L/r_Q-1)/(1-L/r_P)}\) for \(r_Q\lt L\lt r_P\) and real on one side; through intermediate frames the factors multiply and the intermediate clock rates cancel (Section 14: \(\pm2\sqrt{11}\,iE_0\) for A at 200 and D at 1,100); \((dr/d\tau)^2=c^2(e^2-|F|)\) on both sides (outside, \(=c^2f^2(\gamma^2-1)\)), turns at \(L/(1+e^2)\) and, for \(e\lt1\), \(L/(1-e^2)\), \(|dr/d\tau|_L=ce\), \(\Delta\tau\) finite, \(dt/d\tau=e/F\), \(\Delta t\to\infty\) at \(L\) and \(dt/d\tau\lt0\) inside; the speed still needed at \(L\): \(c\) at rest, and \(c(1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\) for a free frame with \(e\le1\), falling in or on its way out; light sent at \(L\) on the way out: \(2eE\). Inside \(L\), read by frames held at rest (premises 3 and 7, H2): \(\gamma(r)=\gamma_0\sqrt{(L/r_0-1)/(L/r-1)}\). What the search looked for and did not find. A surface line of a neutron star above 20 percent whose ion is confirmed and whose mass and radius were measured without the line and without a model of the atmosphere or of the bursts. A measurement that separates gravity from motion for the disk lines or for S2.

What the list shows. Where the redshift is small and everything is measured, the calculation and the observation agree: Sirius B, to within the one percent of the measurement. Above 20 percent no observation is yet free of dispute. In the four that have a published mass and radius the line is redder than the calculation: 0.72 against 0.43, 0.65 against 0.50, 0.64 against 0.31 (there the line itself was among the inputs of the mass and radius), and 0.35 against 0.27.

## Appendix: The Full Audit of This Paper
This appendix holds the AI audit of this paper in full, so that a reader, or an AI asked to check the paper, can see how it was reviewed and check the review itself. It has five parts: how the audit was run; the prompt, word for word; the results, word for word; what was done with each finding; and the discussion with the auditor that followed, word for word. The auditor was Codex, OpenAI’s GPT-6.2-Astra model, at “ultra”, the highest of the reasoning levels it offers, working read-only. In the auditor’s replies, links to files on the author’s computer are reduced to their text; nothing else in them is changed.

### 1. How the audit was run
The audit was run on 26 November 2026, on draft v0.75 of this paper, the version before the corrections it led to. It was one run with no memory of earlier runs, in an empty working folder that held only the manuscript’s text copy, read-only and with web search off. Its message was the review prompt, word for word, followed by a run block with the author’s rules 7 to 9 for every reviewer (Part 2). The auditor read the whole manuscript, 12,028 lines, and returned its Parts I to III (Part 3): 4,274,737 input tokens (4,134,016 of them cached), 28,105 output tokens, 15.6 minutes. Every number in its Part II was recomputed independently, 37 values, and all agree.

The author’s instruction for the audit was: “Don’t make any of the changes it suggests. We’ll discuss them first.” Each finding was discussed with him, and then put in or not; Part 4 records what was done. Two findings needed more mathematics, and each went back to the auditor, at the same level of reasoning, as a check of its own (Part 5).

### 2. The prompt, word for word
The message of the audit run: the review prompt (“Gravity, Geometry and Conservation: Constructive Audit and Repair”, in its second version, with its Section 0 of standing rules), then the run block, into which the author’s rules 7 to 9 are copied from his rule file.

## The message of the audit run

```
# Gravity, Geometry and Conservation: Constructive Audit and Repair

## Assignment

Evaluate the supplied manuscript's proposed explanation of gravity through geometry, curvature and overlaps. Identify precise mathematical and physical errors, determine the conditions needed for a workable derivation, provisionally adopt consistent additional assumptions, and carry out the repairs. Then evaluate the resulting model's conservation of mass-energy and momentum and its relationship to general relativity under the manuscript's stated conditions.

You are authorized to produce corrected equations, a complete revised derivation and replacement manuscript passages. Preserve the original as a reference and identify every substantive change. Complete the repair work that the available information permits; do not stop at a list of suggestions.

Replacement passages are limited by Section 0. Propose replacement text only where you have demonstrated a mathematical error (arithmetic, sign, unit or scope, a formula used outside its domain, or a declared test that was not met), and keep the author's words everywhere else. Do not supply replacement text that restates the manuscript's thesis, premises or conclusions in weaker or different terms. A repaired branch that changes a premise is reported as a branch, never as replacement text for the manuscript.

A successful repair is a verifiable derivation from explicitly stated, jointly consistent premises. The desired conclusion is the question to investigate, not an assumption available to prove itself.

## 0. Standing Rules for This Manuscript

Read this section first. Where any later instruction in this prompt seems to allow something that this section rules out, this section governs.

**Your job.** The author asks every reviewer to test general relativity, not to defend it. The premise under attack is the step by which general relativity merges the different values that frames of reference read into one event horizon: one metric for all observers, continued across the event horizon with the same mass. For every result, find the premise of general relativity that it touches and test that premise by mathematics or by a raw observation. Agreement with general relativity is never a result. Where the manuscript and general relativity disagree, the burden is on general relativity's premise: name the premise, and name the observation that could decide.

**No watering down.** Do not write a result as weaker than its mathematics shows. Do not call a result "not derived", "not shown", "unsupported" or "open" when the manuscript derives it: find the place where it is derived first. Do not add a caveat, a softer word or a "but" that no calculation requires. Do not move the burden from general relativity's premise onto the manuscript. Do not leave a derived result out. Legitimate mathematical corrections are welcome: an arithmetic, sign, unit or scope error, a formula used outside its domain, or a test that the manuscript declared in advance and did not meet.

**The manuscript's definitions govern.**

- Conservation of mass-energy means that an observer's complete count of everything inside a closed surface, each kind of energy counted once in that observer's units, does not change (Section 2).
- The premises of Section 3 are the author's, stated with their arguments from the conservation laws. Premises 7 and 8 state what holds at and beyond the event horizon. They are the manuscript's premises; do not replace them by general relativity's continuation.
- The author's terms stay. Where a term differs from standard usage (for example "the curvature between two points is the integral of f dot dr"), propose a one-line definition, never a replacement.
- The author's bold statements are his words. Do not remove, narrow or reinterpret them. If a premise has a mathematical consequence that looks unphysical, state the consequence exactly and leave the decision to the author.
- The first paper ("Why Is It Impossible to Escape from a Black Hole?") is not a source. Passages that still rest on it are flagged in the manuscript by working notes. You may show where they conflict with the premises; they are not the manuscript's position.

**Do not do the following.** Each was done by an earlier run of this prompt, and each would have weakened the paper.

1. Do not use general relativity's causal structure inside the event horizon (its light cones; "every future-directed path has decreasing r") to deny that objects move beyond their event horizon. That structure belongs to the continuation under attack. Premise 8 states what holds there, and Section 3 derives the passage: the speed c·e at L, reached in a finite time of the body's own.
2. Do not judge the manuscript's conservation claims by general relativity's standards (the conservation of a particle's symmetry charge, ∇·T = 0) and conclude that the manuscript "does not prove" that general relativity violates conservation. Use the manuscript's definition (Section 2). Report general relativity's standards on the comparison side, labelled.
3. Do not recast the manuscript's thesis as "adopted postulates", and do not write replacement text for its summaries of what it derives. You may name an import (special relativity at one place, Planck's relation, Newton's law far away), as the manuscript itself does in Section 4.
4. Do not cut or narrow a premise by reading it as a claim about a different quantity, for example premise 4 read as a claim about light exchanged between two distant events. Premise 4 concerns a frame's own clock, rulers and mass; Section 4 derives it (statements 3 and 4).
5. Do not repair the manuscript with relations of general relativity: its interior ruler 1 − 2Gm(r)/(c²r), the lapse of its constant-density interior, geodesic motion. They are imports. With the interior ruler, for example, the 73.2 percent limit of Section 17 would become general relativity's 200 percent. If you find a real problem in a premise (for example, premise 5 continued to the centre of a body makes the centre a conical point), report it as a finding, and derive repairs from the manuscript's own premises only. A repair taken from general relativity, if you give one, is labelled as the comparison and is never offered as replacement text.
6. Do not present a law of motion, for example the Hamiltonian of a static metric (straightest-path motion, Einstein's assumption A6), as a derived result of the manuscript. Label it as an import.
7. Do not state as a general rule that a change of reference frame "does not relocate a causal boundary". For frames at rest the boundary is the one circle L (Section 3). The manuscript's frame-dependence of the causal boundary concerns frames in motion (Section 9, statement 3).
8. Do not write a verdict on whether general relativity is correct in general. State what the manuscript's derivations establish on its own definitions and premises, and what the comparison with general relativity shows, each at its demonstrated strength.

**Objections that do not count, with the place in the manuscript that answers each.** An objection of one of these kinds is not a finding.

1. The result agrees with general relativity, so general relativity is confirmed. Agreement is never a result. Section 6 names where the two derivations part.
2. A change must move at the speed of light. That is general relativity's premise. Premise 6 states the opposite, and Section 3 gives its mathematics.
3. An event horizon is the same surface for every frame and is crossed one way only. That is the step under attack. Premises 7 and 8 (Section 3) stand in its place.
4. No frame can be held at rest below L, so nothing can be computed there. That is general relativity's premise about its own inside. An objection counts only if a step of the manuscript's mathematics is shown wrong.
5. The premises do not follow from the conservation laws alone. The premises are stated as premises in Section 3. An objection counts only where a step uses something that is in neither Section 2 nor Section 3 nor the derivation's own list of what it uses.
6. The sum over point masses cannot be exact because Einstein's equations are not linear. Einstein's equations are on the comparison side. Section 4, statement 7, derives the sum from premises 1, 3 and 5 in the frame of the calculation.
7. Inside the event horizon every future-directed path moves inward, so an outward solution is no escape. That is general relativity's continued causal structure, the step under attack (item 3). Section 3 derives the passage under premise 8.
8. General relativity conserves its symmetry charge and ∇·T = 0, so the manuscript shows no violation of conservation. Those are general relativity's standards. On the manuscript's definition (Section 2), general relativity's continuation inside the event horizon keeps no count of mass-energy: no observer at rest is left there, and the conserved e is a momentum (Section 9, statement 3).
9. A change of the reference clock does not move the zero of f, so causal boundaries do not depend on the frame. For frames at rest the zero is the circle L, as Section 3 states. The frame-dependence concerns frames in motion (Section 9, statement 3).
10. The interior of a body should be made regular with general relativity's interior ruler. That is an import, and it removes the manuscript's result of Section 17.

## 1. Fix the Question, Physical System and Original Premises

State the precise question being investigated and the result the author intends to establish. Preserve the distinction between:

- Deriving the proposed gravitational interaction from the manuscript's ideas.
- Establishing whether that interaction conserves mass-energy and momentum.
- Establishing agreement or disagreement with GR.
- Establishing whether a particular GR prediction violates a specified conservation law.

Identify which statements are definitions, physical postulates, supplied observations, derived results or proposed conclusions. Accept declared postulates provisionally for the internal mathematical investigation; assess their empirical support separately.

Do not silently change the thought experiment, replace an observer, introduce a different boundary, or substitute an easier physical question. If a repair requires changing a physical premise, identify that change explicitly and treat the repaired model as a distinct branch of the original investigation.

## 2. Track the Origin of Every Material Assumption

Give each material premise or added rule an identifier and classify it:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Definition | A quantity or convention explicitly defined in the manuscript. |
| Manuscript premise | A physical assumption explicitly adopted by the manuscript. |
| Mathematical result | A theorem or identity whose hypotheses have been checked. |
| Derived result | A consequence established from identified earlier premises. |
| Provisional addition | A new assumption introduced to complete or repair the model. |
| Empirical input | A measurement, calibration or observational constraint actually supplied or sourced. |
| Comparison assumption | A premise used only to calculate the predictions of GR or another comparison theory. |

Every substantive step must have a traceable origin. Use citations or equation references for supplied material and external results. Do not invent unavailable source content or numerical inputs.

Maintain a compact dependency list. An assumption introduced during a repair must remain identifiable in every result that depends on it; it must not later be described as a result derived from the original manuscript alone.

## 3. Do Not Inherit Requirements from Quantum Mechanics

**No quantum-mechanical requirement may constrain the independent derivation merely because the manuscript uses waves, amplitudes, probabilities, particles or overlaps. A requirement must be explicitly present in the manuscript's stated premises or follow by a demonstrated derivation from those premises.**

In particular, do not automatically impose:

- The Schrödinger equation, Klein–Gordon equation or other conventional quantum dynamics.
- The Born rule or standard measurement and collapse postulates.
- A Hilbert-space interpretation, operator-observable correspondence or canonical commutation relations.
- Unitary evolution, quantum superposition or standard uncertainty relations.
- Quantization, tensor-product composition or conventional quantum-field assumptions.

For each proposed requirement associated with quantum mechanics, identify the exact manuscript premise that supplies it or derive it from the paper's ideas. If neither is possible, it is not an admissible requirement of this independent derivation. A rule explicitly stated by the manuscript remains a premise unless it is independently derived.

The permission to add provisional assumptions is not permission to import quantum mechanics under another name. Any proposed dynamics, probability rule or coupling must have an explicit motivation in the manuscript's mechanism and must be labeled as an addition when the manuscript does not supply it. For each addition, check that its justification and imposed constraints do not depend on accepting quantum mechanics. Resemblance or mathematical equivalence to a conventional quantum equation neither justifies nor disqualifies it; justify it from the manuscript's mechanism and explicitly declared independent assumptions.

Ordinary mathematics still applies to the structures actually defined. For example, a quantity defined as a normalized probability density must satisfy its stated nonnegativity and normalization conditions relative to its specified measure. These follow from that definition, not from an automatic adoption of the Born rule. Mathematical tools may be used when their hypotheses hold, without importing their usual physical interpretation. If supplied observations are part of the target, compare with those observations without treating their conventional quantum interpretation as an additional axiom.

Apply the same separation to GR: do not import the Einstein field equations, Einstein–Hilbert action, Schwarzschild metric or conventional matter model into the independent derivation unless the manuscript explicitly supplies them. They may be used in the separately identified GR comparison. Using GR to calculate its own predictions does not establish those premises for the independent model.

A provisional addition that reproduces a relation of general relativity, such as the interior ruler 1 − 2Gm(r)/(c²r), the lapse of its constant-density interior, geodesic or straightest-path motion, or the causal cones of its continued metric, is an import of general relativity. Label it so, never call it a repair of the manuscript, and state which of the manuscript's results it would change.

Before extensive calculations, give a finite sequence of stages leading from the available premises to the requested result. For each stage state:

2. The equation, operation or construction to perform.
3. The result that would complete the stage.
4. The check needed to verify it.

Perform the immediate consistency checks available before calculation, then establish further consistency through construction and verification of the solution. Check the repaired equations by substitution into the retained system. Verify relevant dimensions, signs, boundary conditions, domains, limiting behavior and conservation balances. Where the claim requires an admissible solution, provide at least one nontrivial solution or an adequate existence argument; a formal conditional statement with no admissible realization is not a constructed physical model.

Use independent symbolic or numerical checks when they resolve a concrete mathematical risk. Distinguish exact derivations from approximation results and numerical evidence. State the regime and errors of an approximation where they affect the verdict.

1. **Scope and finite plan:** the original question, fixed physical system and calculation route.
2. **Exact error register:** every material error or missing specification, with its demonstration and correction.
3. **Conditions and assumptions:** necessary conditions, sufficient sets, selected additions, their provenance and their empirical status. State material limitations here once.
4. **Completed repaired derivation:** explicit equations, essential intermediate steps and replacement passages, with additions identified by their assumption labels.
5. **Verification:** substitution checks, an admissible worked solution or existence result where needed, and the calculated conservation balances.
6. **GR comparison:** the matched predictions and every established agreement, discrepancy or conservation violation, with its responsible equation.
7. **Final verdict:** what the original manuscript establishes, what the repaired model establishes, and what the calculation establishes about GR.

Use the strongest wording justified by the mathematics. If a result is proved, say so. If its proof uses named additional assumptions, state them as part of the theorem. If a conservation violation is established, explain precisely what fails and by how much. If only incompatibility with an added premise is established, state that incompatibility explicitly. Conditions essential to the theorem's truth belong in its statement; unrelated or repeated caveats do not.

State the verdict about general relativity in the terms of the manuscript's own definitions and premises. Where general relativity's own standards give a different reading, report both, each labelled. Do not say that the manuscript "does not prove" a claim that it derives on its stated definitions; name the definition instead. Do not weaken a valid result because it challenges an established theory. Do not strengthen a result beyond what was demonstrated because it matches the author's intended conclusion.

**Stopping rule:** Once the specified calculations and checks establish the verdict, state it precisely and terminate. Do not append speculative reconciliations, alternative thought experiments, new proof obligations, repeated qualifications or recommendations for further research.

---

**Governing instruction:** Identify the exact error; determine what must be true or what consistent completion can be chosen; state and provisionally adopt those assumptions; repair and complete the derivation; verify the result; and report exactly what it establishes. Quantum mechanics supplies no automatic requirements, and every substantive addition must remain visible.

**DERIVED on C, P1–P5 and I.** Use the positive outward holding acceleration \(g\). Local work on the body’s current energy gives \(dm/m=\mathbf g_{\rm pull}\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell/c^2\). The cancellation in P3 therefore gives
\[
\frac{m_B}{m_A}=\frac{f_A}{f_B},\qquad
d\ln f=\frac{g\,d\ell}{c^2},\qquad f\gamma=e .
\]
Counting a held probe gives \(dE_\infty=mc^2\,df=mf g\,d\ell\). The counted holding force is defined per unit of **local** displacement. Spherical symmetry and the areal-radius definition give
\[
4\pi r^2 f g=4\pi G\mathcal M,\qquad
d\ell=\frac{dr}{f},\qquad
fg=c^2 f\frac{df}{dr}=\frac{c^2}{2}F'(r).
\]
Integrate with \(F(\infty)=1\):
\[
\boxed{F=f^2=1-\frac Lr,\qquad L=\frac{2G\mathcal M}{c^2}.}
\]
The inverse square comes from the area and the flux law. Its attractive sign comes from the inward pull opposite the holding force. \(G\) is calibrated far away. The far-counted pull per unit rest mass is \(G\mathcal M/r^2\); the exterior held frame measures \(G\mathcal M/(r^2f)\). It weighs the source at \(\mathcal M/f\).

For the freely falling frame released from rest far away, \(e=1\), so its relative \(\gamma=1/f\). P4 and local SR give the §4 comparison of the held clock and longitudinal ruler; transverse rulers retain the stated scale. A common transition and \(E=h\nu\) give \(\nu_\infty=f\nu_{\rm own}\). In a static arrangement successive crests traverse the same path. For emission at \(a\) and reception at \(b\),
\[
\frac{\nu_b}{\nu_a}=\frac{E_b}{E_a}=\frac{f_a}{f_b},
\qquad 1+z=\frac{f_b}{f_a}.
\]
This checks the clock, ruler, frequency, photon energy and massive-body entry separately. The exact cancellation can be seen directly:
\[
K_\infty=f(\gamma-1)mc^2=(e-f)mc^2,\qquad
U_\infty=(f-1)mc^2,\qquad
mc^2+K_\infty+U_\infty=e\,mc^2 .
\]
In the weak, slow regime,
\[
e=1+\frac{v^2}{2c^2}-\frac{G\mathcal M}{rc^2}
+O\!\left((v^2/c^2+L/r)^2\right).

Multiplication by \(mc^2\) gives the energy expansion needed in §13. Section 4 derivation

# Part II. The inward body, the light and A’s time

## A. Worked example for §14 — a body falling in

**Premises of the step that tests the author’s hint.** P3 supplies \(e=\gamma f\). P8 supplies a real increasing body time \(\tau\), the radial law in both directions, the far-time passage integral and the specified inward initial direction. P7 supplies the two roots for a held-frame comparison. §4 supplies \(F=1-L/r\) and the reciprocal radial ruler. No GR interior law enters. **HINT, 26 November, C2:** “What happens is that once it hits the causal boundary, time flips. It also move in the complex dimension. This is REALLY important because it explains why there are two solutions.”

**1. DERIVED on P8 — the body’s own clock.** Put \(q(r)=\sqrt{e^2-F(r)}\), \(e>0\). Keeping the sign selected by an inward initial velocity gives
\[
\dot r\equiv\frac{dr}{d\tau}=-cq,\qquad
\dot r(L)=-ce,\qquad
\ddot r=-\frac{c^2}{2}F'(r)=-\frac{c^2L}{2r^2}.
\]
Near \(\tau_L\), \(r=L-ce(\tau-\tau_L)+O((\tau-\tau_L)^2)\). The body crosses \(L\). At every \(0<r<L\), \(q^2=e^2+(L/r-1)>e^2\). An inward body continues inward with increasing \(|dr/d\tau|\). A differentiable reversal requires \(\dot r=0\). The only positive solution of that equation is
\[
r_{\rm turn}=\frac{L}{1-e^2}>L,\qquad 0<e<1.
\]
It is the **outer** turning point reached by an initially outgoing body. Switching the inward root to the outward root at \(L\) would change \(\dot r\) by \(2ce\) instantaneously, in conflict with the finite \(\ddot r\) above. Thus the body falling in does not turn back on its own clock. Premise 8 gives both directions of passage; initial conditions distinguish their trajectories.

For \(e=0.5\) an explicit proper-time primitive is available. Set \(k=1-e^2\), \(r=(L/k)\sin^2\theta\). Then
\[
c\int\frac{dr}{q}
=\frac{L}{k^{3/2}}(\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta).
\]
For \(L=1000\), the inward intervals \(c\Delta\tau\) are \(223.3013\) from D to C, \(676.2692\) from C to 500, and \(883.0485\) from C to A. The mathematical limit from C to \(r=0\) is \(945.5994\). At zero radius the equation itself is singular. The calculation gives no outgoing continuation from that endpoint.

**2. DERIVED on P3, P8 and §4 — the far clock and ruler.** In the exterior \(d\tau=f\,dt/\gamma\), giving \(dt/d\tau=e/F\). The signed form of the manuscript’s passage integral gives, on the two open radial intervals,
\[
\frac{dt}{d\tau}=\frac eF,\qquad
\frac{c\,dt}{dr}=-\frac e{Fq},\qquad
\frac1c\frac{dr}{dt}=-\frac{Fq}{e}.
\]
Near \(L\), \(F=(r-L)/L+O((r-L)^2/L^2)\), \(q\to e\). Consequently
\[
ct=-L\ln\left|\frac{r-L}{L}\right|+O(1).
\]
For inward passage, \(t\to+\infty\) on approach to \(L\) from either side, with separately selectable finite integration constants. Outside, \(dt/d\tau>0\); inside, its inferred value is negative. **This is the time derivative that flips.** The body’s own \(\tau\) continues forward. The far signed \(dr/dt\) is negative outside and positive inside, even though \(dr/d\tau\) is negative throughout. No finite tick of the far clock records the body turning and coming back out.

e_A(e)^2=\frac{F}{F_A}+J(r)^2(e^2-F).
\]
Subtract the equations for two distinct incoming counts. Their difference forces \(J^2\) to be constant in \(r\). Differentiate either equation where \(F'\ne0\): it then requires \(J^2=1/F_A=-1/4\). **No real universal radial calibration realizes those identifications.** The decision left to the author is which additional relation would connect a native interior reading to an incoming body’s far count. P8 already decides the areal trajectory, and P7 already decides the two inferred phases.

**5. DERIVED on P8 and local SR — outward check.** The outgoing solution reaches \(L\) with \(+ce\). For \(e<1\) it reaches the outer turning point above; for \(e\ge1\) it escapes. The relative outward boost to marginal escape follows by comparing \(\beta_e=\sqrt{1-F/e^2}\) with \(\beta_1=\sqrt{1-F}\) from the exterior. The limit of \((\beta_1-\beta_e)/(1-\beta_1\beta_e)\) is \((1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\). For the incoming body the corresponding relative escape speed tends to \(c\). For a held frame it also tends to \(c\).

The manuscript gives the circumferences and clock ratios. A circumference difference does not measure the radial distance between the spheres on A’s native grid. At B this gives \(5517.7662\,\kappa\). At \(990,999,999.9,999.99\) it gives \(14368.1065\,\kappa,\ 23542.4469\,\kappa,\ 32749.1873\,\kappa,\ 41959.1677\,\kappa\). The conclusion about this interval holds also for a positive continuous \(J\) with a finite nonzero limit at C. Its coefficient and its finite times depend on the calibration.

There is a physical reason to keep this example out of the manuscript as a universal clock-and-ruler repair. If one also reuses the same real areal spheres and the original flux prescription with \(h^2=F/F_A\), the inferred native outward holding law is \(r^2 h g_{\rm hold}=G\mathcal M/(F_A J)\), negative for positive \(J\). **5. DERIVED — joining the two sides and the state at C.** Even on the far grid, integrating the clock gives two constants,
\[
ct_{\rm in}=\sigma H+C_{\rm in},\qquad
ct_{\rm out}=\sigma H+C_{\rm out}.

Rate ratios cannot determine \(C_{\rm out}-C_{\rm in}\). Equal offsets in radius give \(H(L+\delta)-H(L-\delta)=2\delta\). Unequal offsets \(a,b>0\) give

As the offsets shrink this finite part depends on their ratio. Neither limit is an elapsed crossing time; each one-sided travel integral to C diverges. Even on one side a change of remote synchronization \(T_A\mapsto T_A+\chi(r)\), \(\chi(200)=0\), preserves A’s actual clock and all fixed-station rate ratios.

**Answer about every A-time and the edge.** On the calibrated emitted inner leg just calculated, every finite time after emission has a state, and C occurs at no finite time. In v0.75, A’s own clock ticks are real, the exterior interval assigned through P7 has the two values calculated above, and no rest clock exists at C. The premises supply **no unique real all-times map** \(T_A\mapsto\) photon state covering both legs, no prescribed match of their offsets, and no native A timestamp at the edge. **Verdict: ADDED RULE.** The passage integrals determine the coefficient \(\pi L/c\) exactly. Premises 7 and 8 leave freedom in how the interior far time is joined to the exterior far time.

**The rule, in one sentence.** Fix the exterior time origin and the positive exterior clock root, then continue the far-time integral and the clock root along the same upper or lower half-turn about \(r=L\), with no additional winding.

This rule replaces the two independent constants of Part II, B.5 with one exterior constant and a determined interior offset on each branch. For \(L=1000\), the imaginary offset has magnitude \(3141.592654/c\) for both matter and light. The sign depends on the contour **and** on which passage integral is being continued.

The only new physical rule used below is the proposed matching rule. The contour integration itself is mathematics. No GR interior law enters.

### 1. The continuation and its real part

**DERIVED on the two passage integrals.** Write \(z=r-L\). Fix the orientation **from exterior to interior**, from \(z=b>0\) to \(z=-a<0\). Let \(s=+1\) denote the upper detour and \(s=-1\) the lower. For matter take the branch with \(q(L)=e>0\).

Both integrands have a simple pole. Their regular parts can be isolated exactly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
-\frac{e}{Fq}
&=-\frac1F-\frac1{q(e+q)}
=-\frac{L}{z}-1-\frac1{q(e+q)},\\[2mm]
\frac{\sigma}{F}
&=\frac{\sigma L}{z}+\sigma .
\end{aligned}
\]
The first identity follows from \((e-q)(e+q)=F\). Thus, writing \(c\,dt/dr=R/z+h(z)\), the residues are \(R=-L\) for the inward body and \(R=\sigma L\) for light. In each case \(h\) is analytic near the detour and real on the real radius. The matter detour stays clear of any zero of \(q\).

A continuous logarithm changes by \(\ln(a/b)+s i\pi\). The regular part has a primitive through zero. Consequently the **exact endpoint difference** is
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
c\Delta t
=R\bigl[\ln(a/b)+s i\pi\bigr]+\int_b^{-a}h(z)\,dz .}
\]
The last integral can be taken on the real interval because its integrand is regular there.

- **Fixed endpoints.** Deforming the detour without changing its winding or crossing another singularity leaves the entire answer unchanged.
- **Equal offsets \(a=b=\rho\).** The imaginary contribution is exactly \(s i\pi R\) for every admissible \(\rho\). The real contribution depends on \(\rho\) and tends to zero. For light it is exactly \(-2\sigma\rho\). For the body \(h(0)=-1-1/(2e^2)\), so at \(e=0.5\) the leading real term is \(6\rho\).
- **Unequal offsets.** As \(a,b\to0\) with \(a/b\to k>0\), the real difference tends to \(R\ln k\). For light the exact real difference is \(\sigma[L\ln(a/b)-a-b]\). Thus the rule matches the *regular parts* at C. It preserves the logarithmic difference between unequal endpoints.

Direct integration on the semicircles gives the following values. The final column is the coefficient of \(i\).

| Exterior-to-interior arc, \(L=1000\) | \(\rho\) | \(\operatorname{Re}(c\Delta t)\) | \(\operatorname{Im}(c\Delta t)\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Inward body, \(e=0.5\) | 1 | \(6.00000933337\) | \(-s\,3141.592654\) |
| Inward body, \(e=0.5\) | 0.01 | \(0.0600000000093\) | \(-s\,3141.592654\) |
| Light, \(\sigma=+1\) | 1 | \(-2\) | \(+s\,3141.592654\) |
| Light, \(\sigma=+1\) | 0.01 | \(-0.02\) | \(+s\,3141.592654\) |

The reported \(6\) and \(0.06\) are rounded matter values. The reported light values are exact. Traversing the same arc in reverse negates the entire increment.

### 2. Why the matching is an added rule

**DERIVED on P7 and P8.** Choose a real regular primitive \(U\) with \(U'=h\) and \(U(0)=0\). On each open real interval the time equation integrates to
\[
ct=R\ln\left|\frac{r-L}{L}\right|+U(r-L)+C_{\rm side}.
\]
Changing \(C_{\rm in}\) leaves every P7 clock ratio, every P8 differential equation and the infinite far-clock time at C unchanged. That freedom is the exact step the existing premises leave open.

**DERIVED on the ADDED RULE.** Continuing the exterior primitive fixes
\[
\boxed{C_{\rm in}-C_{\rm out}=s i\pi R.}
\]
Its real part is zero in the common normalization above. Each one-sided time integral to C still diverges. The finite complex endpoint difference assigns a relation between the branches while preserving P8’s result that the far clock records no finite crossing time.

### 3. How the two contours correspond to P7’s two roots

**DERIVED on P7 and the common-contour rule.** Near C, \(F=z/(L+z)\). The denominator has an analytic logarithm there and is positive at the real endpoints. Starting with \(f>0\) outside therefore gives, inside,
\[
\log F=\ln|F|+s i\pi,\qquad
f=\exp\!\left(\tfrac12\log F\right)=s i\sqrt{|F|}.
\]

| Exterior-to-interior route | Interior \(f\) | Imaginary term in \(ct\), inward body | Imaginary term in \(ct\), light |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upper | \(+i\sqrt{|F|}\) | \(-i\pi L\) | \(+\sigma i\pi L\) |
| Lower | \(-i\sqrt{|F|}\) | \(+i\pi L\) | \(-\sigma i\pi L\) |

**On the two prescribed detours there is a one-to-one correspondence.** For the inward body the upper route gives a positive imaginary clock root and a *negative* imaginary time offset. For light with \(\sigma=+1\) both imaginary signs are positive on the upper route. Changing the direction of propagation changes the residue’s sign. Choosing the other clock root leaves the direction of propagation unchanged.

P7 alone cannot recover the contour choice with its winding information. For a path with argument change \((2n+1)\pi\), the interior root is \(i(-1)^n\sqrt{|F|}\), whereas the time offset is \(i(2n+1)\pi R/c\). Arguments \(\pi\) and \(5\pi\), for example, produce the same clock root and different times. This is why “no additional winding” matters in the rule.

### 5.3 The energy half of the second central claim
A fresh review of draft v0.79 found that the paper had not shown a step of general relativity’s derivations that leaves the store \(U\) of Section 1’s machine out. The author chose to have the auditor derive the missing step, with his review prompt, which asks the auditor to identify and then fix gaps (Part 2, word for word), and this run block. Run: 2,557,942 input tokens (2,445,312 of them cached), 19,138 output tokens, 9.4 minutes. The auditor found the first clause of the author’s sentence, that the extension breaks enclosed energy conservation, carried in the sense of Section 2: inside \(L\) the continuation leaves no frame held at rest to keep the count. It found no closed experiment whose two complete counts differ. An independent Claude check, with the author’s integrity-audit prompt, agreed on all 23 items. The author then pointed to the general rule that closes the gap, on 26 November 2026: “We've already explained how to close the gap in (b). It's the bridge that shows how to equate the redshift and change of clock/ruler/scale between frames of different frames of reference in a field that requires a net f dot dr and the f dot dr that is required to move between two frames of reference with no field, but either relative motion or acceleration. The bridge is f dot dr and the energy required to go from one frame of reference to another.” The repair is in Section 9, statement 3 (“The bridge, and the loophole it closes”), and a targeted review of it, with the same prompt, follows.

### 1. One closed charged-particle cycle, counted twice

The exterior observer \(A\) uses the manuscript’s far-normalized energy units. For a finite held reference \(A\), replace every exterior \(f_i\) in a conversion by \(f_i/f_A\).

\[
Q=mc^2+H+U=mc^2+H+K,\qquad K=U.

The electrostatic configuration and its field are two ways of calculating the same \(U\).

**Manuscript count — DERIVED, C and P1–P5.** At a held station the transported entry is \(fQ\). The local holding force on the compact load is \(Qg_{\rm hold}/c^2\). Converting the incremental work into far units at the place where it is done gives
\[
dW_A=f\,\frac{Q}{c^2}g_{\rm hold}\,d\ell
     =fQ\,d\ln f=Q\,df .

Thus \(W_{\rm up}=Q(f_2-f_1)\). The conversion \(U\to K\) at the top changes the two far entries by \(-f_2U\) and \(+f_2K\), which sum to zero.

On the descent the load’s centre of mass starts at rest at station 2. P3 gives \(\gamma_{\rm bulk,1}f_1=f_2\) just before braking at station 1. The **bulk** kinetic energy delivered to the brake, in \(A\)’s units, is therefore

This is separate from the **internal** \(K\) that restores the charge configuration at the bottom. The bottom reset changes the internal entries by \(-f_1K+f_1U=0\). The internal work store has delivered and recovered the same independently calculated work. §4, clock, work and free-body count

Compare two orientations at the same separation, with a station at distance \(D>a\) on the calculation grid. The pair’s contributions give

## Part II. The repairs and derivations

### 1. What the general bridge charges

Let \(E_{\mathrm h}\) be an energy read by a held frame, and let \(f\) convert it to \(A_\infty\)’s energy units. For a free massive body, §4 gives
\[
E_{\mathrm h}=\gamma m_0c^2,\qquad
E_\infty=fE_{\mathrm h},\qquad
e=f\gamma.
\]
Between two held stations in the domain of this real conversion,
\[
I_g=\int_1^2\frac{\mathbf g\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{c^2}
=\ln\frac{\gamma_2}{\gamma_1}
=\ln\frac{f_1}{f_2}.
\]
Here \(d\boldsymbol\ell\) is measured on the encountered station’s ruler and \(\mathbf g\) denotes the pull in the work integral. In the field-free acceleration calculation, let the force, displacement and \(m=\gamma m_0\) all be evaluated in the specified field-free inertial account. Then
\[
I_F=\int_1^2\frac{\mathbf F\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell}{mc^2}
=\int_1^2\frac{d(mc^2)}{mc^2}
=\ln\frac{\gamma_2}{\gamma_1}.
\]
This proves the bridge for matched energy ratios. Both integrals are **dimensionless**. In the field-free account the energy actually supplied is \(m_0c^2(\gamma_2-\gamma_1)\). The displacement in that work calculation is measured in the frame in which the force generates the motion. Switching the observer of an already moving body supplies no such displacement or work history.

The exact scale accounting, valid also for a nonconstant local store, is
\[
\boxed{dE_\infty=f\,dE_{\mathrm h}+E_{\mathrm h}\,df},
\qquad
\Delta E_\infty
=f_2(E_{\mathrm h,2}-E_{\mathrm h,1})
 +E_{\mathrm h,1}(f_2-f_1).
\]
For the free body the terms cancel at every step. In §2’s kinetic and potential entries the cancellation reads
\[
\Delta\!\left[f(\gamma-1)m_0c^2\right]
 +m_0c^2\Delta f
=m_0c^2\Delta(f\gamma)=0 .
\]
Both terms are in \(A_\infty\)’s units. This verifies the balance for that trade without counting the potential release twice. The same calculation on one interior side uses a fixed interior reference station \(a\), \(h=k/k_a\), and gives \(\Delta(h\gamma)=0\) in that station’s units.

If a ledger **does** substitute a fixed \(f_*\) for the changing scale of a free body, the unbalanced change it records is
\[
\Delta E_{\mathrm{frozen}}
=f_*m_0c^2(\gamma_2-\gamma_1).
\]
It is positive when \(\gamma_2>\gamma_1\). Conversely, assigning a scale change to a locally fixed entry \(E_{\mathrm h}\) changes the reference ledger by \(E_{\mathrm h}\Delta f\). Calling this a physical surplus requires the specified ledger to acquire that entry without the corresponding transfer. Section 1 supplies exactly this test for the store \(U\). With \(\Delta f=f_2-f_1>0\), the far-account work returned less work supplied is
\[
(mc^2+K)\Delta f-(mc^2+U)\Delta f
=(K-U)\Delta f=0.
\]
Omitting \(U\) on ascent gives the stated spurious \(+U\Delta f\). This is an actual computation of the omitted term and its sign.

**The exact failed inference in §9.3** is the move from “no frame held at rest” to “nothing in it charges a body or an energy” if the latter is asserted of all transfers. In the frozen-scale calculation, \(f_*\), \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) are defined readings. In GR’s interior held-frame test, the proposed observer fails normalization. Consequently the corresponding \(E_{\mathrm h}\,df\) is undefined. Setting that term equal to zero, retaining a nonzero gain, and attributing the difference to GR would introduce a new accounting law. The general bridge takes the derivation as far as this exact result: **the continuation removes the observer needed to implement the compensating scale update, so it fails the manuscript’s held-frame count inside \(L\).**

### 2. The release, the clock and the match at \(L\)

For \(0<r_0<L\), an interior held frame reads the released body at
\[
\gamma(r)=\frac{k_0}{k(r)},\qquad k_0^2=\frac L{r_0}-1.
\]
Since \(k\) increases inward, an inward step would give \(\gamma<1\). On the allowed side, let \(v_{\mathrm h}=d\ell/dt_{\mathrm h}\) be the local radial speed as the body passes a held frame. Local special relativity gives \(dt_{\mathrm h}/d\tau=\gamma\) and hence
\[
\frac1{c^2}\left(\frac{d\ell}{d\tau}\right)^2
=\frac{\gamma^2v_{\mathrm h}^2}{c^2}=\gamma^2-1 .
\]
Using the real held ruler \(dr=k\,d\ell\) gives
\[
\boxed{\dot r^2=c^2 k^2(\gamma^2-1)
=c^2(k_0^2-k^2)
=c^2L\,\frac{r-r_0}{r r_0}},\qquad \dot r=\frac{dr}{d\tau}.
\]
Section 14.10 supplies the outward pull at release. In local ruler units its magnitude is
\[
-c^2\frac{d\ln(k/k_0)}{d\ell}\bigg|_{r_0}
=\frac{c^2L}{2r_0^2 k_0}>0.
\]
On the departing solution, differentiating the radial equation gives \(\ddot r=c^2L/(2r^2)\). Its release value is exactly \(k_0\) times the local acceleration, as \(dr=k\,d\ell\) requires at rest. This supplies the direction and start of motion using the manuscript’s own pull.

The outward proper-time integral has the explicit value
\[
\begin{aligned}
c[\tau(r)-\tau(r_0)]
&=\sqrt{\frac{r_0}{L}}\int_{r_0}^{r}\sqrt{\frac{x}{x-r_0}}\,dx\\
&=\sqrt{\frac{r_0}{L}}\left[
\sqrt{r(r-r_0)}
+r_0\,\operatorname{arcosh}\sqrt{\frac r{r_0}}\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Differentiation recovers the integrand, and the expression vanishes at release. The initial inverse-square-root singularity is integrable. At \(L\), \(k=0\), and the outward limit is \(\dot r=ck_0\).

The junction uses the meaning of **at \(L\)** in premise 8. The interior solution has a left derivative \(ck_0\) there. Premise 8 assigns the body’s speed at that same circle, on that same clock, the value \(c e_{\mathrm{out}}\) on departure. A derivative at the crossing must agree with its one-sided derivative. For the positive exterior count,
\[
\boxed{e_{\mathrm{out}}=k_0.}
\]
This identifies the precise condition that makes the proof work. Two curves can meet continuously at \(L\) with unequal slopes. The manuscript supplies the stronger statement of a body-clock speed at the crossing. No held observer at \(L\) is used.

There is also a direct construction verifying the match. Set \(q=k_0\). The real outgoing motion in the two accounts can be written compactly as
\[
\dot r^2=c^2(q^2-|F|).
\]
Inside, this is the equation derived with the real ruler. Outside, it is premise 8 with \(e_{\mathrm{out}}=q\). The exterior solution is given near \(L\) by
\[
\tau(r)-\tau(L)=\int_L^r\frac{dx}{c\sqrt{q^2-F(x)}}.
\]
It exists for every \(q>0\) in an exterior neighborhood of \(L\). Its initial derivative is \(cq\), giving a differentiable crossing when joined to the calculated interior solution. One further consequence is that the one-sided radial accelerations at \(L\) are \(+c^2/(2L)\) inside and \(-c^2/(2L)\) outside. The speed matches exactly.

**The account distinction in the preceding §14.6 paragraph is essential.** The far observer infers an interior count \(e_{\mathrm{inf}}=\pm i k_0\). Substitution into the far-inferred equation gives
\[
c^2(e_{\mathrm{inf}}^2-F)
=-c^2(k_0^2-k^2)
=-\dot r_{\mathrm{real,in}}^{\,2}.
\]
At the crossing its limiting square is \(-c^2k_0^2\). The real body-clock calculation gives \(+c^2k_0^2\). Thus the result actually established is \(e_{\mathrm{out}}=|e_{\mathrm{inf}}|\). Identifying the two interior squared rates as the same real measurement would produce a sign error. Using a single real \(e=k_0\) in the far-inferred formula throughout the interior would already give \(2c^2k_0^2\) at release, where the body is at rest. The passage’s real-ruler derivation avoids both errors.

Outside, the turning and escape results follow from
\[
\dot r^2=c^2(e^2-1+L/r).
\]
For \(0<e<1\) the outer turning radius is \(L/(1-e^2)\); the exterior acceleration \(-c^2L/(2r^2)\) points inward there. For \(e\ge1\) there is no finite outer turning radius. At infinity \(f\to1\), so \(\gamma_\infty=e\) and the speed in the far frame is \(c\sqrt{1-e^{-2}}\).

Finally, on the outgoing exterior branch,
\[
\frac{dt_\infty}{dr}
=\frac{e}{cF\sqrt{e^2-F}}
=\frac{L}{c(r-L)}+O(1/c).
\]
Thus \(t_\infty=(L/c)\ln[(r-L)/L]+O(1)\) as \(r\downarrow L\). This verifies the sign of the far-time divergence and the distinction from the finite proper time.

**GR comparison only.** In §7’s solution \(\xi=\partial_t=\partial_v\) has norm \(-Fc^2\). A held observer would require \(u=\alpha\xi\) and hence

Outside, \(\alpha=1/\sqrt F\). At \(L\) the direction is null. Inside it is spacelike, and no real \(\alpha\) satisfies the normalization. This proves the incompatibility for the specified observer independently of the choice between the displayed coordinate systems.

Outside, the held observer’s proper acceleration has magnitude
\[
a_{\mathrm{held}}=\frac{c^2 F'}{2\sqrt F}
=\frac{GM}{r^2 f}.
\]
The weighing operation specified in §4.2 therefore gives \(a_{\mathrm{held}}r^2/G=M/f\), while the metric still contains the parameter \(M\). This verifies §9.2’s distinction. r_-\operatorname{arsinh}\sqrt{(r-r_-)/r_-}}{\sqrt b}.
\]
Thus \(c\Delta\tau_{L\to r_-\to L}=2S_i(L)\). Outside, a primitive \(S_o\) is
\[
S_o(r)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{r_+}{\sqrt{1-e^2}}\bigl(\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta\bigr),
\quad \theta=\arcsin\sqrt{r/r_+},&0<e<1,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{2r^{3/2}}{3\sqrt L},&e=1,\\[5pt]
\dfrac{\sqrt{r(r+d)}-d\,\operatorname{arsinh}\sqrt{r/d}}{\sqrt{e^2-1}},
\quad d=L/(e^2-1),&e>1 .
\end{cases}
\]
Differentiation gives \(S_i'=1/\sqrt{e^2-k^2}\) and \(S_o'=1/\sqrt{e^2-F}\). Both tend to \(1/e\) at \(L\). At each finite turn the inverse-square-root singularity is integrable. For a bound body the full own-clock period is \(2[S_i(L)+S_o(r_+)-S_o(L)]/c\).

### Far time and the two solutions

**DERIVED \([T,F]\) with the radial law.** Put \(w=\sqrt{e^2-|F|}\) and \(\sigma=\operatorname{sgn}\dot r\) on a moving leg. Then
\[
\dot r=\sigma cw,\qquad
\frac{dt}{d\tau}=\frac eF,\qquad
\frac{dr}{dt}=\sigma c\frac{F}{e}w.
\]
Far time runs forward outside and backward inside along increasing \(\tau\). On infall \(dr/dt\) changes from negative outside to positive inside. On return it is negative inside and positive outside. There are **two distinct effects**. The far-time orientation flips at \(L\), where \(|\dot r|=ce\). The body reverses on its own clock at \(r_-\), where \(\dot r=0\).

**DERIVED \([T,J]\), with finite parts matched at \(L\).** The far-time differential has the exact decomposition
\[
c\frac{dt}{dr}=\sigma J_e(r),\qquad
J_e(r)=\frac{e}{Fw}
=\frac{L}{r-L}+1+\frac{\operatorname{sgn}F}{w(e+w)}.
\]
The coefficient of the pole is independent of \(e\). For the real part define
\[
P(r)=L\ln\left|\frac{r-L}{L}\right|
+\int_L^r\left[1+
 \frac{\operatorname{sgn}F(u)}{w(u)[e+w(u)]}\right]du .
\]
This matches the finite constants at equal \(|r-L|\), continues the logarithm on the prescribed half-turn, and uses each side’s own differential for the regular part. Write \(\eta=+1\) for the upper exterior-to-interior half-turn and \(\eta=-1\) for the lower. With \(t(D)=0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
ct_{\rm in}(r)&=P(D)-P(r) &&(r>L),\\
ct_{\rm in}(r)&=P(D)-P(r)-\eta i\pi L &&(r<L),\\
ct_{\rm out}(r)&=P(D)+P(r)-2P(r_-)-\eta i\pi L &&(r_- \le r<L).
\end{aligned}
\]
The incoming real part tends to \(+\infty\) at \(L\) from either side. The returning real part tends to \(-\infty\) there from either side. **Neither passage has a finite far-clock time.** At the ordinary turn \(r_-\), the continued time is finite and continuous, with the same imaginary part on arrival and departure.

There is a precise limit to analytic continuation here. After subtracting \(L/(r-L)\), the exterior and interior limits of \(J_e\) are
\[
1+\frac{1}{2e^2},\qquad 1-\frac{1}{2e^2},
\]
respectively. One meromorphic differential with that simple pole cannot have these two different regular coefficients. The half-turn of the common logarithm gives exactly the manuscript’s offset. If the joining rule means analytic continuation of the whole exterior differential, it conflicts with Law II. The finite-part match above is the consistent implementation used for the figures.

For a **single complex time carried through both crossings**, there is a further sign to track. Returning on the inverse half-turn restores the positive exterior clock root. The radial sign has also reversed, so the return crossing adds another \(-\eta i\pi L/c\). The exterior return then has the listed real part and an accumulated offset \(-2\eta i\pi L/c\). An outward leg normalized independently to real exterior time has its own time origin. Neither convention assigns a finite elapsed far-clock time through \(L\).

**DERIVED \([C,S,R,T,J]\).** Inside, \(f=\eta i k\). The far observer’s inferred held-clock and ruler steps are
\[
\gamma_{\rm inf}=\frac e f=-\eta i\,\frac e k,\qquad
d\theta_{\rm inf}=\frac e f\,d\tau,\qquad
d\ell_{\rm inf}=\frac{dr}{f}=-\eta i\,\frac{dr}{k}.
\]
Each differs from the corresponding real local reading by the same phase \(-\eta i\). Their ratio is consequently real,
\[
\frac{d\ell_{\rm inf}}{d\theta_{\rm inf}}
=\frac{\dot r}{e}=\sigma c\,\frac{w}{e}.
\]
These equations locate the complex dimension exactly. The two inferred steps and the continued far time are complex conjugates across the two choices. The areal derivative \(\dot r\) on the body’s clock is real.

### Conservation and the GR comparison

**DERIVED \([C,S,R,X]\), manuscript accounting.** On either side, in the real normalization of that side, the two terms counted once give
\[
a(\gamma-1)m_0c^2+a\,m_0c^2=e\,m_0c^2 .
\]
In the units of a particular held interior observer at \(R\), divide both sides by \(k(R)\). The motion realizes this balance: substituting \(\dot r^2/c^2=e^2-a^2\) into the real SR identity gives \(a\gamma=e\) throughout each leg, including at the turn by continuity. The body returns to D with the same mass-energy entry and opposite radial momentum. The calculation verifies the body’s energy entry. Section 3 premise 6 supplies the closed-system momentum law; the fixed-source trajectory specifies no recoil history with which to calculate a separate total-momentum residual.

**IMPORT, GR comparison only.** Match the source, \(L\), initial D event, inward velocity and exterior \(e\). The same-mass Schwarzschild continuation uses \(e=F\dot t\) and timelike geodesic normalization,
\[
-c^2=-Fc^2\dot t^{\,2}+\frac{\dot r^{\,2}}F
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dot r_{\rm GR}^{\,2}=c^2(e^2-F).
\]
Inside, wherever the manuscript’s body can go,
\[
\dot r_{\rm GR}^{\,2}-\dot r_{\rm II}^{\,2}=2c^2k^2.
\]
At the manuscript’s turn, GR predicts \(\dot r_{\rm GR}^{\,2}=2c^2e^2\). For this body that is \(0.5c^2\), with inward velocity in the future black-hole interior. The manuscript predicts **zero velocity followed by outward motion**. Thus the exterior radial equation, the same incoming state and the same speed at \(L\) do **not** require GR’s interior continuation. The two interior predictions already differ at an explicitly calculated event.

For the manuscript’s Section 2 count, the continued GR metric requires a held observer \(u=\alpha\partial_t\) to satisfy \(\alpha^2F=1\). For \(F<0\) there is no real such observer. The continued solution therefore cannot realize the interior held-observer count of §9 statement 3. On GR’s own comparison side the Killing quantity there is a momentum component. The established conservation discrepancy is the absence of the required observer and count; the calculation yields no numerical amount of energy lost. The manuscript identifies the deciding observation as “anything, light or matter, arriving outside from inside an event horizon.” No such observation is supplied in this run.

### 5.6 The speed a frame needs to escape
An independent Claude check of the reply of 5.5 and of draft v0.84, made by an agent that had not seen our own check, derived the law of free motion inside \(L\) for itself, agreed with the auditor’s derivation and reproduced every number in the reply and in the draft by two methods. It disagreed with one claim of the reply: that the speeds a moving frame still needs at \(L\) to escape keep their derivation from outside \(L\). Under the one law every body that goes inward comes back out with its count, so a frame falling in needs, along its motion, only what a frame on its way out needs. Its derivation steps went to the auditor word for word, for a targeted check and repair with the same prompt; the message held the prompt (Part 2), the author’s rules 7 to 9 (Part 2) and the manuscript’s passages that the check needs, word for word, and the parts of its run block that are not copies of those texts are given here word for word, followed by the reply. Run: 647,308 input tokens (617,984 of them cached), 15,199 output tokens, 6.6 minutes. The auditor agreed: under the one law the least push at \(L\) is the same for a frame falling in and a frame on its way out with the same count, \(c(1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\) along its motion for \(e\lt1\) (\(0.6\,c\) inward for \(e=0.5\), after which the frame turns at \(L/2\) and goes away for good) and none for \(e\ge1\); the value \(c\) is the limit for turning a frame that is falling in back at \(L\) itself, which no finite push reaches; and a frame in free motion needs less than \(c\) at every radius it reaches. It agreed with every step of the check but one inference: premise 4 alone does not make the count inside \(L\) equal to the count outside; premise 3 at the real size of the clock rate does, which the paper now names. It made one precision: that a body cannot go deeper than its turn rests on no ruler, while its arrival there and its reversal also use the law of motion and the outward pull. Sections 3, 14 and 18 carry the correction.

## D. The independent check's derivation steps, word for word

**A.6 The match at L.**
- From outside, |ṙ| → ce. From inside, |ṙ| → cq.
- The free body passes L (premise 8), and nothing acts on it there (premise 4: it keeps its clock and ruler). So the rate at which it passes the circles on its own clock does not jump, and q = e.
- The same follows from premise 3 at the real size of the clock rate: |γf| = e outside and γk = q inside. This is the step the ruler rule takes for the ruler.
- **DERIVED** [premise 8, premise 4, or premise 3 at real size]. Premise 8's words say that the body passes, not with what speed. What makes the two speeds equal is premise 4 or premise 3.

**A.8 Turns.**
- The body turns where |F| = e²: r₋ = L/(1 + e²) inside, where the held frame reads γ = 1, and r₊ = L/(1 − e²) outside for e < 1.
- At r₋ the outward pull (Part 10: its direction from premises 3 and 7, for every real ruler) makes the rest a reversal. The squared law alone would also allow the body to stay at r₋.
- The turn exists without any ruler. γ = q/k ≥ 1 (H2) gives k ≤ q, so r ≥ L/(1 + q²) > 0. A ruler is needed only to fix q in terms of e: a scale λ gives q = λe and a turn at L/(1 + λ²e²), and the ruler rule gives λ = 1.
- Nothing with e > 0 reaches the centre.
- **DERIVED.**

**A.11 Escape speeds.**
- Every body that goes inward comes back out with its count (A.7, A.8). So escape for good means count ≥ 1, in either direction.
- Frame held at rest at r, with a = √|F|: it needs c√(1 − a²).
  - Outside that is c√(L/r) = √(2GM/r).
  - Inside, for L/2 ≤ r < L, it is c√(2 − L/r).
  - From L/2 or deeper it needs nothing.
  - On both sides the needed speed rises to c only at L.
- Free frame with count e < 1 at radius r: a boost along its motion raises its count to e′ = a cosh(|η| + β).
  - The speed needed for e′ = 1 is c·tanh(arccosh(1/a) − arccosh(e/a)).
  - At L this tends to c(1 − e²)/(1 + e²), **whether the frame is falling in or on its way out**.
  - At its turns it is c√(1 − e²). It is below c at every radius the frame reaches.
  - For e ≥ 1 it needs nothing.
  - Reversing a frame that is falling in at L needs c. That is the value v0.84 states, and it is not the least speed for escape under the one law.
- **DERIVED** [A.7, A.2].

**A.12 The far clock.**
- Take the far observer's own time t and the radius r as real.
- The far observer works out the held clocks and rulers as dT = f dt and dℓ = dr/f (premise 5 with premise 7's f). The count is kept in its units, γ_inf·f = e (premise 3).
- So dt/dτ = e/F on both sides of L: positive outside, a pole at L, negative inside. Time flips.
- This is the convention Part 10 uses for light, dr/dt = cf² = cF.
- If one instead converts the held frames' own real clock step, dt = γ_loc dτ/f, the increments are imaginary: dt/dτ = ±ie/F. The paper does not use that route.
- **DERIVED** on the Part 10 convention.

## Part I. The speeds needed to escape

**Under the adopted one law, the least boost at \(L\) is the same size for a freely falling frame and a freely outgoing frame of the same count \(e\).** For \(0<e<1\), its magnitude is \(c(1-e^2)/(1+e^2)\), directed **along the frame’s motion**. For \(e\ge1\), the required boost is zero. At \(e=0.5\), the falling frame needs **\(0.6c\) inward**. That boost raises its count to one. It then turns at \(L/2\), crosses \(L\) outward and escapes for good. The \(c\) in draft v0.84 is the limiting requirement for **immediate outward reversal** of an ingoing frame at \(L\).

The manuscript specifies the setup in §14 Part 5. “Its numbers below are on its own clock and in the radius of the circles, with \(e\) in the far observer's units.” I use that radius \(r\), body time \(\tau\), fixed \(L=2G\mathcal M_{\rm enc}/c^2\), one boost measured locally at one event, and free motion thereafter. Escape for good means that the subsequent trajectory goes to arbitrarily large \(r\). The calculation proceeds from the radial law to the escape criterion, from local boost composition to the minimum, and from the held-frame readings to a separate audit of the match and turn. The checks are substitution at the threshold, the two limits at \(L\), and the quoted numerical trajectories.

### Premises and laws used

Premise 4, concerning the frame’s own clock, ruler and mass, is examined in Part II. The example values are supplied calculation data. No raw observation or new empirical constant enters the result.

### 1. Which post-boost counts escape?

**DERIVED \([C,J,A]\).** Write \(e'\) for the count immediately after the boost. In the exterior,
\[
\frac{\dot r^{\,2}}{c^2}=e'^2-1+\frac Lr .
\]
For \(e'<1\) there is a finite outer turning radius \(L/(1-e'^2)\). For \(e'=1\), the outgoing branch has \(\dot r=c\sqrt{L/r}>0\) at every finite exterior radius and goes to infinity. For \(e'>1\), it also goes to infinity. An initially inward branch turns at \(L/(1+e'^2)\) and returns with the same count, as verified in Part II. Hence
\[
\boxed{\text{Escape for good}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ e'\ge1}
\tag{1}
\]
for the radial free motions in question, in either initial direction. The equality in (1) matters for a *least* speed.

### 2. Frame held at rest

**DERIVED \([C,H,J,A]\).** At \(a>0\), launch speed \(u\) in the held frame gives \(e'=a/\sqrt{1-u^2/c^2}\). If \(a\ge1\), release at rest already meets (1). Otherwise solving \(e'=1\) gives
\[
\boxed{
\frac{u_{\rm held}}c=
\begin{cases}
\sqrt{L/r},& r>L,\\
\sqrt{2-L/r},& L/2<r<L,\\
0,&0<r\le L/2 .
\end{cases}}
\tag{2}
\]
Outside this is \(\sqrt{2G\mathcal M_{\rm enc}/r}\) in speed units. Both one-sided limits at \(L\) are \(c\). This is a held-frame **limit**. The held clock factor itself vanishes there. Equation (2) reproduces the manuscript’s rest-frame result throughout its stated domains.

### 3. Frame in free motion, inward or outward

**DERIVED \([C,H,J,A]\).** First take \(a>0\) and \(a\le e<1\). The magnitude of the frame’s rapidity relative to the held frame is \(\eta=\operatorname{arcosh}(e/a)\). A boost of rapidity magnitude \(b\), measured in the free frame and directed along its motion, gives
\[
e'_{\max}=a\cosh(\eta+b)
         = e\cosh b+\sqrt{e^2-a^2}\sinh b .
\tag{3}
\]
This is a maximum at fixed boost size. In local boost composition, a boost at angle \(\theta\) to the initial motion multiplies the second term by \(\cos\theta\le1\). The aligned radial launch attains the bound and has the escaping trajectory of (1). At a turn the second term vanishes, and either radial direction gives the same threshold.

Setting (3) equal to one therefore gives the minimum
\[
\boxed{
u_{\rm free}(r,e)=
\begin{cases}
c\tanh\!\left[\operatorname{arcosh}(1/a)-
                    \operatorname{arcosh}(e/a)\right],&0<a\le e<1,\\
0,&e\ge1,\quad a\le e .
\end{cases}}
\tag{4}
\]
The domain \(a\le e\) is precisely the set of radii the frame can reach. At either turn for \(e<1\), (4) gives \(c\sqrt{1-e^2}\).

The limit at \(L\) can be taken **before** solving for the boost. Let \(s=\operatorname{sgn}\dot r\), let \(b_{\rm out}\) be signed rapidity with outward positive, and put \(p=\dot r/c\). Local boost composition gives the finite expressions
\[
e'=e\cosh b_{\rm out}+p\sinh b_{\rm out},\qquad
p'=p\cosh b_{\rm out}+e\sinh b_{\rm out}.
\]
At the crossing \(p\to se\). Thus \(e'\to e\exp(s b_{\rm out})\) and \(p'\to s e'\). For \(0<e<1\), the threshold is \(b_{\rm out}=s\ln(1/e)\), giving
\[
\boxed{\frac{u_{\rm signed}(L,e)}c
       =s\,\frac{1-e^2}{1+e^2}.}
\tag{5}
\]
No finite boost reverses the sign of \(p\) at that crossing. If an ingoing frame is required to launch **immediately outward** onto an escaping trajectory, the required exterior boost magnitude is \(c\tanh[\operatorname{arcosh}(e/a)+\operatorname{arcosh}(1/a)]\). That tends to \(c\). It answers a different minimization from (1).
